- OEIS A090904, A090905, A090906 and A090907 (Murthy, Dec 2003; last edited Dec 2016) state the claim only as a conjecture. A090907 adds "verified for 4<n<21".
- A090906 has an unproved %F by M. Bouayoun (Mar 2004) giving the row lengths as 2*(A006992(n)-A006992(n-1)). It is off by one index.
- A381901 (A. Niedermaier, Mar 2025) defines the same triangle with no bound on row length and asserts a(n) = 2*A006992(n-1) for n >= 5, without proof.
- Related: A113117 and A113118 (L. Quet, 2006), A093911 (Murthy's variant), and A006992 (Bertrand primes).
- The key analytic input is Nagura's theorem (J. Nagura, Proc. Japan Acad. 28 (1952) 177-181: for x >= 25 there is a prime between x and 6x/5). The Lean development reproves the form it needs (a prime in (5x/3, 2x) for x >= 83) from scratch.
- Searches of arXiv, MathOverflow/MSE, SeqFan-style queries and the formal-conjectures repository found no prior resolution and no prior formalization.

assessment.follows_from: Nagura's theorem (1952: a prime in (x, 6x/5) for x >= 25), which gives the ratio bounds 5/3 between consecutive Bertrand primes (A006992), combined with Legendre's formula for the factorial divisibility (2a)!^2 | (2b)!(2c)! and a finite computer check of the first rows
assessment.justification: Take consecutive Bertrand primes b < a < c, so that row n is [2b+1, 2a]. The prime c lies in row n, and the first multiple of c after 2a is 2c, so the next row must reach 2c. Ending at 2c is enough because (2a)!^2 divides (2b)!(2c)!, which follows from a short Legendre-formula check on floor functions plus a small prime-power case. The only deep input is a known prime-gap bound (Nagura 1952), and the first rows are checked by computer. The whole argument is elementary and fits in about a page; the scouting pass found it straight away. The long Lean file mostly reproves Nagura's bound with Chebyshev weights, which is formalization work, not a new idea.

results.title: Quet's integrality conjecture for A091817 holds
results.summary: For every prime p >= 3, write H(p-3) = 1 + 1/2 + ... + 1/(p-3) = N/D in lowest terms (H(0) = 0/1). Then p divides 2N - 3D. Equivalently, every term a(n) = (2N - 3D)/p of OEIS A091817 (p the (n+1)-th prime, n >= 1) is an integer.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: Leroy Quet conjectures that the terms are always integral. This is true for p < 3*10^4. (Entry: (2*numerator(H(p-3)) - 3*denominator(H(p-3)))/p, Bouayoun and Stephan, Mar 07 2004)

Referees: - OEIS A091817 and its history (oeis.org/history?seq=A091817): the conjecture is still stated as open, verified for p < 3*10^4, and has no proof note.
- Classical source: H(p-1) ≡ 0 (mod p) (Wolstenholme 1862; Hardy & Wright, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers, Thm 115).
- Explicit reflection congruence H_{p-k} ≡ H_{k-1} (mod p), 1 <= k <= p-1: Z.-W. Sun & L.-L. Zhao, "Arithmetic theory of harmonic numbers (II)", Colloq. Math. 130 (2013), 67-78, arXiv:0911.4433 (proof of (2.2)). Taking k = 3 gives H_{p-3} ≡ 3/2 (mod p), which settles the conjecture at once.
- The same lemma is cited in arXiv:1108.2361 (Lemma 2.1 of its ref. [13]) and arXiv:1803.02966.
- Analogous k = 2 fact in OEIS A064169 (Adamchuk, Jun 09 2006: p divides a(p-2)).
- No prior formalization found:
  - not in google-deepmind/formal-conjectures (checked locally at commit c77fdd4);
  - not among the OEIS Open benchmark statements (Adamczewski, arXiv:2608.11941);
  - no other formal proof turned up in searches.

results.title: Convergents of [1; 1/2, 1/3, ..., 1/n]: numerator + denominator = 2^(v2(n!) + v2((n+1)!)) (A092054)
results.summary: For every n >= 1, write the convergent [1; 1/2, 1/3, ..., 1/n] = 1 + 1/(1/2 + 1/(1/3 + ... + 1/(1/n))) in lowest terms as p/q. Then p + q is a power of 2, namely p + q = 2^a(n). Here a(n) is the base-2 logarithm, and a(n) = Sum_{k=1..n} A001511(floor((k+1)/2)) = 2n + 1 - s2(n) - s2(n+1) = A011371(n) + A011371(n+1). In these formulas A001511 is the ruler function, s2 = A000120 is the binary digit sum, and A011371(m) = m - s2(m).
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: It appears that a(n) = Sum_{k=1..n} A001511(floor((k+1)/2)). Equivalently, a(n) = 2n + 1 - A000120(n) - A000120(n+1) = A011371(n) + A011371(n+1). - _Franklin T. Adams-Watters_, Feb 02 2006

Referees: No prior explicit proof of A092054's conjectured formula found. Relevant partial or adjacent sources:
- OEIS A092054 (#43, Aug 09 2026): the formula is still marked "It appears".
- M. A. Suchenek, "Elementary Yet Precise Worst-Case Analysis of Floyd's Heap-Construction Program", Fundamenta Informaticae 120 (2012) 75-92, doi:10.3233/FI-2012-751. It proves 2N-2s2(N)-e2(N) for heap construction, which is algebraically equivalent to the conjectured formula. It does not prove the continued-fraction statement; the link to A092054 rests only on an OEIS comment.
- OEIS A001901: reduced Wallis numerators, "Subsequence of A000079" (powers of 2). Ordowski (2024): A001901(n) = numerator of [1;1,1/2,...,1/n].
- OEIS A056982 (Weisstein): 4^A005187(n) = denominator of prod_{k<=n}(1-1/(4k^2)). This gives the even-index exponent.
- OEIS A001902 and A092053 (Hanna 2004): the convergent numerators are the Wallis denominators.
- N. A. Draim, "Pi in the form of a continued fraction with infinite terms", Fibonacci Quarterly 7.3 (1969) 275-276, https://www.mathstat.dal.ca/FQ/Scanned/7-3/draim.pdf: Wallis partial products equal the convergents of a continued fraction with partial numerators (n-1)n.
- Kummer/Legendre: v2(C(2m,m)) = s2(m), v2(m!) = m - s2(m).

assessment.follows_from: The cross-referenced entries already link the convergents to the partial Wallis products (A001902 and A092053 comments; Ordowski's [1;1,1/2,...,1/n] formula in A001901/A001902; Draim 1969), and A001901 is recorded as a subsequence of the powers of 2. Combine this with the closed form W(2m) = 16^m/((2m+1)·C(2m,m)^2), Kummer's theorem v2(C(2m,m)) = s2(m) (also in A056982 for even n), and Legendre's formula v2(m!) = m - s2(m).
assessment.justification: The proof writes the convergents as P(n)/Q(n) using a three-term recurrence and checks closed forms for P and P+Q by a short induction. The odd parts of the factorials divide the odd double factorial because C(2m,m) is an integer, and Legendre's formula gives the exponent. Each step is standard: the link to Wallis products and the power-of-2 property are already recorded in the cross-referenced entries, and the manuscript itself calls the result a short consequence of classical facts. The informal argument is about a page; most of the work went into the Lean formalization.

results.title: Imaginary parts of the convergents of [1+i; 1+i, 1+i, ...] are A317974(n+1)/A138573(n)
results.summary: Let c_n = (1+i) + 1/((1+i) + ... + 1/(1+i)) be the continued fraction with n partial quotients 1+i, so c_1 = 1+i and c_{n+1} = (1+i) + 1/c_n. Write c_n = (A093725(n) + a(n) i)/A093727(n) in Mathematica's Numerator/Denominator form (A093727(n) = lcm of the denominators of Re c_n and Im c_n). Let A317974 be 0,0,1,1 and A138573 be 0,1,2,5, both continued by u(n) = 2(u(n-1)+u(n-2)+u(n-3)) - u(n-4). Then for every n >= 1, a(n)/A093727(n) = A317974(n+1)/A138573(n) as rational numbers.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: Conjecture: a(n)/A093727(n) = A317974(n+1)/A138573(n). - _Zhuorui He_, Jun 16 2026

Referees: OEIS A093726 rev #13 (Jun 20 2026): the formula is still marked "Conjecture: a(n)/A093727(n) = A317974(n+1)/A138573(n). - Zhuorui He, Jun 16 2026"; there is no later %E edit recording a proof. Related prior work: Peter Bala's 2014 formula in OEIS A138573 that A138573(n) = |U(n)|^2 for the Gaussian Lucas sequence U(n) = (1+i)U(n-1) + U(n-2), which covers the denominator part only. A317974 (rev #35, Jun 30 2026) has no relevant formula. Not covered by S. Fried, "Further proofs of conjectures from the OEIS", arXiv:2607.24832 (Jul 2026); I checked its full text for the A-numbers. Fried's earlier papers (arXiv:2410.07237; JIS 2025 and 2026) predate the conjecture. No MathOverflow, Math StackExchange, SeqFan or arXiv resolution found. Sources: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/oeis/oeisdata/main/seq/A093/A093726.seq, https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24832

assessment.follows_from: The classical continuant formula c_n = U(n+1)/U(n) for U(n) = (1+i)U(n-1) + U(n-2), together with Peter Bala's 2014 formula in A138573: A138573(n) = |U(n)|^2, and the o.g.f. as a Hadamard product of x/(1-(1+i)x-x^2) and x/(1-(1-i)x-x^2). The same Hadamard-product argument puts Im(U(n+1) conj U(n)) in the signature-(2,2,2,-1) recurrence space, so four initial values match it with A317974(n+1).
assessment.justification: The convergent is c_n = U(n+1)/U(n) = U(n+1)conj(U(n))/|U(n)|^2 for the Gaussian continuants U. A138573 already records that the denominator |U(n)|^2 equals A138573(n). The numerator's imaginary part Q(n) = Im(U(n+1)conj U(n)) is built from the same characteristic roots, so it satisfies the same order-4 recurrence. Matching four initial values identifies it with A317974(n+1). The whole argument is standard continued-fraction and linear-recurrence bookkeeping, plus a short check that a(n)/A093727(n) is just Im c_n. It fits in well under a page and leans mainly on a formula already in a cross-referenced entry.

results.title: The only fixed points of reverse(x) - maxdigit(x) are 0 and 89
results.summary: For a natural number x, let rev(x) be its decimal reversal (rev 0 = 0, trailing zeros are dropped) and maxdig(x) its largest decimal digit (maxdig 0 = 0). Let f(x) = rev(x) - maxdig(x). Then f(x) = x if and only if x = 0 or x = 89.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: "a(89)=-1 because 89 is the first number that will not reach zero: 98-9=89. It is conjectured that 0 and 89 are the only fixed points of f." (A097154, entry by _Jason Earls_, Aug 01 2004. The same sentence appears in A097155 and A097157.)

Referees: **OEIS (local mirror, cross-checked against the current raw GitHub oeisdata files).**
- A097154 (#4, Dec 15 2017), A097155 (#11, last edited Aug 29 2025) and A097157 (#3) all still say "It is conjectured that 0 and 89 are the only fixed points of f".
- None has an %E line, comment, formula or link recording a proof or counterexample. A097155's only %E is a 2011 data correction by Harvey P. Dale.
- The cross-referenced entries A097153, A097156 and A097158 (Earls, Aug 2004; extensions by Robert G. Wilson v and Klaus Brockhaus) are purely computational.
- A grep of the whole local oeisdata mirror finds no other entry that references A097153 through A097158.

**Web searches.** Queries covered the exact map text, "reversal minus largest digit", SeqFan 2004, Math StackExchange/MathOverflow-style phrasing, and an extended search. None found a proof.
- Hits were only the OEIS pages themselves.
- Unrelated digit-reversal work also came up: arXiv 2410.11784 (1089 attractor), arXiv 2404.06656 (reverse divisors), arXiv math/0511366, and OEIS A393794 (fixed points of the 1089-trick map, Havenaar 2026, a different map).
- A GMAT forum problem covers only the two-digit equation reverse(n) = n + 9, which has eight solutions (12, ..., 89). That is a different condition and does not address this conjecture.

No prior resolution was found, so this appears to be the first written proof, and it is Lean-verified.

assessment.follows_from: The standard fact that a number is congruent to its digit sum mod 9, so rev(x) ≡ x (mod 9). This forces maxdig(x) = 9 at a nonzero fixed point. A units-digit comparison mod 10 and a size bound then finish it.
assessment.justification: A fixed point satisfies rev(x) = x + maxdig(x). Reversal keeps the digit sum, so maxdig(x) must be divisible by 9, which leaves only rev(x) = x + 9. Comparing the leading and units digits mod 10 and bounding the middle block then gives x = 10a + (a+1), and the largest-digit condition picks out 89. That is under a page of textbook digit arithmetic that a competent mathematician would find quickly. The entry itself carries the keyword 'easy', and the length of the Lean proof reflects formalization effort, not mathematical depth.

results.title: A106505: common sides of A/2A primitive triangles are periodic mod 8, so a(n+5) = a(n) + 8
results.summary: Let IsSide(c) mean there are natural numbers x, y such that x, y, c are the sides of a non-degenerate triangle in which the angle opposite y is twice the angle opposite x, and gcd(x, y, c) = 1. Let a(n) be the n-th smallest such c (1-indexed): 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15, 16, 17, ... Then a(n+5) = a(n) + 8 for every n > 2 (Ralf Stephan's conjecture in OEIS A106505).
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: "Conjecture: for n>2, a(n+5) = a(n) + 8. - _Ralf Stephan_, Nov 16 2010." Also: "Empirical g.f.: ... - _Colin Barker_, Oct 05 2013"

Referees: No earlier proof found. OEIS A106505 (GitHub oeisdata main, rev #21, Apr 23 2021) still states it as a conjecture (Ralf Stephan, Nov 16 2010), with an empirical g.f. by Colin Barker (2013). OEIS A321499 (M. F. Hasler, Nov 2018; rev #24, Feb 2025) proves that {d²(2m+d)} = odd numbers > 1 together with multiples of 8 > 8, and records a(n+5) = a(n) + 8 for A321499 (D. A. Corneth). It still says "Cf. A106505 (conjectured to be the sequence without the 3)". The closely related A321501 complement analysis (Hasler) is also there. Related OEIS entries: A343063 and A343064 (B. Schott, 2021), which give the parametrization a = m² − k², b = mk, c = k² with gcd(m,k) = 1 and k < m < 2k, but no set characterization; and A229849, which says A106505 "seems" to give those values. Parametrization background: M. N. Deshpande, Math. Gazette (2002); K. Zelator, arXiv 1208.0497; R. S. Luthar (1984). None of these addresses the conjecture. Not covered in S. Fried, arXiv 2410.07237 or arXiv 2607.24832, nor in Adamczewski's OEIS Open benchmark (arXiv 2608.11941), which uses the Tsoukalas et al. dataset in epoch-research/LeanOpenProblems; also absent from google-deepmind/formal-conjectures.

assessment.follows_from: The entry's own %F formula: the terms are the values s^2 - r^2 with r < s < 2r and gcd(r,s) = 1 (classical parametrization of A/2A triangles, Luthar 1984; A343063). With that formula, a parity argument mod 8 plus the families (m, m+1) and (2j+1, 2j+3) give the set {odd >= 5} together with {8m : m >= 2}. Cross-reference A321499 (Hasler) already proves the same set with 3 added and records a(n+5) = a(n) + 8 there.
assessment.justification: The proof works out the set of common sides. A coprime difference of squares s^2 - r^2 is either odd or divisible by 8. Two one-line families of triangles realize every odd c >= 5 and every multiple of 8 from 16 on, and the small cases are checked by hand. Since the set is periodic mod 8 with five residues per period, the recurrence follows at once. This is about half a page of elementary number theory, using the formula already given in the entry, and the cross-referenced A321499 already contains the same set characterization. The Lean work (deriving y^2 = x(x+c) from the arccos definition, plus the counting with Nat.nth) is formalization effort and adds no mathematical depth.

results.title: The Golomb-row triangle A113676 and Levine's sequence A014644
results.summary: Let G be Golomb's sequence A001462 (G(1)=1, G(2)=G(3)=2, G(4)=G(5)=3, ...; n occurs G(n) times, nondecreasing). Let H be G with one 2 removed: H(1)=1 and H(j)=G(j+1) for j>=2. Cut H into consecutive rows: row 1 is [H(1)], and row n+2 has as many terms as the sum of row n+1. Let a(n) be the length of row n. Levine's array has row 1 = [1,1], and row k+1 lists 1 c_1 times, 2 c_2 times, ..., where row k = [c_1, c_2, ...]. A014644(k) is the last term of Levine row k. Claim (both conjectures of van Lamoen and Hanna, 2005): (1) for every n>=2, a(n) = A014644(n+2) - A014644(n+1); (2) the last term of row 1 is A014644(1), and for every n>=2 the last term of row n is A014644(n+1).
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: %C Conjecture: a(n) for n>1 gives first differences of Lionel Levine's sequence A014644(n) for n>=3. %C Conjecture: Final elements of the rows form A014644 except for duplicate 2. (Floor van Lamoen and Paul D. Hanna, Nov 06 2005)

Referees: No prior proof found.
- OEIS A113676 (van Lamoen & Hanna, Nov 2005; rev #9, Mar 2025) still lists both conjectures.
- OEIS A001462 has van Lamoen's related conjecture (Nov 06 2005), still unresolved in the Aug 2026 revision.
- OEIS A014643 has the %Y note "Rows converge to A001462".
- J. Claes and R. Miyamoto, "Golombic and Levine sequences", arXiv:2602.10992 [math.CO] (Feb 2026), p. 3, eqs. (3)–(4). It observes that Γ maps the first n Golomb terms to the first A001463(n) terms (so the A014643 rows are Golomb prefixes), and that |a| = #Γa and #a = (Γa)(|a|). These are the key ingredients, but the paper does not mention A113676 or prove its conjectures.
- Cross-checked entries: A014644, A014643, A011784, A012257, A001463, A113722, A113724, A113730 and A304679. None records a resolution.

assessment.follows_from: The fact that from row 2 on, the rows of Levine's array (A014643) are initial segments of Golomb's sequence A001462. A014643's cross-reference note "Rows converge to A001462" points to this, and Claes and Miyamoto, arXiv:2602.10992, p. 3, eqs. (3)-(4) state it: the Levine step maps the first n Golomb terms to the first A001463(n) terms. Golomb's self-describing property gives it at once.
assessment.justification: The one real idea is that each Levine row from row 2 on is a prefix of Golomb's sequence, so its sum is the length of the next row. That is immediate from Golomb's self-describing property and is already known: A014643 hints at it and Claes and Miyamoto state it. Everything else is a telescoping sum and a short induction showing that the triangle's rows are the blocks of G between consecutive Levine row lengths; both conjectures then follow. The whole argument fits in about a page of elementary steps, and the manuscript itself calls the result "a short consequence" of known facts.

results.title: A115026 has a term greater than 370: a(119) = 371
results.summary: Let F(m) be the sum of d^L over the decimal digits d of m, where L is the number of digits of m (A101337). For n >= 1, a(n) is the smallest element of the cycle that the orbit n, F(n), F(F(n)), ... eventually enters (A115026). Harvey P. Dale conjectured that a(n) <= 370 for all n >= 1. This is false: a(119) = 371.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: "Conjecture: no term is greater than 370. - _Harvey P. Dale_, Jun 08 2022"

Referees: OEIS A151543, "Smallest precursor of n-th cycle in the 'Recurring Digital Invariant Variant' problem" (N. J. A. Sloane, May 15 2009, based on an email from Eric Angelini, Feb 18 2009, with a cycle table by Hans Havermann). Its table entry "13 { 119, 1, {371}}" names 119 as the smallest number whose orbit under A101337 ends in the fixed point 371, so a(119) = 371. The same table has "19 { 407, 1, {407}}" and other cycles with minima above 370. Related pre-2022 OEIS entries: A151544 (2009) lists the cycle elements, including 371 and 407. A157714 (Havermann, Mar 2009) lists numbers in cycles of period greater than 1, such as 2929 and 18829. A005188 lists the narcissistic numbers 153, 370, 371, 407, 1634, ...; since 371 is a fixed point, a(371) = 371 > 370 trivially. Angelini's page "A Recurring Digital Invariant Variant" is at cetteadressecomportecinquantesignes.com/RecurDigit.htm, with a cached copy at oeis.org/A151543/a151543.pdf. The A115026 entry itself (revision #12, Jun 08 2022, unchanged upstream) still states the conjecture and has no correction or %E extension. Web searches found no explicit published retraction of Dale's comment. Sources: https://oeis.org/A115026, https://oeis.org/A151543, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narcissistic_number

results.title: A116184: Adamchuk's conjectures on 37^3 dividing the numerator of sum_{k=1}^{36} 1/k^n
results.summary: Let H(n) = sum_{k=1}^{36} 1/k^n, a rational number. Claim (a): for every k >= 0, 37^3 divides the numerator of H(3 + 36k). Claim (b): if p > 37 is a prime and 37^3 divides the numerator of H(p), then p = 37k - 1 for some natural number k, that is, p ≡ -1 (mod 37).
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: Conjecture: All terms of the arithmetic progression 3+36k belong to a(n). ... It appears that all primes in a(n) that are greater than 37 are of the form 37k-1. (Alexander Adamchuk, Apr 08 2007)

Referees: No explicit prior resolution of the A116184 conjecture found. OEIS A116184 is unchanged (rev #6, Feb 16 2025) with no %E line or resolving comment, and no other mirror entry cross-references it. Classical ingredients that make it an easy corollary:
- J.W.L. Glaisher, Q. J. Math. 31 (1900) 321-353: H(p-1,m) ≡ -m(m+1)/(2(m+2))·p^2·B_{p-2-m} (mod p^3) for odd m ≤ p-3.
- Z.-H. Sun, "Congruences concerning Bernoulli numbers and Bernoulli polynomials", Discrete Appl. Math. 105 (2000) 193-223: Thm 5.1(a) (k ≤ p-4) and the power-sum formula S_k ≡ pB_k + (p^2/2)kB_{k-1} + (p^3/6)k(k-1)B_{k-2} (mod p^3), as quoted in C. Levaillant, arXiv:2005.09434, Results 2 and 4.
- J. Zhao, arXiv:math/0301252: (p, p-2n-1) is irregular iff H(p-1, 2n-1) ≡ 0 (mod p^3) for p ≥ 2n+3.
- Kummer congruences, plus (37,32) being an irregular pair.
- R. Meštrović, arXiv:1111.3057, eq. (22).
- OEIS A007408 comment (Adamchuk 2006): 37^3 | numerator of H(36,3), i.e. the k=0 case.

assessment.follows_from: Euler's theorem: since 37 does not divide k for 1 <= k <= 36, whether 37^3 divides the numerator of H(36,n) depends only on n mod phi(37^3) = 49284, so both claims reduce to checking one period. Alternatively, it follows from the classical power-sum congruence of Glaisher/Sun, S_m = p B_m + (p^2/2) m B_{m-1} + ... (mod p^3), together with Kummer's congruences and the fact that (37,32) is the only irregular pair of 37.
assessment.justification: Both claims are about one fixed modulus, 37^3, and the denominator of H(36,n) is prime to 37. By Euler's theorem, whether n is a term depends only on n mod 49284. Both conjectures therefore reduce to a finite computation over one period. For (b), a prime above 37 is coprime to 49284, so only the residues coprime to 49284 need checking. The manuscript's truncated binomial expansion only makes this check cheaper. Its alternative derivation also takes just a few lines from Sun's power-sum congruence, Kummer's congruences and the irregular pair (37,32). No new idea was needed.

results.title: The row-LCM of denominators of the cube of the mean matrix is n · lcm(1..n)²
results.summary: Let A be the lower-triangular matrix with A(i,j) = 1/i for j ≤ i and 0 otherwise. Its cube has entries r(n,m) = (1/n) Σ_{m ≤ l ≤ k ≤ n} 1/(k l) for 1 ≤ m ≤ n. Let a(n) be the lcm, over m = 1..n, of the reduced denominators of r(n,m). Then for every n ≥ 1, a(n)/n³ = A002944(n)² = (lcm(1..n)/n)². Equivalently, a(n) = n · lcm(1,…,n)². This is the equation that OEIS A119936 (Wolfdieter Lang, 2006) labels a conjecture.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: %F A119936 a(n)/n^3 = A027451(n) = A002944(n)^2 (the second equation is a conjecture). (Wolfdieter Lang, Jul 20 2006)

Referees: I found no prior proof or counterexample.
- OEIS A119936 (Lang 2006, edit #22 Nov 2019) still calls a(n)/n^3 = A002944(n)^2 a conjecture.
- A027451 states (lcm(1..n)/n)^2 as a formula (Meijer, 2009) without proof. Detlefs' comment there begins "It appears".
- A120078 and A120079 say "conjectured to be A027451".
- Crowley, arXiv:1207.1126, says only that a denominator "appears to be" A119936.
- Fried's OEIS-conjecture series does not mention A119936 or the related sequences: arXiv:2410.07237 / JIS 25.4.3, JIS 26.1.8, arXiv:2606.09913, arXiv:2607.24832.
- Sloane, math/0409509: no mention.
- Web, MSE/MO and SeqFan searches turned up nothing.

assessment.follows_from: The standard p-adic argument in which a sum has a single term of minimal valuation, the same idea as the classical proof that the harmonic numbers H_n are not integers (Taeisinger/Kürschák), applied to the explicit formula r(n,m) = (1/n) Σ_{m≤l≤k≤n} 1/(kl) and to v_p(lcm(1..n)) = floor(log_p n).
assessment.justification: The divisibility a(n) | n·lcm(1..n)^2 is immediate, because each product kl divides lcm(1..n)^2. For the reverse divisibility, take each prime p separately and use the column m equal to the largest multiple of p^e that is at most n, where p^e ≤ n < p^{e+1}. In that column, k = l = m is the only term whose valuation reaches -2e, so the full p-power survives in the denominator. This is the textbook unique-minimal-valuation trick used for harmonic sums. The whole argument fits in under a page, and the scout record set it out almost in full before any formalization, so it is a short, standard proof and not a new idea.

results.title: Denominators of Sum C(k)/4^(k-1): Groux's and Staunton's conjectures (A120069)
results.summary: Let C(k) be the Catalan numbers, r(n) = Sum_{k=1..n} C(k)/4^(k-1), and a(n) the denominator of r(n) in lowest terms (A120069). Let A283208(n) be the least e >= 0 such that 2^e (2n+1)/(n+1) c(2n) is a nonnegative integer, where c(2n) = Pochhammer(1/2,n)/n!. Then for every n >= 1: (Groux) a(n) = denominator(C(n)/4^(n-1)), and (Staunton) a(n) = 2^(A283208(n) - 2), with the exponent taken in the integers.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: A120069 (Denominators of partial sums r(n) = Sum_{k=1..n} C(k)/2^(2(k-1)), C = Catalan): "Conjecture: a(n) = denominator(Catalan(n)/4^(n-1)). - _Groux Roland_, Dec 11 2010" and "Conjecture: a(n) = 2^(A283208(n)-2). - _Alexander Staunton_, Feb 28 2026"

Referees: OEIS sources (read from the local mirror; A120069 also checked against GitHub oeisdata main):
- A120778, formula by Groux Roland, Jan 04 2011: sum_{k=0..n} C(k)/4^k = 2(1 - binomial(2n+2,n+1)/4^(n+1)).
- A119951, comment by Pieter Mostert, Oct 12 2012: r(n) = sum_{k=1..n} C(k)/4^(k-1) = 4 - binomial(2n+2,n+1)/2^(2n-1).
- A120777, which records:
  - Johannes W. Meijer, Jul 06 2009: a(n) = denominator(C(2n+2,n+1)/2^(2n+1)).
  - Peter Luschny's new name, Apr 2024: a(n) = 2^(2n - v2(Catalan(n))).
  - Amiram Eldar, Apr 18 2024: a(n) = 2^(2n - A048881(n)) = 2^A283208(n).
  - A comment that its terms coincide with the denominators of sum_{k=0..n} C(k)/4^k.
- A283208:
  - Comment: 2^a(n) is the denominator of 2^(-2n)·A001700(n).
  - Formula by Zabolotskii, 2021: a(n) = A005187(n+1) - 1.

Combining these gives A120069(n) = A120777(n)/4 = 2^(A283208(n)-2) = den(C(n)/4^(n-1)). No explicit paper, MSE/MO post or SeqFan message resolving the A120069 conjectures by name was found. A120069 #30 (Mar 10 2026) still lists both as conjectures.

Web pages:
- https://oeis.org/A120778
- https://oeis.org/A120777
- https://oeis.org/A119951
- arXiv:0906.4290, "Asymptotics of partial sums of central binomial coefficients and Catalan numbers". Found in search; related, but I did not read it.

results.title: Mathar's order-6 recurrence for A121750 (even-length columns in deco polyominoes) holds for all n >= 7
results.summary:
Let a(n) be the total number of columns of even length over all deco polyominoes of height n (OEIS A121750). The polyominoes are encoded as column lists, as in the statement file. Then for every n >= 7:
a(n) - (n+2)a(n-1) + (-n^2+4n-2)a(n-2) + (n^3-3n^2-4n+11)a(n-3) - (n-1)(n^2-11n+26)a(n-4) + (-n^3+5n^2+7n-43)a(n-5) + (n-3)(n-5)^2 a(n-6) = 0.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: %F Conjecture D-finite with recurrence a(n) +(-n-2)*a(n-1) +(-n^2+4*n-2)*a(n-2) +(n^3-3*n^2-4*n+11)*a(n-3) -(n-1)*(n^2-11*n+26)*a(n-4) +(-n^3+5*n^2+7*n-43)*a(n-5) +(n-3)*(n-5)^2*a(n-6)=0. - R. J. Mathar, Jul 26 2022

Referees: I found no published proof of this recurrence. Sources checked:
- OEIS A121750, local mirror and upstream raw oeisdata (revision #13, 2024-08-20, still says 'Conjecture'). Cross-references A121748, A121747, A121749, A121751 also contain no proof.
- E. Barcucci, S. Brunetti, F. Del Ristoro, 'Succession rules and deco polyominoes', RAIRO ITA 34 (2000) 1-14. Full text read; it does not treat even-length columns.
- E. Barcucci, A. Del Lungo, R. Pinzani, TCS 159 (1996) 29-42.
- E. Deutsch, E. Pergola, R. Pinzani, 'Six bijections between deco polyominoes and permutations', arXiv:0810.2876. It gives the definition of directed height and has no even-column results.
- S. B. Ekhad, X. Yang, D. Zeilberger, arXiv:1707.04654. It predates the 2022 conjecture.
- S. Fried, arXiv:2410.07237; JIS 28 (2025) Art. 25.4.3; JIS vol. 29 fried21; arXiv:2607.24832. None covers A121750.
- T. Niu, arXiv:2605.15500, 2605.04369, 2605.08444, 2605.16553 (2026). None covers A121750.
- M. Kauers, C. Koutschan, arXiv:2303.02793. Does not cover A121750.

Note: the order-6 recurrence would follow routinely from Deutsch's first-order recurrence in the same entry (holonomic closure). That recurrence is stated in the entry without proof.

assessment.follows_from: Deutsch's first-order recurrence in the same entry, a(n) = n*a(n-1) + d(n-1) + (n-1)!*floor((n-1)/2), together with the closure properties of D-finite sequences (Stanley 1980). The row-polynomial recurrence for Q[n] in the cross-referenced A121748 gives the same route. Both are stated in OEIS without proof.
assessment.justification: The proof splits each deco polyomino at its first column, the standard recursive decomposition, and uses the fact that shifting columns does not change the count. This gives a small first-order system for the counts and even-column totals. The order-6 recurrence then follows by unrolling the system six steps in each parity class and expanding a polynomial identity, which is a mechanical computation. The manuscript itself says the recurrence follows by routine closure arguments from Deutsch's first-order recurrence in the same entry. The new part is deriving that first-order relation from the definition, which takes about a page of standard combinatorics and needs no new idea.

results.title: Hanna's conjecture A124418(n,k) = k! * A124526(n,k) (partitions with k mixed-parity blocks) proved
results.summary: For all n >= 0 and 0 <= k <= floor(n/2): the number A124418(n,k) of set partitions of {1,...,n} with exactly k blocks containing both an odd and an even entry equals k! * A049020(floor(n/2),k) * A049020(floor((n+1)/2),k), where A049020(m,k) = sum_{i=0}^{m} S2(m,i) * C(i,k) and S2 is the Stirling number of the second kind. (The proof does not need the bound k <= floor(n/2); the identity holds for every k.)
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: A124526: "A124418(n,k) = k!*T(n,k) (conjecture)."; A124418 %F: "Conjecture: T(n,k) = k!*A049020([n/2],k)*A049020([(n+1)/2],k) ... - _Paul D. Hanna_, Nov 08 2006"

Referees: OEIS entries read from the local mirror: A124526, A124418 (Hanna's 2006 conjecture in %F; Heinz's 2013 alternative Maple program uses the equivalent product formula), A049020 (cites East–Gray and Halverson–Jacobson), A244489, A124419 (k=0 column: Bell(floor(n/2))·Bell(ceil(n/2))), A124529, A362495.

Prior proofs, stated in partition-monoid and partition-category language:
- J. East and R. D. Gray, "Diagram monoids and Graham–Houghton graphs: Idempotents and generating sets of ideals", J. Combin. Theory Ser. A 146 (2017) 63–128, doi:10.1016/j.jcta.2016.09.001, arXiv:1404.2359. Proof of Theorem 7.5 and Remark 7.7: |J_r(P_n)| = ρ_{nr}^2·r!, with ρ_{nr} = Σ_j S(n,j)C(j,r). This is the even-n case.
- T. Halverson and T. N. Jacobson, "Set-partition tableaux and representations of diagram algebras", arXiv:1808.08118 (Algebraic Combinatorics 2020), Remark 3.23: the rank-m diagrams in P_k number |W^m_k|^2·m!, where |W^m_k| = A049020(k,m).
- I. Đurđev, I. Dolinka and J. East, "Sandwich semigroups in diagram categories", arXiv:1910.10286 (Internat. J. Algebra Comput. 2021), Proposition 4.11 and Remark 4.12: for the partition category P_{mn}, |D_r| = r!·[Σ_q C(q,r)S(m,q)]·[Σ_q C(q,r)S(n,q)]. Taking m = ⌈n/2⌉ and n = ⌊n/2⌋ gives the full conjecture.

Checked and not relevant: Yaqubi–Mirzavaziri arXiv:2608.30097; Ehrenborg–Hedmark–Hettle (JIS 2017, odd/even block sizes); Shattuck arXiv:1401.6588.

results.title: A127752 mod 2 is the first Feigenbaum symbolic sequence A035263
results.summary: Let A(n,k) = 1/(3n+1) if k <= n <= 2k and 0 otherwise (n, k >= 0), and let a(n) be the row sums of the inverse of this lower-triangular matrix. Equivalently, a is defined by forward substitution: a(n) = 3n+1 - sum_{j<n, n<=2j} a(j). Let A035263 be the trajectory of 1 under the morphism 0 -> 11, 1 -> 10 (offset 1). Then for every n >= 0, a(n) mod 2 = A035263(n+1). This is Paul Barry's 2007 conjecture.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: a(n) mod 2 is first Feigenbaum symbolic sequence A035263 (conjecture). (Paul Barry, Jan 28 2007; checked to 2048 terms by Antti Karttunen, Sep 29 2018)

Referees: OEIS A127752 (P. Barry, Jan 28 2007; current version #11, Feb 11 2021) still says "(conjecture)", with A. Karttunen's 2018 check of the first 2048 terms. A127751 (#5) still calls it conjectural, and the related A127750, A127749 and A111967 conjectures (Fredholm-Rueppel parity for the 1/(2n+1) triangle) remain open. Checked and not relevant: S. Fried, "On the inverse of a certain triangular matrix and its connection to the largest odd divisor", NNTDM 32(2) (2026) 255-262, which covers A127793 and A000265, not A127752; S. Fried, JIS 28 (2025) Art. 25.4.3 and JIS 29 (2026) Art. 26.1.8; S. Fried, arXiv:2607.24832. No prior proof or counterexample found, and no existing formalization in formal-conjectures.

assessment.follows_from: The row-n equation of the lower-triangular system A s = 1, i.e. sum_{ceil(n/2)<=j<=n} s(j) = 3n+1. Taking differences of consecutive rows gives s(0)=1, s(2m+2)=3 and s(2m+1)=s(m)+3. Compare this with the formula a(2n)=1-a(n), a(2n+1)=1 already listed in A035263 (equivalently, the parity of the 2-adic valuation of 2n).
assessment.justification: The whole argument is to write row n of A s = 1 as a window sum, sum_{j=ceil(n/2)}^{n} s(j) = 3n+1, and subtract consecutive rows. This gives s(2m+2)=3 and s(2m+1)=s(m)+3, which also yields a closed form in terms of the 2-adic valuation of n+1. Parity then follows by a one-line induction against the recursion a(2n)=1-a(n), a(2n+1)=1, which is already listed in A035263. This is a half-page, standard telescoping argument that a competent mathematician would find within minutes. Most of the effort went into the formalization (morphic-word indexing, matrix-inverse link), not into new mathematics.

results.title: The inverse of the triangle 1/n! [k ≤ n ≤ 2k] is an integer triangle
results.summary: Let A(n,k) = 1/n! if k ≤ n ≤ 2k and A(n,k) = 0 otherwise (n, k ≥ 0), viewed as an infinite lower-triangular matrix over Q. Let T be its inverse, computed by forward substitution: T(n,k) = n!·([n = k] − Σ_{j<n} A(n,j) T(j,k)) for k ≤ n, and T(n,k) = 0 for k > n. Then T(n,k) is an integer for all 0 ≤ k ≤ n. This was conjectured by Paul Barry in OEIS A127755.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: %C A127755 It is conjectured that this is an integer triangle. Row sums are A127756. (_Paul Barry_, Jan 28 2007)

Referees: I found no prior proof or counterexample for A127755. Sources checked:
- Local mirror and current GitHub oeisdata entry for A127755 (revision #5, Sep 29 2018), still marked conjectured.
- Related OEIS entries: A127756; A101688 (the 0/1 triangle [k<=n<=2k]); A111967 (its inverse, by Barry, 2005), with A127755(n,k) = k!·A111967(n,k).
- A127749: R. J. Mathar (Apr 21 2021) gives T(n,k) = (2k+1)·A111967(n,k), the same diagonal-scaling argument applied to the 1/(2n+1) sibling.
- A127793: FUNG Cheok Yin (Sep 2022) gives a formula implying integrality for the 1/floor((n+2)/2) sibling. Sela Fried, "On the inverse of a certain triangular matrix and its connection to the largest odd divisor", Notes Num. Theor. Disc. Math. 32(2) (2026) 255-262, doi:10.7546/nntdm.2026.32.2.255-262, proves it; the paper does not mention A127755.
- Sibling integrality conjectures that are also still open in OEIS: A127710, A127711, A127771.
- Web searches (OEIS/SeqFan/arXiv/MathOverflow/MSE-style queries) found nothing more.

results.title: The inverse of the 1/Catalan band triangle (A127767) has integer entries
results.summary: Let C(n) be the Catalan numbers. Let A be the infinite lower-triangular matrix with A(n,k) = 1/C(n) if k ≤ n ≤ 2k and A(n,k) = 0 otherwise. Let T be its inverse, which is also lower triangular. Then every entry T(n,k) with 0 ≤ k ≤ n is an integer. In the frozen statement, T is defined by forward substitution: T(n,k) = C(n)·([n=k] − Σ_{j<n} A(n,j)·T(j,k)) for k ≤ n, and T(n,k) = 0 for k > n.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: %C It is conjectured that all elements of the triangle are integers. (Paul Barry, Jan 28 2007)

Referees: - OEIS A127767 (P. Barry, Jan 28 2007). Local mirror and current GitHub oeisdata, #11 Sep 30 2018: the conjecture is still marked as conjectured, with no proof or formula. Cross-references: A127768, A127769, A127770, A000108.
- OEIS A101688: the 0/1 triangle [k<=n<=2k].
- OEIS A111967: inverse of A101688. It is an integer triangle because A101688 is unitriangular. T(n,k) = A000108(k)·A111967(n,k) is the identity that settles A127767.
- OEIS A127749, R. J. Mathar, Apr 21 2021: T(n,k) = (2k+1)·A111967(n,k). This is the same factorisation applied to a sibling triangle. It is the closest prior use of the method, but it does not resolve A127767.
- OEIS A127793: the integrality conjecture for the 1/floor((n+2)/2) sibling was proved by FUNG Cheok Yin (Sep 2022) and by S. Fried, "On the inverse of a certain triangular matrix and its connection to the largest odd divisor", Notes Num. Theor. Disc. Math. 32(2) (2026) 255-262, doi:10.7546/nntdm.2026.32.2.255-262 (https://nntdm.net/papers/nntdm-32/NNTDM-32-2-255-262.pdf). This covers A127793 only; there is no general remark that would cover A127767.
- Siblings with the same still-open integrality conjecture, all settled by the same argument: A127710, A127711, A127755, A127771.
- No relevant hits on arXiv, MathOverflow/MSE or SeqFan for A127767.

assessment.follows_from: The factorization A = diag(1/C_n) * M, where M(n,k) = [k <= n <= 2k] is the lower unitriangular 0/1 triangle A101688. Its inverse is the integer triangle A111967, so T = M^{-1} * diag(C_k), that is, T(n,k) = C_k * A111967(n,k). The same factorization appears in R. J. Mathar's 2021 formula for the sibling triangle A127749.
assessment.justification: The conjecture follows from one observation. Every nonzero entry in row n of A equals 1/C(n), so A is the 0/1 band matrix [k<=n<=2k] with each row scaled by 1/C(n). That band matrix is lower unitriangular, so its inverse has integer entries. Inverting A then just multiplies column k of that integer inverse by C(k). This is standard linear algebra that fits in a few lines. The method was already used for the sibling triangle A127749, and the manuscript itself calls the result an elementary observation. The integrality conjecture was meant literally, and the proof settles it as stated.

results.title: The triple-gcd Pascal triangle A129455: T(n,k) is an integer, divisible by C(n,k), and T(n,k)/C(n,k) is a sixth power
results.summary: Let G(m) = A129454(m+1) = prod_{i,j,k=1..m} gcd(i,j,k), so G(0) = 1. For all 0 <= k <= n: (1) G(k)·G(n-k) divides G(n), so T(n,k) = G(n)/(G(k)G(n-k)) is an integer; (2) the binomial coefficient C(n,k) divides T(n,k); (3) T(n,k)/C(n,k) = m^6 for some natural number m. This is Peter Bala's 2007 conjecture from OEIS A129455, with the Lean T defined by natural-number division as in the frozen statement.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: It appears that the T(n,k) are always integers. This would follow from the conjectured prime factorization given in A129454. Calculation suggests that the binomial coefficients C(n,k) divide T(n,k) and that T(n,k)/C(n,k) are perfect sixth powers. (Peter Bala, Apr 16 2007)

Referees: OEIS A129455, A129454 and A129453: the local mirror matches GitHub oeisdata (revisions #9, #8 and #9, Feb 2024), and all three still state the claims as conjectures. OEIS A092287: Greathouse (Apr 2013) confirmed the square-case prime factorization. Wanli Ma, "Generalized factorials characterized by Dirichlet convolution", arXiv:2509.13354 (Sept 2025), Section 2.2 and Theorems 2.5-2.6: proves that the q-tuple gcd product equals prod_p p^{sum floor(n/p^i)^q}, and that the generalized binomial coefficients for superadditive x are integers. With q=3 this implies only the integrality part of A129455; the paper does not mention A129454/A129455, C(n,k) divisibility or sixth powers. A.B. Mingarelli, "Abstract factorials", arXiv:0705.4299 / NNTDM 19 (2013): general framework, no gcd products. A224479/A224497 (Forgues, Luschny 2013): square-case formulas G2(n) = n!*A224479(n)^2, the analogue of the perfect-square property of A129453, but nothing for the cubic case. I found no source proving that C(n,k) divides T(n,k) or that T(n,k)/C(n,k) is a sixth power for A129455.

assessment.follows_from: The prime factorization v_p(A129454(n+1)) = sum_t floor(n/p^t)^3 conjectured in A129454 (cubic analogue of the A092287 formula Greathouse confirmed; stated for general q in Ma, arXiv:2509.13354), together with Legendre's formula and Kummer's carry theorem for v_p(C(n,k)).
assessment.justification: Counting multiples of each prime power gives the Legendre-type formula v_p(G(n)) = sum_t floor(n/p^t)^3, which A129454 already points to and which is published in general form. With A = floor(k/p^t), B = floor((n-k)/p^t) and a carry c in {0,1}, the identity (A+B+c)^3 = A^3+B^3+c+3[AB(A+B)+c(A+B)(A+B+1)] has an even bracket. By Kummer's theorem the carries c add up to v_p(C(n,k)), so all three claims follow at once. The whole argument is under a page of standard elementary number theory and needs no new idea. Bala's comment itself says integrality would follow from the factorization.

results.title: Denominators of Curtz's polynomials are Farhi's d(n+1,k+1) (A141412, Marcus's conjecture)
results.summary: Let P(0,x)=1 and P(n+1,x) = (-1)^(n+1)/(n+2) + x * sum_{i=0}^{n} (-1)^i/(i+1) * P(n-i,x) over Q, and let c(n,k) = [x^k] P(n,x) (computed by the matching recursion c in the statement file). Let T(n,k) be the reduced denominator of c(n,k), and let d(n,k) be the reduced denominator of |s(n,k)| * k!/n!, where |s(n,k)| is the unsigned Stirling number of the first kind (Nat.stirlingFirst). Then T(n,k) = d(n+1,k+1) for every 0 <= k <= n. The proof gives this for all n and k.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: "Conjecture: T(n, k) = d(n+1, k+1), with d(n,k) = denominator(A000254(n, k)*k!/n!) where A000254 are the unsigned Stirling numbers of the 1st kind. See d(n,k) in Farhi link. - _Michel Marcus_, Oct 18 2018"

Referees: P. Flajolet, X. Gourdon and B. Salvy, "Sur une famille de polynômes issus de l'analyse numérique", Gazette des Mathématiciens 55 (1993) 67-78, also INRIA Research Report RR-1857 (Feb 1993), https://inria.hal.science/inria-00074815/document. Eq. (3) is the generating function log(1+z)/(z(1-x·log(1+z))), and eq. (6) is P_n(x) = (-1)^n/(n+1)! Σ_k s_{n+1,k+1}(k+1)!(-x)^k, which gives the conjecture at once. This paper is cited in A141412's own %D line. The OEIS records the same identity in A140749 %F (Paul Curtz, Jul 17 2008, numerators = those of A048594(n+1,k+1)/(n+1)!) and A141412 %F (G. C. Greubel, Oct 24 2023, "Equals denominators of A048594(n+1,k+1)/(n+1)!"), with A048594's column e.g.f. log(1+x)^k. Farhi's d(n,k) comes from B. Farhi, arXiv:1810.07560 (Funct. Approx. Comment. Math. 61 (2019)). I found no earlier formal proof.

results.title: A144637: (1/18) 6^n a(n)/n! is odd iff n = 2^k with k >= 1
results.summary: Let S(n,k) be A144385: the number of partitions of {1,...,k} into exactly n blocks, each of size 1, 2 or 3. Let T = A144633 be the transpose of the inverse of the upper unitriangular matrix M(i,j) = S(i,j). Let a(n) = T(n,2), and y(n) = (1/18) 6^n a(n) / n!. Then for every n >= 0, y(n) is an odd integer if and only if n = 2^k for some k >= 1.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: Conjecture: (1/18)*6^(n)*a(n)/n! is odd iff n = 2^k for k >= 1. (End) - _Peter Bala_, Feb 19 2026

Referees: OEIS A144637 (Bala conjecture, Feb 19 2026; entry revision #25, Mar 14 2026; no proof recorded). The companion conjecture in OEIS A144636 (Bala, Feb 16 2026) is also unresolved. OEIS A144633 and A144385 give the definitions. Checked with nothing found on either conjecture: S. Fried, "Proofs of Ten Conjectures From the OEIS", J. Integer Sequences 29 (2026), Art. 26.1.8; S. Fried, "Further proofs of conjectures from the OEIS", arXiv:2607.24832 (full text grepped); Epoch AI, "OEIS Open", arXiv:2608.11941 and github.com/epoch-research/LeanOpenProblems (no A14463x file); Engbers–Galvin–Smyth, "Restricted Stirling and Lah number matrices and their inverses", JCTA 2019 (integrality of inverses, not parity). No prior proof or counterexample found.

results.title: Barker's order-20 recurrence for the lines through an 8 x n grid holds
results.summary: Let a(n) be the number of lines in the plane through at least 2 points of the 8 x n grid {0..n-1} x {0..7} (OEIS A160848). Then for every n > 21: a(n) = -a(n-2) + a(n-5) + a(n-6) + 2a(n-7) + a(n-8) + a(n-9) - a(n-11) - a(n-12) - 2a(n-13) - a(n-14) - a(n-15) + a(n-18) + a(n-20) (Colin Barker's 2017 conjecture).
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: Conjectures from _Colin Barker_, Dec 25 2017: "a(n) = -a(n-2) + a(n-5) + a(n-6) + 2*a(n-7) + a(n-8) + a(n-9) - a(n-11) - a(n-12) - 2*a(n-13) - a(n-14) - a(n-15) + a(n-18) + a(n-20) for n>21", with g.f. denominator (1-x)^3(1+x)(1-x+x^2)(1+x^2)(1+x+x^2)(1+...+x^4)(1+...+x^6).

Referees: - OEIS A160848 (local mirror, revision #13 of Dec 25 2017): Barker's g.f. and order-20 recurrence are labelled "Conjectures from Colin Barker, Dec 25 2017", with no later %E. Siblings A160845, A160846, A160847, A160849 and A160850 are likewise still conjectural or empirical; A295707 is the parent array.
- S. Mustonen, "On lines and their intersection points in a rectangular grid of points", http://www.survo.fi/papers/PointsInGrid.pdf (2009). Section 3 proves L(m,n) = ½[f(m,n,1) - f(m,n,2)]. Appendix 2, eq. (38), gives the second-difference recursion L(m,n) = 2L(m,n-1) - L(m,n-2) + 2ψ1 + 2ψ4 with periodic residuals, supported by a heuristic "bearing points" argument and numerical checks; that recursion is the basis of the Mathematica code in the OEIS entry.
- P. Haukkanen and J. K. Merikoski, arXiv:1108.1041 (2011), Remark 2: for n1 ≠ n2, "Mustonen [5] conjectured a recursive formula", and the question is "more difficult".
- A.-M. Ernvall-Hytönen, K. Matomäki, P. Haukkanen and J. K. Merikoski, "Formulas for the number of gridlines", Monatsh. Math. 164 (2011) 157-170: proves Mustonen's recursions only for n×n and (n-1)×n grids.
- S. Mustonen, "On lines through a given number of points in a rectangular grid of points", LinesInGrid2.pdf: covers square grids only.

No prior proof or counterexample of Barker's A160848 recurrence was found.

assessment.follows_from: The entry's own formula a(n) = (1/2)(f(8,n,1) - f(8,n,2)), with f(m,n,k) = Sum (n-|kx|)(m-|ky|) over coprime (x,y), proved by Mustonen (PointsInGrid.pdf, Section 3) and repeated in the parent array A295707. Taking the second difference in n gives a periodic residual, which is Mustonen's eq. (38) for m=8.
assessment.justification: The conjecture follows readily from the slope-sum formula already in the entry. With 8 rows, y ranges over a bounded set, and for each fixed y the second difference in n of Sum_x (n-|kx|)[gcd(x,y)=1] is a gcd indicator that is periodic with period at most 7 (at most 6 for the k=2 term). So the second difference of a(n) is eventually a combination of sequences with periods 1..7. That means a(n) is annihilated by (1-x)^2 times lcm(1-x^q : q<=7), which is exactly Barker's denominator (1-x)^3 Phi_2...Phi_7. The manuscript re-derives the counting formula via "first pairs" and checks the period-420 identity by kernel computation, but the underlying idea is a standard half-page quasi-polynomial argument.

results.title: A172164: the second differences of the Theodorus-spiral turns are always 18, 19, 20 or 21
results.summary: Let S(k) = sum_{i=1}^{k} arctan(1/sqrt i) be the total central angle of the first k triangles of the spiral of Theodorus. Triangle i covers the angular sector [S(i-1), S(i)], and turn n is the angle range [2pi(n-1), 2pi n]. Let c(n) be the number of triangles i >= 1 that lie entirely inside turn n, that is, with 2pi(n-1) <= S(i-1) and S(i) <= 2pi n. Then for every n >= 2, the difference a(n) = c(n) - c(n-1) is one of 18, 19, 20, 21. This is Dumortier's conjecture in OEIS A172164.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: "Conjecture : The terms are only 18,19,20,21 (From the first thousand turns, there are 2,3% of 18, 36,5% of 19, 46,2% of 20 and 15% of 21). No period found. Probably due to Pi transcendence." (Sebastien Dumortier, Jan 27 2010)

Referees: I found no prior proof or counterexample.

OEIS entries (local mirror, identical to the raw GitHub copy):
- A172164 (Dumortier, 2010): the conjecture, with numerical frequency checks by R. G. Wilson v (1e5 turns) and H. Kociemba (1e7 turns), 2013. Still listed as a conjecture at edit #25, Aug 2026.
- A137515: "the number added grows by 18, 19, 20 or 21 (tested up to 5000 terms)"; restated by H. P. Dale in 2019 with no proof.
- A072895: Kociemba's comment that floor((pi n + c)^2 - 1/6) with c = -K/2 = 1.0788914983... differs from A072895(n) by at most 1, and equals it for n < 1e9 (numerical only).
- A105459: Hlawka's Schneckenkonstante K, with the formula Sum_{x<n} arctan(1/sqrt x) = 2 sqrt n + K + o(1).
- A296179, A296181, A295338, A295339 (W. Lang): related revolution counts; nothing on this bound.

Background sources for the asymptotics:
- E. Hlawka, "Gleichverteilung und Quadratwurzelschnecke", Monatsh. Math. 89 (1980) 19-44.
- P. J. Davis, "Spirals: From Theodorus to Chaos" (1993).
- D. Brink, Amer. Math. Monthly 119 (2012) 779-786.
- J. Waldvogel, "Analytic Continuation of the Theodorus Spiral" (2008).
- Kociemba, "The Spiral of Theodorus" (kociemba.org/themen/spirale/theodorus.html): unreachable, seen only through search snippets, which cover the asymptotics and turn counts but no proof of the 18–21 bound.

Unrelated papers checked: arXiv 2403.20207 (Stouten, about hypotenuses on a common line; withdrawn) and arXiv 2407.07109 (the Fibonacci–Theodorus spiral).

The result follows from effective versions of the Hlawka/Davis asymptotics, but no source I found writes the bound down.

assessment.follows_from: Hlawka's asymptotic Sum_{x<n} arctan(1/sqrt x) = 2 sqrt n + K + o(1) (A105459 %F; Hlawka 1980, Davis 1993), made effective, together with Kociemba's form K_n ~ (pi n - K/2)^2 - 1/6 in A072895 and the elementary fact that the second difference of floor(y_n) is within 2 of the second difference of y_n, where 2 pi^2 = 19.74.
assessment.justification: The heuristic is immediate: the turn boundaries are roughly floor((pi n + c)^2), whose second differences are within 2 of 2 pi^2 = 19.74, which leaves only 18..21 with about 0.26 of slack. The proof turns this into an effective argument in a standard way. Two elementary one-step inequalities show that S(k) - 2 sqrt k is nonincreasing and that S(k) - 2 sqrt k - 2/sqrt k is nondecreasing (the usual sum-versus-integral comparison). A squeeze over three consecutive turns then gives |a(n) - 2 pi^2| < 2.13 for n >= 71, and a finite interval computation covers n <= 70. This is about a page of standard effective asymptotics plus a finite check, and the scout's own plan (Euler-Maclaurin plus a check of small n) already calls every step standard. The Lean work, including the kernel-evaluated interval certificate, was heavy, but that is formalization effort and not new mathematics.

results.title: ∑_{i=1..n} C(2n-i-1, i-1)/i is never an integer for n > 1 (A175385)
results.summary: For every integer n ≥ 2, the rational number S(n) = ∑_{i=1}^{n} C(2n-i-1, i-1)/i is not an integer. This is the Shevelev–Seidov conjecture from OEIS A175385.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: We conjecture that Sum_{i=1..n} ((1/i)*C(2n-i-1,i-1)) is not an integer for n>1. (Vladimir Shevelev, Zak Seidov, Apr 24 2010)

Referees: OEIS A175386 (cross-reference of A175385), comment by Ralf Stephan, May 25 2026: the conjecture was proved by an autonomous AI agent (AlphaProof Nexus). Lean file: https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphaproof-nexus-results/blob/main/APNOutputs/OEIS/oeis_175386_conjecture_0.lean (theorem target_theorem_0: for n > 1, the denominator of S(n) is not 1; checked, no sorry). Papers: G. Tsoukalas et al., "Advancing Mathematics Research with AI-Driven Formal Proof Search", arXiv:2605.22763 (May 2026); T. Adamczewski, "OEIS Open: How many conjectures can language models turn into theorems?", arXiv:2608.11941 (Aug 2026), cited by OEIS for the proof on p. 15, Appendix A. Classical implication: P. S. Bruckman, "Lucas Pseudoprimes Are Odd", Fibonacci Quarterly 32(2) (1994) 155-157 (https://www.mathstat.dal.ca/FQ/Scanned/32-2/bruckman2.pdf). No even composite N has N | L_N − 1, and with 2n·S(n) = L_{2n} − 1 this settles the conjecture. The A175385 entry itself (https://oeis.org/A175385, history up to #14, Mar 2023) records no proof.

results.title: Divisors of the terms of row n of A176206 are the parts of the partitions of n
results.summary: Row n of A176206 lists n - k repeated p(k) times for k = 0, ..., n-1, where p is the partition function. Pol's conjecture says that for every n >= 1, the multiset of all divisors of all terms of row n equals the multiset of all parts of all partitions of n. Divisors and parts are counted with multiplicity: each term t of the row contributes each divisor of t once, and each partition contributes all of its parts.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: %C Conjecture: all divisors of all terms in row n are also all parts of all partitions of n. (Omar E. Pol, Nov 2020)

Referees: OEIS A066633 (number of k's in all partitions of n): g.f. x^k/(1-x^k)*Prod 1/(1-x^m) by V. Jovovic (Jan 2002); T(n,k) = Sum_{j<n, j==n mod k} P(j) by J. L. Arregui (Apr 2002); T(n+k,k) = T(n,k) + A000041(n), proved in M. Ghosh Dastidar and S. Sen Gupta, "Generalization of a few results in Integer Partitions", arXiv:1111.0094, Lemma 1. A related classical bijection appears in arXiv:1610.01863 ("On Stanley's theorem and its generalizations") and arXiv:1007.3459. M. Merca, "A note on a classical connection between partitions and divisors" (aos.ro), also counts the k's in all partitions of n. OEIS A338156 states the A176206 divisor/partition correspondence as fact. Sources: https://oeis.org/A066633 (read from local mirror), https://arxiv.org/abs/1111.0094, https://arxiv.org/pdf/1610.01863, https://arxiv.org/pdf/1007.3459, https://aos.ro/?p=14363

results.title: A178295: collinear 4-subsets of {0,...,4}^n number 9^n/2 + 3*7^n/2 - 2*5^n (Mathar's conjecture, all three formulas)
results.summary: Let a(n) be the number of 4-element subsets of the grid {0,...,4}^n whose points lie on one line. Collinearity means that all 2x2 minors of the difference vectors vanish. Then three things hold. (1) a(n) = 9^n/2 + 3*7^n/2 - 2*5^n for every n >= 0. (2) a(n) = 21 a(n-1) - 143 a(n-2) + 315 a(n-3) for every n >= 3. (3) As formal power series over Q, sum a(n) x^n = x(-5+41x) / ((9x-1)(7x-1)(5x-1)).
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: Conjecture: a(n) = 9^n/2+3*7^n/2-2*5^n. a(n)= +21*a(n-1) -143*a(n-2) +315*a(n-3). G.f.: x*(-5+41*x)/((9*x-1)*(7*x-1)*(5*x-1)). [_R. J. Mathar_, May 24 2010]

Referees: No published resolution of the A178295 formula was found. Local mirror oeisdata seq/A178/A178295.seq (%I #15, Jul 22 2025): the formula is still labelled "Conjecture [R. J. Mathar, May 24 2010]", with no %E lines and no cross-references to it.

Related sources:
- **R. J. Mathar, "Points on a line in the finite d-dimensional simple cubic lattice"** (oeis.org/A178294/a178294.pdf). Its abstract calls it a "mostly speculative summary", fitting Hardin's tables to Ehrhart polynomials. I saw only search snippets and an independent report, not the full text: the mirror has only an LFS pointer, and oeis.org and the Wayback Machine were inaccessible.
- **the-omega-institute/trureturing, GitHub issue #7376 (Sep 12–13, 2026).** A Lean proof of sibling A178294 (triples in the 4^n grid). Its literature check found "no proof or refutation as of 2026-09-13" and says the Mathar PDF gives the formula only as a fit. It does not mention A178295.
- **Classical full-line count ((k+2)^n - k^n)/2**, which gives the (7^n-5^n)/2 ingredient (A081200, itself still labelled a Hardin conjecture in OEIS):
  - P. Erdős and J. L. Selfridge, J. Combin. Theory Ser. A 14 (1973) 298-301.
  - S. W. Golomb and A. W. Hales, "Hypercube Tic-Tac-Toe", MSRI Publ. 42 (2002), Theorem 1.
  - L. Moser's proof, via Honsberger.
  - O. Patashnik, Math. Mag. 53 (1980).
- **Same-batch siblings, still labelled conjectures:** A081199, A081200, A081201, A178294, A178296-A178299.
- **Checked, no relevant result:** arXiv:2609.25133 (Kudriashov, Sep 2026), arXiv:2404.02369, arXiv:1107.0327.

assessment.follows_from: The classical tic-tac-toe line count ((k+2)^n - k^n)/2 for the grid {0,...,k-1}^n (Erdos-Selfridge 1973; Golomb-Hales 2002, Theorem 1; Moser's word-counting proof). With k=5 this gives the (7^n-5^n)/2 full lines, which is OEIS A081200. The same word-counting method gives (9^n-5^n)/2 runs of four consecutive collinear points.
assessment.justification: Any line meeting {0,...,4}^n in 4 or more points has a primitive direction in {0,±1}^n, because a coordinate step of 2 or more allows at most 3 points. So a collinear 4-set is either 4 consecutive points on such a line, which Golomb-Hales word counting gives as (9^n-5^n)/2 (9 choices per coordinate, not all constant, up to reversal), or one of the 3 non-consecutive 4-subsets of a full 5-point line, giving 3(7^n-5^n)/2. The recurrence and generating function then follow mechanically from the closed form. This is a standard argument of under a page, an easy variant of the classical count; the manuscript itself calls it short and elementary. The formalized route through a finite classification of columns is formalization engineering, not a new mathematical idea.

results.title: 3 × 3 lower triangles with neighbours differing by at most two: a(n) = 1047 n - 1459 for n > 2 (A195249)
results.summary: Let a(n) be the number of fillings (x0,...,x5) of the six cells of the lower triangle of a 3 × 3 array (rows of lengths 1, 2, 3) with entries in {0,...,n}, such that any two king-adjacent cells (horizontal, vertical or diagonal neighbours) have entries differing by at most 2. The adjacent pairs are 0-1, 0-2, 1-2, 1-3, 2-3, 1-4, 2-4, 3-4, 2-5, 4-5. Then a(n) = 1047 n - 1459 for every n > 2. This is Hardin's empirical formula from OEIS A195249.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: %F Empirical: a(n) = 1047*n - 1459 for n>2. (R. H. Hardin, Sep 13 2011); %F Conjectures from Colin Barker, May 06 2018: G.f.: x*(64 + 601*x + 288*x^2 + 94*x^3) / (1 - x)^2. a(n) = 2*a(n-1) - a(n-2) for n>4.

Referees: I found no prior proof of A195249 or of row 3 of A195248. The local OEIS mirror entries for A195249, A195248 and A195214 have no %E lines and still mark the formulas 'Empirical'. The closest prior work is Robert Israel's comment (Nov 21 2017) on the sibling sequence OEIS A195232 ('one or less' variant), which proves the analogous linearity in k with the same span argument; this is a direct template for the current proof. Israel's Ehrhart-polynomial comment on A195220 (Oct 06 2019) is related. Hardin's own 'Generalizing' note on A195248 gives no proof. Searches I checked that turned up nothing relevant: Dougherty-Bliss & Kauers, 'Hardinian Arrays', Electron. J. Combin. 31(2) P9 (arXiv:2309.00487), which treats a different Hardin family; Ekhad-Yang-Zeilberger arXiv:1707.04654, which treats Mathar's conjectures; and web, arXiv and MathOverflow searches for the formula, the A-numbers and the entry's name text.

assessment.follows_from: The standard bounded-span (translation) argument, written down by Robert Israel (Nov 21 2017) for the sibling table A195232: any two cells of the triangle are joined by at most two neighbouring steps, so every valid filling spans at most 4. Hence a(n) = sum over s of N_s*(n+1-s), which is linear in n once n >= 3. A finite count of shapes (or of T(8,4) = 1047 plus a(3..7)) fixes the constants. This is also Hardin's 'Generalizing' remark in A195248 (slope = A195214(3)).
assessment.justification: The proof uses one standard observation. Every entry lies within 4 of the apex, so fillings are translates of finitely many shapes. That makes a(n) affine in n beyond a small threshold, and a finite computation (T(8,4) = 1047 and a(3) to a(7)) supplies the slope and intercept. The manuscript itself says this is essentially Israel's bounded-span argument from the sibling sequence A195232. No new idea is needed: it is a short argument plus a direct computation, and the work beyond that is formalization.

results.title: Repdigits with repdigit digital product are repunits from a(16) = 1111 on (A201060)
results.summary: Let a(1) < a(2) < ... list the repdigits (all decimal digits equal; 0 counts) whose digital product is also a repdigit. Then a(n) is a repunit (all digits equal to 1) for every n >= 16. Formally: forall n >= 16, IsRepunit (a n), where a n = Nat.nth IsTerm (n - 1).
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: "Conjecture: a(n) is repunit for n >= 16." (A201060, entry by _Jaroslav Krizek_, Nov 26 2011)

Referees: Main citations:
- R. Obláth, "Une propriété des puissances parfaites", Mathesis 65 (1956), 356–364. It shows that the only perfect powers with all decimal digits equal to some a != 1 are 4, 8 and 9.
- Y. Bugeaud and M. Mignotte, "On integers with identical digits", Mathematika 46 (1999), 411–417. It shows that no decimal repunit with two or more digits is a perfect power.
Together these say that no repdigit >= 10 is a perfect power, and the A201060 conjecture follows directly, since d^k >= 16 for 2 <= d <= 9 and k >= 4.

Both results are restated in O. Kihel and F. Luca, "Perfect Powers With All Equal Digits But One", J. Integer Seq. 8 (2005), Article 05.5.7, Introduction (https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL8/Kihel/kihel7.html). See also A. Gica and L. Panaitopol, "On Oblath's Problem", J. Integer Seq. 6 (2003), Article 03.3.5, which is linked from OEIS A018885 and A368049. The Wikipedia article "Repdigit" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Repdigit) covers the related Nagell–Ljunggren equation and cites Bugeaud–Mignotte 2002.

The OEIS entry A201060 (local mirror, revision #11, 2012) still labels the statement as a conjecture, and I found no web or arXiv discussion that names A201060.

results.title: Positivity of the exponential Mertens function (A209802)
results.summary: Let mu_e be the exponential Möbius function (A166234). It is multiplicative with mu_e(p^e) = mu(e), so mu_e(n) = prod_{p | n} mu(v_p(n)). Let a(n) = sum_{k=1}^{n} mu_e(k) (A209802). Then a(n) > 0 for every n >= 1. This is Zumkeller's conjecture in the OEIS entry.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: A209802 (Partial sums of exponential Möbius function, A166234): "Analog of Mertens's function, A002321; conjecture: a(n) > 0." (entry by _Reinhard Zumkeller_, Mar 13 2012)

Referees: No explicit resolution of the A209802 conjecture found:
- OEIS A209802 (https://oeis.org/A209802) and its history (https://oeis.org/history?seq=A209802, versions 1-29) still list "conjecture: a(n) > 0"; nothing about a proof is recorded.
- A166234 (exponential Möbius function) and A368405 add nothing on positivity.

Prior results that imply the conjecture at once:
- K. Rogers, "The Schnirelmann density of the squarefree integers", Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. 15 (1964) 515-516, doi:10.1090/S0002-9939-1964-0163893-X. It proves Q(n) >= 53n/88 for all n, with equality only at n = 176.
- L. Moser and R. A. MacLeod, "The error term for the squarefree integers", Canad. Math. Bull. 9 (1966), doi:10.4153/CMB-1966-039-4.
- The same bound is recorded in an OEIS A013928 comment (M. Marcus 2012; C. R. Greathouse IV 2016).
- L. Tóth, "On certain arithmetic functions involving exponential divisors, II", Annales Univ. Sci. Budapest. Sect. Comp. 27 (2007) 155-166, arXiv:0708.3557. It gives mu_e taking values in {-1, 0, 1} with mu_e(p) = 1, and the asymptotic sum mu_e(n) = c x + O(x^{1/2} log x) with c about 0.36094. That settles positivity only for large x.

Together these give a(n) >= 2Q(n) - n >= 9n/44 > 0 for all n >= 1.

Also checked, with nothing relevant found:
- Lelechenko, arXiv:1405.7597
- Cao and Zhai, J. Integer Seq. 13 (2010)
- Web, MathOverflow and Math StackExchange searches

results.title: A211343: positive entries are smallest parts of consecutive-part partitions; last positive column is A109814(n)
results.summary: Let T(n,k) be the triangle in which column k (k >= 1) begins in row k(k+1)/2 and lists 1, 0^(k-1), 2, 0^(k-1), 3, ... going down. In other words, for 1 <= k and k(k+1)/2 <= n we have T(n,k) = j/k + 1 when k divides j = n - k(k+1)/2, and T(n,k) = 0 otherwise. Two claims are made. (1) For n >= 1 and any entry (n,k) of the triangle with T(n,k) > 0, n has a partition into k consecutive parts m, m+1, ..., m+k-1, and T(n,k) is the smallest part of every such partition. (2) For n >= 1, A109814(n), the largest k such that n is a sum of k consecutive positive integers, is the largest column k of row n with T(n,k) > 0.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: %C Conjecture 1: T(n,k) is the smallest part of the partition of n into k consecutive parts, if T(n,k) > 0. %C Conjecture 2: the last positive integer in the row n is in the column A109814(n). (Omar E. Pol, Apr 30 2017)

Referees: OEIS (local mirror): A261699 comment by Peter Munn, Jul 30 2017 ("A211343(n,k) = abs(n/d - d/2) + 1/2, smallest part"; one-to-one link between odd divisors and partitions into k consecutive parts). A286013 comment by Peter Munn, Jun 18 2017 (trapezoid proof of the largest-part companion conjecture, which carries over directly to smallest parts). A285898 comment by David A. Corneth, Apr 28 2017 (n has a partition into k consecutive parts iff (n - C(k,2))/k is a positive integer). A196020 formula by Max Alekseyev, Nov 18 2013 (T(n,k) = 2n/k - k on the support), combined with the A211343 formula T = floor((1+A196020)/2). A237048 property by Hartmut F. W. Hoft, Oct 2014. A286000 "Theorem" (Pol). A379632 (Pol, Dec 2024: "Positive terms of A211343", "Right border gives A118235"). A118235 (smallest part of partitions into consecutive parts). A109814 (Jaap Spies / David W. Wilson: 2n = k(2m+k-1)). The classical background is Sylvester's enumeration of partitions into consecutive parts. Not retrievable (web.archive.org unreachable): Joerg Arndt, SeqFan, Jun 3 2017, proof of the A285914/A204217 conjectures. Web searches found no counterexample and no paper on A211343 specifically.

results.title: An equiangular decagon with sides in arithmetic progression (A215010)
results.summary: Garcia's conjecture (OEIS A215010) says that hexagons are the only equiangular simple convex polygons whose integer side lengths are the N terms t, t+d, ..., t+(N-1)d (with d ≥ 1) of an arithmetic progression, in some order. Formally: if N ≥ 3, every side t + σ(k)·d is positive, and Σ_k (t + σ(k)d)·exp(2πik/N) = 0 for a permutation σ of Fin N, then N = 6. We prove that this is false. Take N = 10 and t = d = 1, with consecutive sides (1, 4, 5, 8, 9, 2, 3, 6, 7, 10), so σ = (0, 3, 4, 7, 8, 1, 2, 5, 6, 9). This gives an equiangular decagon.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: "Conjecture: hexagons are the only simple convex polygons with equal interior angles with such property, due to the fact that cos(Pi/3) = 1/2." Here 'such property' means integer side lengths in arithmetic progression t+m*d, as in the entry name. (entry by _Robin Garcia_, Jul 31 2012)

Referees: Prior refutations, all at least as old as or published soon after Garcia's 2012 conjecture:

(1) OEIS A118887 (H. Pfoertner, May 03 2006). "Number of ways to place n objects with weights 1,...,n evenly spaced around a circle so it balances." T. D. Noe, Sep 13 2005: "Also number of equiangular polygons whose sides are some permutation of 1,2,3,...,n." The data have included a(10)=24, a(12)=732, a(14)=720, a(15)=48 since the first revision in 2006. W. Edwin Clark (Sep 14 2005) proved there are no solutions when n is a prime power. J. Sondow (Oct 17 2013) records that Murray Klamkin proved solutions exist when n is not a prime power, and adds the formula a(A024619(n)) > 0. The problem was proposed by Brendan McKay on the SeqFan mailing list, Sep 12 2005. https://oeis.org/A118887

(2) G. J. Woeginger, "Nothing new about equiangular polygons", Amer. Math. Monthly 120(9) (2013) 849–850, doi:10.4169/amer.math.monthly.120.09.849. Abstract: "We survey results on equiangular n-vertex polygons with edge lengths in arithmetic progression. Such a polygon exists if and only if n has at least two distinct prime factors." This is exactly the A215010 setting, and it gives n = 10, 12, 14, 15, ... as counterexamples.

(3) Supporting references:
- D. Ball, "Equiangular polygons", Math. Gazette 86 (2002) 396–407.
- A. Bernoff, "Bernoff's Puzzler", MuddMath Newsletter 4(1) (2005), p. 10.
- M. Munteanu and L. Munteanu, "Rational equiangular polygons", Applied Math. 4 (2013) 1460–1465, doi:10.4236/am.2013.410197.
- U. Abel, "Coincidence of the barycentre and the geometric centre of weighted points", Math. Gazette (online Oct 2019). It restates the criterion: at least two distinct prime factors.

A215010 itself (history checked through revision #43, Jan 23 2015) never cites any of these, and its conjecture remains uncorrected. I found no earlier formalization in Lean or any other proof assistant.

results.title: A223395: walks on the 4 x 4 grid graph satisfy Hardin's recurrence, Barker's g.f. and closed form
results.summary: Let a(n) be the number of walks with n vertices in the 4 x 4 grid graph P4 x P4 (the number of n x 1 arrays over the nodes 0..15 where vertically adjacent entries are adjacent nodes). Then (1) a(n) = 3a(n-1) + 2a(n-2) - 4a(n-3) for all n >= 4 (in Z); (2) (1 - x)(1 - 2x - 4x^2) * sum_{n>=1} a(n) x^n = 8x(2 - 3x^2) as formal power series over Z; (3) a(n) = (8 + (11 - 5 sqrt5)(1 - sqrt5)^n + (1 + sqrt5)^n (11 + 5 sqrt5)) / 5 for all n >= 1 (in R).
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: "Empirical: a(n) = 3*a(n-1) + 2*a(n-2) - 4*a(n-3)." and "Conjectures from _Colin Barker_, Aug 20 2018: G.f.: 8*x*(2 - 3*x^2) / ((1 - x)*(1 - 2*x - 4*x^2)) ..."

Referees: OEIS sources (local mirror):
- A223395 (R. H. Hardin, Mar 19 2013; Barker's conjectures added Aug 20 2018; rev #7). The recurrence is still "Empirical" and the g.f. and closed form are still "Conjectures"; there are no %E lines.
- A223402 (rev #8, Oct 03 2025). The column k=1 recurrence is still listed as empirical.
- A223372 (the 3x3 analogue, also empirical).
- A081057 (P. D. Hanna 2003; g.f. and recurrence by M. Somos and V. Jovovic, Mar 2003; R. J. Mathar, Oct 2010: "apparently" counts walks from a corner of the 4x4 board; D. Scambler, Oct 2010: decomposition into independent horizontal and vertical walks, giving a binomial convolution of Fibonacci numbers; I. M. Gessel 2022). It has the same signature (3,2,−4), but for corner-start walks only. I observed that A223395(n) = 2(A081057(n) + A081057(n+1)); this identity is not recorded anywhere.
- A052899 (same signature; R. Jehn's Oct 2024 comment on walks leaving a 4x4 board).

General theory (implies the result routinely but does not state it):
- D. Cvetković, M. Doob, H. Sachs, Spectra of Graphs (1980), Thm 1.11: the generating function of total walk counts, in terms of the characteristic polynomials of G and its complement.
- P. Rowlinson, "The main eigenvalues of a graph: a survey", Appl. Anal. Discrete Math. 1 (2007) 455–471.
- The classical spectrum of P_m□P_n, {2cos(iπ/(m+1)) + 2cos(jπ/(n+1))}.

Checked and not relevant (they concern a different Hardin family):
- R. Dougherty-Bliss & M. Kauers, "Hardinian Arrays", arXiv:2309.00487.
- G. Spahn & R. Dougherty-Bliss, "Rectangular Hardinian Arrays" (2024).

Web searches (arXiv, MathOverflow/MSE, general) found no explicit prior proof of the A223395 recurrence, g.f. or closed form.

assessment.follows_from: The transfer-matrix method, a(n) = 1^T A^(n-1) 1 for the adjacency matrix A of P4 x P4, together with standard main-eigenvalue theory (Cvetkovic-Doob-Sachs). The main eigenvalues of P4 x P4 are 1+sqrt5, 1 and 1-sqrt5, which are the roots of (x-1)(x^2-2x-4). In practice everything reduces to the finite check A^3·1 + 4·1 = 3A^2·1 + 2A·1 on 16 vertices.
assessment.justification: The sequence counts walks in a fixed 16-vertex graph, so it equals 1^T A^(n-1) 1. Its recurrence therefore comes from the polynomial of least degree that annihilates the all-ones vector under A. The proof checks the identity A^3·1 + 4·1 = 3A^2·1 + 2A·1 directly at every vertex, which comes down to three small symmetric 4x4 arrays, and then applies A repeatedly to get the identity for all n. The generating function and the closed form follow from the recurrence and the first three terms by routine algebra. This is a textbook transfer-matrix or main-eigenvalue argument plus a finite computation, and the manuscript itself calls it routine.

results.title: Every odd prime is a side of a Heronian triangle (A229159)
results.summary: For every prime p > 2 there are natural numbers x, y, z, A such that x, y, z satisfy the strict triangle inequalities (x < y + z, y < x + z, z < x + y), Heron's formula 16 A^2 = (x+y+z)(-x+y+z)(x-y+z)(x+y-z) holds in Z, and at least one of x, y, z equals p.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: "Conjecture: for all prime p > 2 there exists an integer-sided triangle with integer area where at least one side is of length p." (entry by _Michel Lagneau_, Sep 17 2013)

Referees: Classical formula (n, (n^2-1)/2, (n^2+1)/2) for odd n, credited to the Pythagoreans (Proclus, Commentary on Euclid's Elements I.47; H. Eves, An Introduction to the History of Mathematics, sec. 3-4; cf. Euclid, Elements X, Lemma 1 before Prop. 29). OEIS A046079, comment by Richard R. Forberg, May 31 2013: "For odd n: L = (n^2-1)/2 and H = L+1". In the same entry, Ant King (Jan 29 2011) notes that for n > 2 the n with exactly one Pythagorean triangle on leg n are the primes and their doubles. OEIS A042965 (Sloane, May 30 2014): the primes that are a difference of two squares are exactly the odd primes. Related: A009004 (short legs of Pythagorean triangles). Mathlib has the Pythagorean triple classification (Mathlib/NumberTheory/PythagoreanTriples.lean) but not this Heronian statement. I found no source that addresses A229159's conjecture directly; it is resolved immediately by the classical formula.

results.title: Stephan's conjectured g.f. for A242396 is false (first failure at n = 97)
results.summary: Let a(n) be the number of rows (closed horizontal strips j*sqrt(3)/2 <= y <= (j+1)*sqrt(3)/2) of the unit equilateral-triangle tiling that meet the circle of radius n. Stephan's conjecture says that sum_{n>=1} a(n) x^n * (x^14 - x^13 - x + 1) = -2x^14 + 4x^13 + 2x^12 + 2x^11 + 2x^10 + 2x^9 + 2x^8 + 4x^7 + 2x^6 + 2x^5 + 2x^4 + 2x^3 + 2x^2 + 4x in Z[[x]]. We prove that this identity is false.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: G.f., conjectured: (-2*x^14 + 4*x^13 + 2*x^12 + 2*x^11 + 2*x^10 + 2*x^9 + 2*x^8 + 4*x^7 + 2*x^6 + 2*x^5 + 2*x^4 + 2*x^3 + 2*x^2 + 4*x)/(x^14 - x^13 - x + 1). - _Ralf Stephan_, May 18 2014  (also: Asymptotics from g.f.: a(n) ~ 30/13 * n. - _Ralf Stephan_, May 18 2014)

Referees: Sources checked:
- The OEIS A242396 entry, from the local mirror and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/oeis/oeisdata/main/seq/A242/A242396.seq. Both show revision #18 (May 31, 2014), and the g.f. is still marked "conjectured" with no correction.
- The cross-referenced entries A242394 and A242395.
- A mirror search for the sequences ⌊2n/√3⌋ and 2⌊2n/√3⌋+2. The only match was A242396 itself.
- Ralf Stephan's conjecture list at ark.in-berlin.de/conj.txt, which covers only the 2004–2005 list.
- Four papers on proving OEIS conjectures, none of which mention A242396:
  - arXiv:2607.24832, "Further proofs of conjectures from the OEIS"
  - arXiv:2410.07237
  - S. Fried, JIS vol. 28 (fried15)
  - S. Fried, JIS vol. 29 (fried21)
- General web searches (arXiv, MathOverflow/Math StackExchange, SeqFan). These found no counterexample or refutation of Stephan's g.f. for A242396.

No prior resolution was found.

assessment.follows_from: Elementary closed form a(n) = 2*floor(2n/sqrt(3)) + 2, which is what the entry's own Small Basic program computes, together with direct evaluation of a(83), a(84), a(96), a(97) and comparison of the x^97 coefficient after clearing the denominator (1-x)(1-x^13).
assessment.justification: A row meets the circle exactly when its vertical extent overlaps [-n, n]. That gives a(n) = 2*floor(2n/sqrt(3)) + 2, which is also what the entry's own program computes for n up to 100. A rational g.f. with denominator (1-x)(1-x^13) would force a(n+13) - a(n) = 30 for every n. Because the slope 4/sqrt(3) is irrational, this cannot hold for all n, and a direct computation of four values gives the first failure at n = 97 (226 instead of 224). The refutation needs only this short argument and a finite check: Stephan's g.f. was a fit to the 61 listed terms, and no new idea was required. The counterexample is a real failure of the g.f. for the sequence as defined, not a degenerate or excluded case.

results.title: A249151(k) = k exactly when k + 1 is prime (Karttunen's conjecture, A249434/A249151)
results.summary: Let P(k) = prod_{j=0..k} C(k,j) be the product of row k of Pascal's triangle. For every k >= 0, k is the largest m with m! | P(k) if and only if k+1 is prime. Equivalently, A249151(k) = k iff k+1 is prime, so A006093 = {k : A249151(k) = k}.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: %C A249434 It seems that A006093 gives all those k for which A249151(k) = k. If that is true, then this is a disjoint union of A006093 and A249429. (_Antti Karttunen_, Nov 02 2014; the same claim appears in A249151: 'A006093 seems to give all such k, that a(k) = k', and %Y A249434 'Subsequences: A006093 (conjectured)')

Referees: OEIS A249434, A249151, A249431 (Antti Karttunen, Oct/Nov 2014; latest revisions Aug–Sep 2025 still say "seems"/"conjectured"; no %E proof record). J. C. Lagarias and H. Mehta, "Products of binomial coefficients and unreduced Farey fractions", arXiv:1409.4145 (Int. J. Number Theory 2016): formulas for ord_p of the row product G_n, including ord_p(G_n) = 0 iff n = a·p^k − 1 with 1 ≤ a ≤ p−1. This is a related ingredient, but the paper does not state or prove the conjecture. L. Du and J. C. Lagarias, arXiv:2006.15439, and Du–Lagarias–Yangjit, arXiv:2112.14422: related, but they do not address the conjecture. The conjecture is not in the AlphaProof Nexus / formal-conjectures auto_oeis set of 492 (Tsoukalas et al., arXiv:2605.22763) or in OEIS Open (Adamczewski, arXiv:2608.11941). No MathOverflow, Math StackExchange or SeqFan resolution was found.

assessment.follows_from: A001142's product formula P(k) = prod_{j=1..k} j^(2j-1-k), giving P(k)/k! = prod_{j<n} j^(2j-n-1) with n = k+1, together with Legendre's formula. Lagarias–Mehta (arXiv:1409.4145) also give closed forms for ord_p of the row product.
assessment.justification: The prime case takes one line: v_p(C(p,j)) = 1 for 0<j<p, so p^(p-1) exactly divides P(p). For composite n = k+1 the proof uses the standard row-product formula in A001142 to write v_q(P(k)/k!) as a sum over j < n. Splitting that sum by powers of q gives a closed form, q^e f(u) - R s(u) + e.
