A short digit-sum inequality, (q-1) f(u) >= s(u) whenever f(u) >= 1, then shows the excess is either negative or greater than e. All of this is about a page of elementary p-adic valuation bookkeeping (Legendre/Kummer-type sums) that someone fluent in such calculations would find quickly, so it is routine. The fact that the conjecture stayed open in the OEIS reflects lack of attention, not hidden difficulty.

results.title: A262957: Israel's b(n), c(n) are coprime integers and a(n) = b(n)
results.summary: Let cf(n) be the value of 1 - 1/(2 + 1/(3 - 1/(4 + ... (n+1) + (-1)^(n+1)/1))), where the integers 1, ..., n+1 are used, the sign after k is (-1)^k, and the innermost tail is 1. Let a(n) be the numerator of cf(n) in lowest terms. Robert Israel defined b and c by b(1)=2, b(2)=3, c(1)=3, c(2)=5 and, for both, x(n+1) = (((-1)^n(n-1) + n(n+2)) x(n) - (1 + (-1)^n(n+1)) x(n-1)) / (n - (-1)^n). Claim (Israel's conjecture, OEIS A262957): for every n >= 1, b(n) and c(n) are integers with gcd(b(n), c(n)) = 1, and a(n) = b(n).
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: Conjecture: b(n) and c(n) are coprime for all n, so that a(n) = b(n). I have verified this for n <= 10000. - _Robert Israel_, Dec 22 2015 [b(1)=2, b(2)=3, c(1)=3, c(2)=5, b(n+1) = (((-1)^n*(n-1)+n*(n+2))*b(n) - (1+(-1)^n*(n+1))*b(n-1))/(n-(-1)^n), same recurrence for c]

Referees: OEIS A262957 (local mirror, rev #80, Mar 2025): Robert Israel's comment of Dec 22 2015 states the conjecture, verified for n <= 10000, and it is still listed as open. Peter Bala, "A note on A262957 and A263295" (Dec 24 2015, linked from the OEIS entry): proves the simple continued fraction expansion [0;1,1,2,1,3,4,1,5,6,...] of the limit, but not Israel's recurrence or the coprimality. The cross-referenced entries A263295, A346590, A244279 and A244280 contain no proof. A262957 is absent from Tom Adamczewski, "OEIS Open: How many conjectures can language models turn into theorems?", arXiv:2608.11941 (2026), and from the epoch-research/LeanOpenProblems and LeanOpenProblems-results repositories. Web searches of arXiv, MathOverflow, Math StackExchange and SeqFan found no prior resolution. The proof uses the classical determinant identity for continued-fraction convergents (p_{k+1}q_k - p_k q_{k+1} = ±1).

assessment.follows_from: The classical fundamental recurrence and determinant identity for continued-fraction convergents, P_k Q_{k-1} - P_{k-1} Q_k = ±1 (e.g. Lorentzen-Waadeland), applied to the finite continued fraction 1 - 1/(2 + 1/(3 - ...)) whose last partial denominator is (n+1) ± 1.
assessment.justification: The n-th iterate is a finite continued fraction with integer partial denominators and numerators ±1. Its value is therefore (P_n ± P_{n-1})/(Q_n ± Q_{n-1}) for the standard convergents, and that numerator and denominator are coprime by the textbook determinant identity. The only remaining step is to check that these sums satisfy Israel's recurrence. That is a polynomial identity in two cases by parity, which a computer-algebra system or ring normalisation settles mechanically. Spotting that Israel's b, c are just the convergent numerators and denominators is the one small insight, and it is the obvious guess, so the whole argument is well under a page of standard continued-fraction theory.

results.title: Ternary digits of 2^n: column k has least period 2*3^(k-1) and balanced digits for k ≥ 2
results.summary: Let T(n,k) be the k-th base-3 digit (from the least significant end) of 2^n, i.e. the digit at the place 3^(k-1). Column k consists of the rows n with 3^(k-1) ≤ 2^n. Then for every k ≥ 1: (i) p(k) = 2*3^(k-1) is a period of column k (T(n+p(k),k) = T(n,k) for every row n in the column), and no q with 0 < q < p(k) is a period; (ii) for k ≥ 2, in every block of p(k) consecutive rows m, ..., m+p(k)-1 (m in the column) the digits 0, 1 and 2 occur equally often (in fact exactly 2*3^(k-2) times each). This is Conjecture 1 of OEIS A265210 (L. Edson Jeffery, 2015).
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: Conjecture 1: The sequence in column k is periodic, with period p(k) = 2*3^(k-1) = A008776(k-1), k >= 1, and in which the numbers 0,1,2 appear with equal frequency, for each k>1. (_L. Edson Jeffery_, Dec 04 2015)

Referees: E. de Faria and C. Tresser, "On Sloane's persistence problem", arXiv:1307.1188 (2013), Section 3.1, Lemma 3 and the paragraph after it. It shows 2^n mod 3^k has minimum period 2*3^(k-1) and that every allowable length-k ternary tail appears exactly once per period. This predates the Dec 2015 OEIS conjecture.
J. C. Lagarias, "Ternary expansions of powers of 2", J. London Math. Soc. 79 (2009) 562-588, arXiv:math/0512006, proof of Thm 1.4, eq. (3.3): 2 is a primitive root mod 3^k, so 2^n runs over all units mod 3^k.
Y. N. Aliyev, "Digits of powers of 2 in ternary numeral system", Notes Number Theory Discrete Math. 29(3) (2023) 474-485, Lemmas 3.2-3.3 and Observation I. It gives ord_{3^(n+1)} 2 = 2*3^n and shows the last-k-digit tails are periodic with period 2*3^(k-1) and run through all endings that don't end in 0.
Also standard textbook material (2 is a primitive root mod 3^k; e.g. LeVeque, Rosen) and the A008776 comment (J. Song, 2021).
OEIS A265210 itself (rev. #18, Dec 2015) still lists the statement as a conjecture and has no proof note. The single-column least-period refinement is not stated explicitly in these sources, but it is a short elementary consequence of the same facts.

results.title: Mathar's generating function for column 3 of A270668 (domino tilings of (4k+1)x5 boards with central hole)
results.summary:
Let c_k = T(2k, 2) be the number of domino tilings of the (4k+1) x 5 board with its central cell removed (c_0 = 1 for the 1 x 5 strip with its middle cell removed). Then, in Q[[x]],
  sum_{k>=0} c_k x^k = (-1 - 4x + 543x^2 - 6238x^3 + 17032x^4 - 6238x^5 + 543x^6 - 4x^7 - x^8) / ((x-1)(x^2-7x+1)(x^2-23x+1)(x^4-161x^3+576x^2-161x+1)).
This is R. J. Mathar's 2016 conjectured g.f. for "column 3" of OEIS A270668. Equivalently, (sum c_k x^k) * den = num.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: %F A270668 Conjectured g.f. for column 3: ( -1 -4*x +543*x^2 -6238*x^3 +17032*x^4 -6238*x^5 +543*x^6 -4*x^7 -x^8 ) / ( (x-1) *(x^2-7*x+1) *(x^2-23*x+1) *(x^4 -161*x^3 +576*x^2 -161*x +1) ). - _R. J. Mathar_, Mar 23 2016

Referees: R. J. Mathar, "A270668: Domino tilings with one monomer in the center", PDF linked from OEIS A270668 (https://oeis.org/A270668/a270668.pdf), dated Apr 13 2016. It counts the 5 x (2m+1) floor with a central monomer by the transfer-matrix method: 50 states, nine centre configurations, and left/right Hadamard products of rational g.f.s in x = z^5. It appears to derive the column-3 g.f. that Mathar had conjectured on Mar 23 2016 in OEIS A270668 (still labelled "Conjectured" there). I saw its content only through search-engine extracts; the full PDF could not be downloaded. Related but not resolving: OEIS A143659 / M. Ciucu arXiv:0710.4500 (diagonal); A189003/A189006 (5xn corner-removed, same characteristic polynomial t^4-15t^3+32t^2-15t+1); A003775, A006238; B. E. Tenner, EJC 11(2) R17 (2005); Byun-Goddard arXiv:2502.05918; Stanley EC1 section 4.2.5 (Hadamard products of rational series). No prior Lean or other formalization found.

results.title: Kagey's conjecture for A278212: a(n) = floor(A275815(n)/2), via exact bishop and queen maxima from flow (LP-dual) certificates
results.summary: For every n >= 1, let a(n) be the largest total number of moves that same-colored bishops can make on an n x n board, and queenMax(n) the same for queens. A piece can only move to an empty square, and every square it passes must be empty. Then a(n) = floor(queenMax(n)/2). More precisely, the proof shows the following. For bishops, a(4) = 20, a(5) = 38 and a(n) = 4(n-2)^2 for n >= 6. For queens, queenMax(4) is 40 or 41, queenMax(5) is 76 or 77, queenMax(6) is 128 or 129, and queenMax(n) = 8(n-2)^2 for n >= 7. That last formula also settles Alec Jones's conjecture on A275815 for n >= 7. The cases n <= 3 come from the listed values.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: "Conjecture: a(n) = floor(A275815(n)/2). - _Peter Kagey_, Nov 24 2016" (also A275815: "Conjecture: a(n) = 8(n-2)^2 for n >= 6. - _Alec Jones_, Nov 16 2016")

Referees: I found no prior resolution, only computation and partial bounds:
- OEIS A278212 (#36, Nov 19 2023): Kagey's 2016 conjecture is still listed as open. It records Chai Wah Wu's bounds 4(n-2)² ≤ a(n) ≤ 4n² (Nov 2016), Andrew Howroyd's a(n) ≤ 4(n-2)²+4 (Oct 2023), and terms a(7)–a(50) computed by Christian Sievers with an ILP (PuLP), after M. S. Branicky's a(6).
- OEIS A275815 (#43, Jul 2021): Alec Jones's conjecture a(n)=8(n-2)² for n≥6 is still a conjecture, with keyword "more". It records Wu's bounds 8(n-2)² ≤ a(n) ≤ 8n² and terms a(7)–a(32) computed by Jim Randell with MiniZinc.
- Jim Randell, Enigma 69 "Maximum queen moves" (enigmaticcode.wordpress.com, 2013, comments through 2025): the 6×6 case is verified by computer and the border formula is called "presumed". There is no general proof.
- Related entries A278211, A278213 and A278214 contain no proof.
- Searches of arXiv, MathOverflow, Math StackExchange, Puzzling, SeqFan and Google Scholar-style queries found no general proof or counterexample.

assessment.justification: The bishop half is routine. Andrew Howroyd's per-diagonal bound of 4(n-2)^2+4, given in the entry, drops to 4(n-2)^2 for n>=6 with a short corner argument: the 8 squares on the length-2 diagonals are exactly the endpoints of the four length-(n-1) diagonals. The conjecture also needs the queen bound A275815(n) <= 8(n-2)^2+1, which is essentially Alec Jones's conjecture, open since 2016. Counting moves line by line does not give that bound; it leaves a slack that grows linearly in n. The proof gets it from a linear-programming dual (flow) certificate found by computer, built on distance-to-edge classes so that one finite table covers every n>=8, and it needs 21 separately certified cases for n=4,5,6. That construction is not standard and does not follow from anything in the entries, so the result as a whole is substantial, though the bishop part on its own is not.

results.title: Schulte's conjectures on A281000, T(n,k) = C(2n+1,2k+1)·Cat(n-k): antidiagonal sums and matrix inverse
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: %F A281000 Conjectures: (1) Antidiagonal sums equal A001003(n+1); (2) Sum_{k=0..n} (-1)^k*T(n,k)*(2*k+1)*A000108(k)*A103365(k) = A000007(n); (3) Matrix inverse equals T(n,k)*A103365(n+1-k). (Werner Schulte, Jan 12 2017)

Referees: No prior resolution found. Sources checked:
- Local OEIS mirror: A281000 (#17, Nov 25 2018), A280580, A103365, A103364, A238390, A097610, A001003, A006318, A126120, A180874. No entry other than A281000 itself mentions A281000.
- arXiv 2607.24832 and 2410.07237 (Sela Fried, proofs of OEIS conjectures); no mention.
- arXiv 2608.11941 (Adamczewski, "OEIS Open") and the epoch-research/LeanOpenProblems-results repo; A281000 is not among its conjectures.
- Web searches on arXiv, MathOverflow, the OEIS wiki and SeqFan; no hits.

Closest prior material, which makes the result routine without explicitly resolving it:
- T. Copeland, comment in A238390 (Jan 30 2016): the inverse pair C(n,k)·A126120(n−k) ↔ C(n,k)·m(n−k), with m(2j) = (−1)^j·A238390(j). Its odd–odd block gives conjecture (3).
- V. Kotesovec, Mathematica in A103365 (2014), and P. D. Hanna's g.f. (2009): link A103365 to x/BesselJ(1,2x), so (−1)^j·A238390(j) = Cat(j)·A103365(j+1).
- P. Bala, A103364 (2013): generalized Riordan array (1/E(y), y).
- P. Barry, A097610 (Apr 2010): diagonal sums of the Motzkin triangle are the aerated large Schröder numbers. Restricting to an odd number of level steps gives half of that, which is conjecture (1).

assessment.follows_from: The scaling T(n,k) = (2n+1)!/(2k+1)! * c(n-k) with c(j) = 1/(j!(j+1)!), together with P. D. Hanna's g.f. in A103365 (A(x) = 1/B(x), B(x) = Sum x^n/[n!(n+1)!/2^n]), gives (3) at once; T. Copeland's inverse-pair comment in A238390 (Jan 30 2016) gives the same. (2) is the first column of (3). (1) follows from P. Barry's comment in A097610 (diagonal sums of the Motzkin triangle are the aerated large Schroeder numbers) plus a short g.f. parity argument, or from a Vandermonde/Narayana binomial identity.
assessment.justification: The inverse in (3) is immediate once you see that T and the Narayana triangle are both diagonal conjugates of the same Toeplitz matrix built from c(j) = 1/(j!(j+1)!). Inverting that Toeplitz matrix is exactly the reciprocal power series that Hanna's g.f. in A103365 already records. Conjecture (2), read as its evidently intended column-0 case, is just the first column of T*T^{-1} = I. Conjecture (1) takes about a page, either with Vandermonde's identity and Cloitre's Narayana formula for A001003 or with the Motzkin bivariate g.f. that Barry's A097610 comment points to. The paper itself calls the result routine, and none of these steps needs a new idea.

results.title: Lang's conjecture a(n) = A250400(n+1)/(n+1) for A294512 fails at n = 164
results.summary: Let V(n) = sum_{k=0}^{n} 1/((k+1)(3k+1)) and let a(n) be the denominator of V(n) in lowest terms (OEIS A294512). Let A250400(m) be the numerator, in lowest terms, of the harmonic mean m / sum_{j=1}^{m} 1/(j(3j-2)) of the first m octagonal numbers. Lang's conjecture (A294512, FORMULA, 2017) says that A250400(n+1)/(n+1) = a(n) in Q for every n >= 0. This is false. The first failure is at n = 164, where A250400(165)/165 = a(164)/11.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: A294512 (Denominators of partial sums of the reciprocals of octagonal numbers), FORMULA: "a(n) = A250400(n+1)/(n+1), n >= 0. [conjecture]." (entry by _Wolfdieter Lang_, Nov 01 2017). Companion A294513 (Lang, Nov 02 2017): "a(n) = 2*A250327(n+1)/(n+1) [conjecture]."

Referees: OEIS A294512 (W. Lang, Nov 01 2017; history #1-#13, last edit Nov 12 2017, formula "a(n) = A250400(n+1)/(n+1), n >= 0. [conjecture]" still present). OEIS A250401 (C. Barker 2014; Lang comment Nov 01 2017 conditional on "n+1 divides A250400(n+1)", still present, history #1-#19). OEIS A250400 (C. Barker, Nov 21 2014, b-file n=1..1000, which contains A250400(165) = 15*a(164)). Sibling Lang conjectures in A294513, A294515 are unresolved there too. Not in google-deepmind/formal-conjectures (FormalConjectures/OEIS); not in Tsoukalas et al. / Epoch OEIS Open (arXiv 2608.11941; github.com/epoch-research/LeanOpenProblems-results; SeqFan thread "Language models resolving OEIS conjectures", Aug 2026). No SeqFan, MathOverflow, MSE or arXiv discussion found. Independent check: the failures for n < 3000 are exactly n = 164 (gcd 11) and n = 2413 (gcd 17).

assessment.follows_from: A harmonic-mean identity that follows straight from the definitions in A294512/A250400: H(n+1) = (n+1)/V(n), so A250400(n+1) = (n+1)*a(n)/gcd(n+1, numerator V(n)). Barker's b-file for A250400 (m <= 1000) already lists A250400(165) = 15*a(164).
assessment.justification: Since the harmonic mean is (n+1)/V(n), the conjecture holds exactly when n+1 is coprime to the numerator of V(n). Checking that condition with exact rational arithmetic finds the first failure at n = 164, where 11 divides both 165 and num V(164). The Lean proof confirms the identity 11*A250400(165) = 165*a(164) by kernel evaluation. The paper's hand argument for why 11 divides the numerator is a nice touch but not needed: the result is a direct finite search, and the relevant value was already in Barker's A250400 table. This is a genuine counterexample to the conjecture as intended, not a degenerate case.

results.title: Domino-tileable Young diagrams are exactly the colour-balanced ones (A300789)
results.summary: For every integer partition y = (y_1 >= y_2 >= ... >= y_m), the Young diagram of y can be tiled by dominoes if and only if the number of odd parts in even positions equals the number of odd parts in odd positions. So the Heinz numbers of domino-tileable partitions (A300789) are exactly the Heinz numbers of partitions whose odd parts appear as often in even as in odd positions. Equivalently, a(n) = b(n) for all n >= 1, where a(n) and b(n) are the n-th smallest Heinz numbers of the two classes.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: %C A300789 This sequence is conjectured to be the Heinz numbers of integer partitions in which the odd parts appear as many times in even as in odd positions.  (_Gus Wiseman_, Mar 12 2018)

Referees: Already known, so the Lean proof is a first formalization, not a new result:
- Classical 2-core / beta-number theory. I.G. Macdonald, Symmetric Functions and Hall Polynomials (2nd ed. 1995), Ch. I §1 Ex. 8, pp. 12-15: the r-core is empty iff the beta-numbers are equidistributed mod r. D.E. Littlewood, Modular representations of symmetric groups, Proc. Roy. Soc. A 209 (1951) 333-353.
- Explicit statement of the parity form. S.P. Albion, "Proof of some Littlewood identities conjectured by Lee, Rains and Warnaar", arXiv:2108.12766, Lemma 2.1: empty 2-core (i.e. domino-tileable) iff {lambda_i + 2n - i} has n even and n odd elements, which is equivalent to the A300789 parity condition.
- Black = white criterion for Young diagrams. Codeforces Round 609 editorial, problem 1268B/1269D "Domino for Young" (Dec 2019, codeforces.com/blog/entry/72358).
- OEIS. A304710 (A. P. Heinz, May 2018) states the equivalence as fact: "number of partitions of 2n where the number of odd parts in even positions differs from the number of odd parts in odd positions". A000712 has Meeussen's 2013 comment and Karlsson's Dec 2025 comment. Heinz's Maple program and b-file for A300789 use the criterion.
- The A300789 entry itself (rev #11, May 22 2018, local mirror = GitHub) still says "conjectured" and has no %E updates.

results.title: A308107: Barker's rational generating function and order-15 recurrence for the sum of smallest sides of scalene integer triangles
results.summary: Let a(n) be the sum of the smallest side k over all integer triples k < i < j with j < k + i and k + i + j = n, i.e. over all scalene integer triangles of perimeter n. Then (1) sum_{n>=0} a(n) x^n = x^9 (2 + 2x + 2x^2 + x^3) / ((1-x)^4 (1+x)^3 (1+x^2)^2 (1+x+x^2)^2) as formal power series over Q, and (2) for every n > 15, a(n) = -a(n-1) + 2a(n-3) + 4a(n-4) + 2a(n-5) - a(n-6) - 5a(n-7) - 5a(n-8) - a(n-9) + 2a(n-10) + 4a(n-11) + 2a(n-12) - a(n-14) - a(n-15).
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: %F A308107 Conjectures from Colin Barker, May 13 2019: (Start) G.f.: x^9*(2 + 2*x + 2*x^2 + x^3) / ((1 - x)^4*(1 + x)^3*(1 + x^2)^2*(1 + x + x^2)^2). a(n) = -a(n-1) + 2*a(n-3) + ... - a(n-15) for n>15. (End)

Referees: The OEIS entry A308107 (local mirror and current GitHub oeisdata, version #14 of Sep 12 2021) still marks Barker's May 13 2019 g.f. and recurrence as conjectures, with no proof note or %E edit. Its cross-reference A307686 and the related entries A308108, A308109 and A308158 also leave their Barker conjectures unproved. A005044 has Roger Cuculière's comment that scalene triangles of perimeter n+6 correspond to all triangles of perimeter n; this gives a reduction, not a proof. Sela Fried's proofs of OEIS conjectures (arXiv:2410.07237; JIS 28, 2025, Art. 25.4.3; JIS 29, 2026, Art. 26.1.8; arXiv:2607.24832) do not cover A308107 or any triangle sequence near it. Andrews–Paule–Riese (MacMahon's Partition Analysis IX, k-gon partitions), Hirschhorn on k-gon partitions, and arXiv:2308.01912 on Alcuin's sequence treat only the unweighted triangle count. I found no prior proof or counterexample.

assessment.follows_from: Standard parametrization of integer triangles (as in Alcuin's sequence A005044 / Andrews-Paule-Riese k-gon partitions): scalene triangles of perimeter n are (k,i,j)=(v+w, v+w+u, 2v+w+u) with u,v,w>=1 and 2u+4v+3w=n, so the g.f. is sum (v+w) x^(2u+4v+3w) = x^9(2-x^3-x^4)/((1-x^2)(1-x^3)^2(1-x^4)^2). Alternatively, Cuculiere's bijection in A005044 reduces it to A307686.
assessment.justification: The proof writes each scalene integer triangle with three positive parameters in one linear relation, 2u+4v+3w=n, with smallest side v+w. Summing this linear weight over the parameters gives the rational generating function in a few lines by a standard MacMahon-type calculation. The order-15 recurrence then follows directly from the denominator. The paper itself calls the argument elementary and a routine computation. The Lean proof's chain of shift bijections is only formalization effort, not a new idea.

results.title: A308121: for odd n > 1, row 2n is row n with its halves swapped
results.summary: Let T(n,k) = b_n·k − a_n·r_k(n), where r_1(n) < ... < r_φ(n)(n) are the totatives of n and a_n/b_n is φ(n)/n in lowest terms (A076512/A109395). Row n is (T(n,1), ..., T(n,φ(n))). Claim (Charlie Neder's conjecture): for every odd n > 1, row n splits into two halves A, B of equal length with row n = A ++ B, and row 2n = B ++ A.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: Conjecture: If n is odd, then row 2n can be obtained from row n by interchanging the first and second halves. (Charlie Neder, Jun 05 2019)

Referees: - OEIS A308121 (Jamie Morken, May 13 2019; last edited Aug 05 2019, revision #47). Charlie Neder's conjecture of Jun 05 2019 is still marked "Conjecture," with no %E or comment recording a proof.
- The two entries that cite it, A307964 and A309497, do not resolve it.
- The cross-referenced entries A109395, A076512, A038566 and A076511 contain nothing about the conjecture.
- The classical background is phi(2n) = phi(n) for odd n and the bijection between totatives of n and of 2n; see arXiv 0907.1689, which treats a related map as a routine exercise.
- A308121 is absent from google-deepmind/formal-conjectures, and so from the OEIS Open benchmark (arXiv 2608.11941).
- Web searches (arXiv, MSE/MO, OEIS wiki) found no prior proof or counterexample. The SeqFan archive could not be reached (503 / connection reset).

assessment.follows_from: The classical fact that for odd n, phi(2n) = phi(n) and the totatives of 2n are the odd residues coprime to n. They are 2r-n for the totatives r > n/2, followed by n+2r for the totatives r < n/2. The symmetry r -> n-r (implicit in the entry's x+y = A109395(n) comment) shows that each half contains phi(n)/2 totatives.
assessment.justification: For odd n, the totatives of 2n are 2r-n for the totatives r of n above n/2, followed by n+2r for those below n/2. The symmetry r -> n-r puts exactly half of the totatives on each side of n/2. The reduced form of phi(2n)/(2n) is (a_n/2)/b_n, and after substituting both facts the identity T(2n,k) = T(n,k±phi(n)/2) is two lines of algebra using a_n n = b_n phi(n). This is a short, standard elementary argument, about a page, and a competent number theorist would find it quickly. The manuscript itself calls the argument elementary. The length of the Lean proof reflects list bookkeeping, not mathematical depth.

results.title: Perimeters of primitive Heronian isosceles triangles: A308222(n) = 2 · A096033(n + 2)
results.summary: Let a(n) be the n-th smallest perimeter of a primitive Heronian isosceles triangle (integer sides with no common divisor, integer area, two sides equal). Let A096033(n) be the n-th smallest difference z - x, where x is a leg and z the hypotenuse of a primitive Pythagorean triangle. Then for every n ≥ 1, a(n) = 2 · A096033(n + 2).
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: %F a(n) = 2*A096033(n+2) (conjectured). (Peter Kagey, May 16 2019)

Referees: Main prior resolution: Math StackExchange answer 3230072 by user "George", 2019-05-17 (https://math.stackexchange.com/a/3230072), answering Peter Kagey's question 3230019, "Semiperimeter of isosceles Heronian triangles". It is linked in the A308222 %H line. It derives that primitive isosceles Heronian triangles are (u^2+v^2, u^2+v^2, 2(u^2-v^2)) or (u^2+v^2, u^2+v^2, 4uv) with semiperimeters 2u^2 or (u+v)^2, citing J. R. Carlson, "Determination of Heronian Triangles", Fibonacci Quarterly 8 (1970) 499-506, Lemma 2.

Also: Wikipedia, "Integer triangle", section "Isosceles Heronian triangles" (the same parametrization: two copies of a Pythagorean triangle joined along a leg). The A096033 comment (Weimholt, 2010) says A096033 is the odd squares together with the numbers 2n^2.

No prior formalization found. OEIS A308222 (local mirror, #20, Aug 12 2022) still marks the formula "(conjectured)".

results.title: Fixed polyominoes with n cells and width n-2: T(n,n-2) = 8n^2 - 51n + 86 (A308359)
results.summary: For every n >= 5, the number T(n, n-2) of fixed polyominoes with n cells whose convex hull has width n-2 equals 8n^2 - 51n + 86. A fixed polyomino is a finite edge-connected set of grid cells, taken up to translation. The statement file encodes it as the normalized set S in N x N that has min x = 0 and min y = 0. The height is unrestricted.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: %F A308359 Conjecture: T(n,n-2) = 8*n^2 - 51*n + 86 for n >= 5.  (Entry by _R. J. Mathar_, May 22 2019; last edit Oct 10 2022.)

Referees: A. Goupil, H. Cloutier, F. Nouboud, "Enumeration of inscribed polyominos", FPSAC 2010, DMTCS proc. AN (2010) 737-748 (https://dmtcs.episciences.org/2808; hal-01186234; cited in OEIS A196593). Theorem 1 gives pmin(b,k) = 2k+2b-3bk-8+8*C(b+k-2,b-1), so pmin(w,3) = 4w^2-3w-2. Theorem 3 (k=2, b>2) gives pmin+1(b,2) = 4b^2-16b+18. Since T(n,n-2) = pmin(n-2,3) + pmin+1(n-2,2) = 8(n-2)^2-19(n-2)+16 = 8n^2-51n+86, Mathar's 2019 conjecture follows directly. The OEIS A308359 entry (last edited Oct 2022) still says "Conjecture" and has no proof note. Related but not resolving: L. Marin, "Counting Polyominoes in a Rectangle b x h", arXiv:2406.16413 (EPTCS 403, 2024), which covers fixed width and any height. I found no MathOverflow, Math StackExchange or SeqFan discussion explicitly proving the A308359 formula.

results.title: Odd terms of A323695 occur only at n = k(k+2)
results.summary: Let a(N) be the coefficient of x^N in Sum_{m>=0} x^m (1 - x^(m+1))^m / (1 + x^(m+1))^(m+1) (OEIS A323695, offset 0). If a(n) is odd, then n = k(k+2) for some natural number k. Equivalently, if a(n) is odd then n + 1 is a perfect square.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: A323695 (G.f.: Sum_{n>=0} x^n (1 - x^(n+1))^n/(1 + x^(n+1))^(n+1)): "Odd terms occur only at n = k*(k+2) for k >= 0 (conjecture);" (_Paul D. Hanna_, Feb 23 2019). A324300 (G.f.: Sum_{n>=0} x^n (x^(n+1)+i)^n/(1 + i x^(n+1))^(n+1)): "Odd terms occur only at n = k*(k+2) for k >= 0 (conjecture);" (Hanna, Feb 21 2019).

Referees: OEIS A323695 (Hanna, Feb 23 2019; still labeled "(conjecture)" at rev #24, Dec 15 2024; history checked) and its cross-references A323696, A324300 (same conjecture for an i-variant, also unproved), A323675 and A323680. Sibling results proved by others, which do not cover A323695: A325046, odd terms iff N = m(m+1), in S. Fried, "Further proofs of conjectures from the OEIS", arXiv:2607.24832 (Thm 50), also in google-deepmind/alphaproof-nexus-results; A323557, odd terms at r(r+1), in T. Adamczewski, "OEIS Open", arXiv:2608.11941 and AlphaProof Nexus (Tsoukalas et al.). A323695 is in neither google-deepmind/formal-conjectures nor epoch-research/LeanOpenProblems. It is not mentioned in Fried's arXiv:2410.07237 (JIS 25.4.3), JIS 26.1.8 or arXiv:2606.09913. MathOverflow, Math StackExchange and SeqFan searches found nothing.

assessment.follows_from: Reduce the entry's own g.f. modulo 2. Since 1 - x^(m+1) = 1 + x^(m+1) mod 2, each summand becomes x^m/(1+x^(m+1)), and the series becomes the standard Lambert series Sum_m x^m/(1-x^(m+1)) = Sum_n d(n+1) x^n. The classical fact that d(N) is odd iff N is a perfect square finishes the proof.
assessment.justification: The proof reduces the generating function modulo 2. There the numerator and denominator of each summand have the same base, so the m-th summand cancels down to x^m/(1+x^(m+1)). The sum is then the classical Lambert series for the divisor function, so a(n) is congruent mod 2 to d(n+1), and d(n+1) is odd exactly when n+1 is a square, by pairing each divisor d with N/d. This is a few lines of standard reasoning that a competent mathematician would find almost at once; the manuscript itself calls the result elementary. Unlike the sibling entries A323557 and A325046, nothing fails to cancel here, and the conjecture is the intended statement, not a degenerate reading of it.

results.title: Prime-Minesweeper on the A060734 array: a(n) < 6, and a(n) = 5 only at n = 6
results.summary: Write the positive integers into the square array A060734. The cell in row r, column c (both counted from 0) holds val(r,c) = (c+1)^2 - r if r <= c, and r^2 + 1 + c if r > c. Every positive integer appears in exactly one cell. Set a(n) = -1 if n is prime. Otherwise a(n) is the number of primes in the king-move neighbouring cells of n's cell. There are up to 8 such cells, 5 on row 0 or column 0, and 3 at the corner (0,0). Claim: for every n >= 1 we have a(n) < 6, and a(n) = 5 holds exactly when n = 6.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: %C a(n) < 6 (conjectured). %C a(n) = 5 for n={6} (conjectured). %C Set of n such that a(n) = 4 is unbounded (conjectured). (Witold Tatkiewicz, Oct 02 2019)

Referees: OEIS A326407 (Tatkiewicz, Oct 2019; last edit #27, Mar 20 2020) still lists "a(n) < 6" and "a(n) = 5 for n={6}" as conjectured, with no %E edits or proof links. OEIS A327893 (hexagonal spiral, De Vlieger 2019) records Tatkiewicz's parity argument bounding its terms by 4. That is the same technique applied to a different grid, not a proof for A326407. OEIS A326408 and A326409 state "a(n) < 5" without "(conjectured)" but give no proof. A326405, A326406, A326410, A060734, A136626 and A136627 contain nothing relevant. Web searches (arXiv, MathOverflow/Math StackExchange, SeqFan, general) found no prior proof or counterexample for A326407.

assessment.follows_from: Checkerboard parity of the A060734 array: val(i,j) is congruent to i+j+1 mod 2. This is the same parity technique that the OEIS records in A327893 (Tatkiewicz's comment bounding the hexagonal-spiral Minesweeper terms by 4), applied to this grid.
assessment.justification: The whole proof rests on one observation: in A060734 the entry in cell (i,j) has the parity of i+j+1. So for any interior cell, either its four orthogonal neighbours or its four diagonal neighbours hold even numbers, and only the cell of 2 can break this. That gives at most 4 primes everywhere except the cell of 6, which is next to 2. The edge cells and the few cells near 2 take a short parity check or direct evaluation. This is a standard argument of well under a page, and the OEIS already uses the same parity method for the sibling hexagonal entry A327893. The conjectures are settled as they were intended. The third conjecture, that a(n)=4 for infinitely many n, is not touched and remains open.

results.title: A326602: a(n) is odd iff n is a square
results.summary: Let A(x) = Sum_{n>=0} (x^(2n-1)+1)^n x^n / (1+x^(2n+1))^(n+1) in Z[[x]] (the n=0 summand is 1/(1+x)), and let a(n) = [x^(2n)] A(x). Then for every n >= 0, a(n) is odd if and only if n is a perfect square (n = k^2 for some k >= 0, so 0 counts as a square).
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: A326602 (G.f.: Sum_{n>=0} (x^(2n-1)+1)^n x^n/(1+x^(2n+1))^(n+1), an even function; a(n) = [x^(2n)]): "a(n) is odd iff n is square (conjecture)." (_Paul D. Hanna_, Aug 08 2019). Same family: A323689 (Sum (x^n+i)^n/(1+i x^n)^(n+1)): "Odd terms occur only at n = k^2 for k >= 0 (conjecture);" (Hanna, Feb 14 2019); A323675 (Sum x^n (x^n+i)^n/(1+i x^(n+1))^(n+1)): "It appears that odd terms occur only at n*(n+1)" (Hanna, Feb 10 2019); A323690 (Sum (x^(n+1)+i)^n/(1+i x^n)^(n+1)): "the first column consists of all the odd terms" (triangle rows start at n(n+1)) (Hanna, Feb 13 2019).

Referees: No prior resolution of A326602 found.
- OEIS A326602 (local mirror and upstream oeisdata) is still at revision #19, Aug 11 2019, and still says "a(n) is odd iff n is square (conjecture)". No later edits or proof links.

Closest prior work (same involution or parity method, different sequences):
- A323557 (odd terms only at n(n+1)): proved by AlphaProof Nexus (github.com/google-deepmind/alphaproof-nexus-results, APNOutputs/OEIS/oeis_323557_conjecture_0.lean) and in T. Adamczewski, "OEIS Open: How many conjectures can language models turn into theorems?", arXiv:2608.11941, Appendix A. Also R. Stephan's comment of Jun 01 2026 on A323557.
- A325046: S. Fried, "Proof of a conjecture stated in A325046" (OEIS a325046.pdf, 2025), and "Further proofs of conjectures from the OEIS", arXiv:2607.24832, Sec. 3.8 / Thm 50.

Neither arXiv paper mentions A326602, and A326602 is absent from google-deepmind/formal-conjectures, so it was not in the Tsoukalas et al. or OEIS Open benchmark sets.

assessment.follows_from: The involution/parity method already used for the cross-referenced sibling A323557: Ralf Stephan's comment of Jun 01 2026 in that entry, the AlphaProof Nexus Lean file, and Adamczewski, arXiv:2608.11941, Appendix A. Fried's proof for A325046 uses the same idea. The new proof also uses the standard fact that the central binomial coefficient C(2k,k) is even for k >= 1.
assessment.justification: The proof expands each summand using the binomial theorem and the series for (1+y)^-(n+1). Modulo 2 it rewrites the coefficient of x^N as a sum of trinomial coefficients T(n,m,i) over triples with n+m+2nm = N+2i. Both the weight and the condition are symmetric in n and m, so the off-diagonal terms cancel in pairs. Each diagonal term is a multiple of a central binomial coefficient, so it is even except when i = n, which forces N = 2n^2. The whole argument fits in about a page, and it is a direct adaptation of the involution proof for the cross-referenced entry A323557, which that entry already cites; the manuscript itself calls it a fairly routine adaptation.

results.title: The gcd of the interior binomial coefficients of row n equals Λ-exp(n)·Λ-exp(n−1) (A328202, Maiga's conjecture)
results.summary: For every n ≥ 4, let G(n) = gcd{ C(n,k) : 2 ≤ k ≤ n−2 }. Let L(m) = p if m = p^t is a prime power (p prime, t ≥ 1), and L(m) = 1 otherwise (A014963, the exponential of the von Mangoldt function). Then G(n) = L(n)·L(n−1).
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: %F A328202 a(n) = A014963(n) * A014963(n - 1) (conjecture). - _Jon Maiga_, Oct 08 2019; also %C (From _Robert Israel_, Oct 16 2019): 'If p is a Fermat prime > 3, a(p)=2*p. If p is a Mersenne prime, a(p+1)=2*p. Conjecture: these are the only cases where a(n)>n.'

Referees: G. Kaplan and D. Levy, "GCD of truncated rows in Pascal's triangle", Integers 4 (2004), #A14 (https://math.colgate.edu/~integers/e14/e14.pdf). Theorem 4 with Theorem 7 at t=1 (h(n,1)=1 for n>=4), or equivalently Theorem 9, gives g(n,2) = lcm(g(n-1,1), g(n,1)) = A014963(n)*A014963(n-1). This proves the A328202 formula in 2004, before the 2019 OEIS conjecture, and the paper's Table 2 matches the sequence data. Also relevant: H. Joris, C. Oestreicher and J. Steinig, "The greatest common divisor of certain sets of binomial coefficients", J. Number Theory 21 (1985) 101-119, which gives a general formula for gcd{C(n,k): r<=k<=s} (not checked directly). Background: Ram (1909) for the g(n,1) case. The OEIS entry (rev #46, Oct 10 2026) still labels the formula "(conjecture)" and does not cite these papers.

results.title: A332010: the average first letter of one-descent derangements has denominator 2^(n-2)
results.summary: For every n ≥ 2, take the derangements of {1, ..., n} (in one-line notation) that have exactly one descent. The average of their first letters, written in lowest terms, has denominator 2^(n-2). This is Kagey's conjecture T(n,1) = 2^(n-2) in OEIS A332010.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: "Conjecture: T(n, 1) = 2^(n-2)." (A332010, entry by Peter Kagey, Feb 04 2020)

Referees: No prior resolution found.
- OEIS A332010 and A332009 (Peter Kagey, Feb 04 2020; last edits Mar 30 2024) still state "Conjecture: T(n,1) = 2^(n-2)" and "Conjecture: T(n,1) = A083329(n-1)", with no proof recorded in comments or %E lines. I checked both the local mirror and raw.githubusercontent oeisdata.
- Related known facts:
  - A219836 (Callan 2012; links to Fu–Lin–Zeng arXiv:1507.05184 and Alexandersson arXiv:2609.07325) gives a recurrence implying there are 2^(n-2) derangements with one descent. That is only the unreduced denominator.
  - M. Conger, arXiv math/0508112, proves E[π(1) | des = k] = k+1 over all permutations; this is the analogue for all permutations that the A332010 comment cites.
  - Kagey, arXiv:2112.05281, treats expected π(1) given k-cycles and does not address derangements by descents.
  - Eriksen–Freij–Wästlund, arXiv:0811.1925 / EJC 16 (2009) R32, and Han–Xin (2007) cover derangements with prescribed descent sets, with no first-letter averages.
- Searches of Math StackExchange, arXiv and SeqFan found nothing. MathOverflow was not reachable through the search tool.

assessment.follows_from: Standard fact that a permutation with one descent is an increasing word on a set A followed by an increasing word on its complement (a Grassmannian permutation). A219836 already implies the count 2^(n-2).
assessment.justification: A permutation with exactly one descent is sorted(A) followed by sorted(complement of A). Checking fixed points run by run shows it is a derangement exactly when 1 is not in A and n is in A. That gives 2^(n-2) such derangements, and their first letter is min A. Summing min A over these sets gives 3*2^(n-2) - 1, which is odd, so the reduced denominator is 2^(n-2). This is a half-page counting argument built on a textbook description of one-descent permutations, and the count itself already follows from A219836. It needs no new idea.

results.title: Domino towers of height 2 and of height n-1, n-2, n-3 (A333650): all four Kagey/Luschny conjectures
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: %C A333650 Conjecture: For n > 1, T(n,2) = A000071(n+2).  [entry author _Peter Kagey_, Mar 31 2020]; Conjecture: T(n,n-1) = A339252(n-2). - _Peter Kagey_, Nov 21 2020; Conjecture: T(n,n-2) = A339254(n-3). - _Peter Luschny_, Nov 29 2020; Conjecture: T(n,n-3) = A339029(n-4). - _Peter Luschny_, Dec 01 2020 (summarised by Luschny as T(2n+k, n+k) = d_n(n+k-1), k>=1, 0<=n<=3).

Referees: OEIS A333650 (Kagey, Mar 2020; conjectures by Kagey Nov 21 2020 and Luschny Nov 29 / Dec 1 2020; still marked Conjecture as of revision #68, Aug 12 2022). A339494 (Luschny, Dec 2020): unproved remark that towers of height <=2 by base size form the binomial triangle C(k,n-k) (A030528), whose row sums are Fibonacci numbers, which is essentially the height-2 argument. A339495 assumes the height-2 formula. A339252, A339254, A339029: closed forms of the target sequences only. Definition of domino towers: A264746, A320314; Bona, Handbook of Enumerative Combinatorics, pp. 25-27; Gouyou-Beauchamps & Viennot 1988; Bétréma & Penaud 1993; Zeilberger arXiv:1208.2258. Related papers with no height enumeration: Ekhad & Zeilberger arXiv:1212.4105; T. M. Brown, Convex Domino Towers (JIS 2017, arXiv:1608.01562) and k-omino towers (arXiv:1608.01563); A. Haupt, S-omino towers (JIS 2021, arXiv:1810.10428); Ardila arXiv:1409.2562. Math StackExchange 2949131 and 3659431 (Kagey): symmetric towers and the 4^(n-1) variant only. No prior proof or counterexample of any of the four conjectures found.

assessment.follows_from: Height 2: a diagonal binomial sum, T(n,2) = sum_b C(b+1, n-b), which equals F(n+2)-1 by the standard Fibonacci identity (Luschny already noted the binomial-triangle link in A339494). Near-diagonals: the standard row-by-row transfer-matrix recursion on translation-normalized rows, compared with the closed forms 2^h times a polynomial already recorded in A339252, A339254 and A339029.
assessment.justification: The height-2 conjecture comes down to one observation: the second-row bricks pick distinct positions among the b+1 positions above a base of b bricks. That gives a diagonal binomial sum, which is a textbook Fibonacci identity. For heights n-1, n-2 and n-3 the excess over one brick per row is at most 3. Then only 13 translation-normalized row states can occur, and a single brick over a single brick always has exactly 2 placements. So the count is a finite transfer-matrix recursion whose solutions are 2^h times polynomials of degree at most 3, checked by induction against a finite table. These are standard enumerative techniques that need no new idea, and once the state space is written down the proof is a finite computation matched to closed forms already recorded in the cross-referenced entries.

results.title: Records of the XOR-triangle zero count A334592 are exactly the powers of two
results.summary: Let a(n) be the number of zeros in the XOR-triangle whose top row is the binary expansion of n, with the most significant bit first. Each later row is the XOR of adjacent pairs in the row above, down to a row of length 1. Then n is a record position (n >= 1 and a(m) < a(n) for all 1 <= m < n) if and only if n = 2^k for some k >= 0.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: %C A334592 Conjecture: Records occur at powers of two. (entry by _Peter Kagey_, May 07 2020)

Referees: The key fact is published. H. Harborth, "Solution of Steinhaus's problem with plus and minus signs", J. Combin. Theory Ser. A 12 (1972) 253-259, is credited with observing that the minimum weight of a nonzero binary Steinhaus triangle of size n is n. J. M. Brunat and M. Maureso prove it in "Small and large weights in Steinhaus triangles" (arXiv:1707.06698, 2017), Theorem 4.4: for n >= 4, w1 = n and W1 = {1^n, 10^(n-1), 0^(n-1)1}. Their extended abstract is "Extreme weights in Steinhaus triangles", Electron. Notes Discrete Math. 54 (2016) 349-354. The A334592 record conjecture is an immediate corollary: a(n) <= T(L) - L = T(L-1) = a(2^(L-1)). The OEIS entries A334592 and A334593 (local mirror, still at #19 / #22 from May 2020) have no %E note marking the conjecture resolved. The MathOverflow thread q/359138 linked from the entry could not be fetched. Other sources seen: arXiv:1702.03236 (Chappelon, periodic balanced binary triangles) and arXiv:2508.05159 (balanced Steinhaus triangles, which mentions Chang 1983 on the smallest weights).

results.title: A334595: a(n) = 1 iff n is a power of two, and the records occur exactly at 1 and 2^k + 1
results.summary:
Let a(n) be the number obtained as follows. Write n in binary, most significant bit first. Build the XOR-triangle whose first row is that bit string; each later row is the pairwise XOR of adjacent entries of the row above. Read the right side of the triangle from the top-right corner downward, and interpret it as a binary numeral with the first entry as the most significant bit. Then:
(1) For n >= 1, a(n) = 1 if and only if n is a power of two.
(2) The record positions are exactly {1} together with {2^k + 1 : k >= 1}. Here n >= 1 is a record position when a(n) > a(m) for every 1 <= m < n.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: Conjecture: Records occur at 1 and at 2^n + 1.  /  Conjecture: a(n) = 1 if and only if n is a power of two. (_Peter Kagey_, May 07 2020)

Referees: I found no earlier proof or counterexample for either A334595 conjecture.
- OEIS A334595 (Peter Kagey, May 2020): unchanged since revision #18 (May 09 2020), with both statements still labeled "Conjecture".
- MathOverflow 359138, "Number triangle" (user DSM, with answers by YCor and Ilya Bogdanov): treats the boundary operator φ_k with φ_k^3 = 1 and counts rotationally symmetric triangles (A334556/A334596). It does not address records or a(n) = 1.
- OEIS A334727 (Rémy Sigrist, 2020): states that the left-diagonal map is a self-inverse permutation.
- Paul D. Hanna's XOR binomial transform entries (OEIS A099884, A099900, A099902): note that the transform is self-inverse.
These are the known ingredients that make the result elementary. Web searches of SeqFan, arXiv, MathOverflow and Math StackExchange found no resolution.

assessment.follows_from: The classical fact that the binomial transform over GF(2) (the Pascal matrix mod 2) is an involution. This is the self-inverse XOR binomial transform of A099884, and also the self-inverse permutation stated in the sibling entry A334727, which gives the left-diagonal version of A334595. Reading the right diagonal of a row is the same as reading the left diagonal of the reversed row.
assessment.justification: Reverse the row, so that the right diagonal becomes the left diagonal. The digits of a(n) are then the GF(2) binomial transform of the bits of n. That transform is a classical involution, and A334727 already records it for this family. So a is a bijection on L-bit strings with a(n) < 2^L. Both conjectures then come down to working out three explicit preimages, of 1, of 2^L-1 and of 2^L-2, which takes about a page of elementary argument. No new idea was needed. The length of the Lean formalization does not make the mathematics substantial.

results.title: The period of 1/11^n is 2 * 11^(n-1)
results.summary: For every n >= 1, the period of the decimal expansion of 1/11^n is 2 * 11^(n-1). Equivalently, the multiplicative order of 10 modulo 11^n is 2 * 11^(n-1). This is the FORMULA conjecture of OEIS A334603.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: Comment: "Conjecture proposed by the authors in References page 205: if p is a prime with gcd(p,30) = 1 and if the period of 1/p is m then the period of 1/p^n is m*p^(n-1)." Formula: "a(n) = 2 * 11^(n-1) [conjectured, see comments]." (_Bernard Schott_, May 07 2020)

Referees: The result is classical; no formalization of this specific statement was found.

Classical theory: Gauss, Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801), on orders modulo p^n and on periods of decimal fractions with prime-power denominators (Arts. 85-89, 312-318). Standard elementary number theory texts (Ireland-Rosen; Niven-Zuckerman-Montgomery) state the lifting lemma: if p is odd and a^{ord_p a} = 1 + p*c with p ∤ c, then ord_{p^n}(a) = p^{n-1} * ord_p(a). Mathlib's ZMod.orderOf_one_add_mul_prime is that lemma for 1 + p*a.

Explicit decimal-period statements:
- K. A. Ross, "Repeating Decimals: A Period Piece", Mathematics Magazine 83 (2010), 33-45. If n is the largest exponent with period(1/p^n) = period(1/p), then period(1/p^a) = period(1/p) * p^(a-n) for a > n. For p = 11, period(1/121) = 22 ≠ 2, so n = 1.
- S. Yao and A. Toyohara, "The length of the repeating decimal", arXiv:2507.01295 (2025), Theorem 2.1: l_{p^n} = p^{n-(m_p+1)} * l_p, where m_p = v_p((10^{l_p} - 1)/p). For p = 11 this gives m = v_11(9) = 0, so l_{11^n} = 2*11^(n-1).
- Wikipedia, "Repeating decimal": the period of 1/p^2 is usually p*T_p, with the only known exceptions 3, 487 and 56598313.
- OEIS A045616 (primes with 10^(p-1) ≡ 1 mod p^2) lists exactly these exceptions, and 11 is not among them.
- John D. Cook, "Reciprocals of prime powers" (blog, 2021-09-28) checks 1/121 explicitly: period 22.

In the OEIS itself, A055272 has a Sep 2026 comment by E. Rodríguez proving the analogous 7^n case with the same lifting argument.

Side note: the general conjecture of De Koninck and Mercier quoted in the A334603 comments (not the formalized statement) is false at p = 487.

Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.01295 ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Repeating_decimal ; https://www.johndcook.com/blog/2021/09/28/reciprocals-of-prime-powers/ ; https://oeis.org/A045616 (read from the local mirror)

results.title: Repunit residues: a(n) = n - 1 exactly for long period primes
results.summary: For n >= 1 let a(n) be the number of distinct values R_k mod n for 1 <= k <= n, where R_k = (10^k - 1)/9 is the k-th repunit. Then a(n) = n - 1 if and only if n is a long period prime (A006883): n is prime and either n = 2 or the multiplicative order of 10 modulo n is n - 1.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: Conjecture: a(n) = n-1 if and only if n is a long period prime (A006883), that is, n is a prime and the decimal expansion of 1/n has period n-1. (entry by _Sen-Peng Eu_, May 19 2020)

Referees: OEIS A335012 (Sen-Peng Eu, May 19 2020): the current revision #31 (Mar 12 2026) still lists this as a conjecture, with no %E line recording a resolution. In the same entry, Robert Israel's comment (Jun 25 2020) gives a(n) = A084680(n), the order of 10 mod n, when gcd(n,30) = 1. That implicitly settles the coprime-to-30 case but not n divisible by 2, 3 or 5. Cross-references: A006883 (long period primes, including 2) and A084680; neither mentions a proof. Background only: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Repunit (pigeonhole argument that some repunit is a multiple of n; R_k ≡ k mod 3), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Full_reptend_prime, https://mathworld.wolfram.com/FullReptendPrime.html. Web searches of arXiv, MathOverflow, Math StackExchange, SeqFan and the Google index found no earlier proof or counterexample.

assessment.follows_from: Robert Israel's comment in A335012 itself, a(n) = A084680(n) (the order of 10 mod n) when gcd(n,30)=1, together with ord_n(10) <= phi(n) <= n-1 (equality forcing n prime), and the standard congruence R_k ≡ k (mod 3).
assessment.justification: The proof is an elementary argument of about a page. If n is even or a multiple of 5, every repunit is odd, or is 1 mod 5, so too few residues are hit. For gcd(n,10)=1 the residues are purely periodic with period L = min{k : n | R_k}. When 3 does not divide n, L = ord_n(10) <= phi(n), and L = n-1 forces n to be prime. When 3 divides n, R_k ≡ k (mod 3) forces 3 | L, while n-1 ≡ 2 (mod 3). The main case, gcd(n,30)=1, is essentially Israel's comment in the entry, and the cases of multiples of 2, 3 and 5 are quick standard observations, so a competent number theorist would find the whole proof quickly.

results.title: A338885: the smallest number in row 655 is 104, not A228286(655) = 115
results.summary: Kagey's conjecture in OEIS A338885 says that for every n ≥ 2, the smallest k for which a diagonal lattice rectangle (integer vertices, no side parallel to the x-axis) lies in the n X k box [0,n]×[0,k] and touches all four of its sides is A228286(n) = min{x + y*z : x, y, z ≥ 1, x*y + z = n}. This is false. For n = 655, the value k = 104 is in the row, but A228286(655) = 115 ≥ 105. So A228286(655) is not the least element of row 655.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: "Conjecture: The smallest number in the n-th row is A228286(n)." (entry by _Peter Kagey_, Nov 14 2020; a second conjecture in the same entry, "The largest number in the n-th row is A033638(n)", is true; see approach)

Referees: I found no prior resolution.
- OEIS A338885 (Kagey, Nov 14 2020): I checked both the local mirror and the latest raw oeisdata version (rev #22, Sep 11 2021). The conjecture is still listed, with no counterexample noted, and the b-file covers only rows 2..101.
- Cross-references (local mirror): A228286, A228287, A228288, A338886, A338887, A033638, A085582, A113751. None of them mentions a resolution.
- Code Golf SE question 213754 "Rectangles in rectangles", read via the Stack Exchange API: neither the answers nor the comments mention the conjecture.
- Web searches (OEIS/A338885, Kagey, SeqFan, the min x+yz / ab+cd formulations, ARML 2013) turned up nothing relevant.
- Independent computation: n = 655 is the smallest counterexample (row min 104 vs A228286 = 115). Further counterexamples are at n = 845, 909 and 1019 for n <= 1200.

assessment.follows_from: Finite computer search, using the elementary parametrization that k is in row n iff n = a+b, k = c+d and ab = cd for positive a, b, c, d (the explicit rectangle with vertices (4,0),(655,42),(651,104),(0,62); 4*651 = 42*62 = 2604)
assessment.justification: The conjecture is refuted by one counterexample, n = 655, found by a direct search. The row minimum there is 104, from an explicit lattice rectangle, while A228286(655) = 115; the lower bound is a finite check over about 2400 pairs (x, y). The only setup is the observation that the side vectors' coordinates satisfy a+b = n, c+d = k and ab = cd, which takes a few lines, and after that the search is mechanical (I reproduced it independently: counterexamples at n = 655, 845, 909 and 1019 below 1100). The counterexample is an ordinary row of the triangle and falls within the conjecture's intended meaning, so the result is not literal-only, but no new mathematical idea was needed.

results.title: The subword complexity polynomial S(n,x) has leading coefficient n(n+1)/2 (A341761, Guo's conjecture)
results.summary: For a word w, complexity(w) is the number of distinct nonempty factors (contiguous subwords) of w. Let S(n,x) be the sum of complexity(w) over all x^n words w of length n on an alphabet of x letters. For every n >= 0 there is a polynomial P in Q[X] with P(x) = S(n,x) for every natural number x, and the coefficient of x^n in P is n(n+1)/2.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: Conjecture: the coefficient of x^n in S(n,x) is n*(n+1)/2. (Shiyao Guo, entry author, Feb 19 2021)

Referees: OEIS A341761 (Shiyao Guo, 2021; still labelled "Conjecture" in rev #33, Mar 2024), cross-referenced with OEIS A340885. Shiyao Guo (Mivik), "On the Expected Subword Complexity of Random Words", https://mivik.moe/2021/research/expected-subword-complexity-en/, and the Chinese version https://mivik.moe/2021/research/expected-subword-complexity/ (updated 2026-03-26, still calls it an unproven conjecture). Related work that does not settle it: S. Janson, S. Lonardi, W. Szpankowski, "On average sequence complexity", TCS 326 (2004); I. Gheorghiciuc, M. D. Ward, "On correlation polynomials and subword complexity", DMTCS Proc. AH (AofA 2007), https://dmtcs.episciences.org/3553; Ahmadi and Ward, "Asymptotic Analysis of the kth Subword Complexity" (Entropy, 2020); Ivanko (Trudy IMM UrO RAN, 2008). I found no prior proof.

assessment.follows_from: Standard grouping of words by equality pattern (set partition of positions), giving S(n,x) = sum over patterns p of c(p)·x(x-1)...(x-k(p)+1). This is the same falling-factorial reasoning behind Guo's own remark in his linked blog post that S(n,x) is a polynomial of degree at most n.
assessment.justification: The proof groups words by which positions carry equal letters, so S(n,x) becomes a sum of c(p) times falling factorials of x, and only the pattern with all letters distinct reaches degree n. A word with n distinct letters has n(n+1)/2 distinct factors, which settles it. Put another way, once S(n,x) is known to be a polynomial of degree at most n (as Guo already noted), its leading coefficient is the limit of the expected complexity as x grows, and almost every word then has distinct letters. This is a standard argument of a few lines that a competent combinatorialist would find right away, and the paper itself calls it elementary. Proving the conjecture as stated is what the author intended, so the result is not literal-only.

results.title: Every n not divisible by 5 has a multiple with only prime digits (A342992)
results.summary: For every integer n >= 1 with 5 not dividing n, there is some k such that k*n is positive and every decimal digit of k*n is prime (in {2,3,5,7}). Equivalently, a(n) > 0 for A342992 (Sariyar's conjecture).
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: "Conjecture: a(n) > 0 for all n that are not divisible by 5." (A342992, entry by _Metin Sariyar_, Apr 13 2021. Corneth added that a(625k) = 0.)

Referees: No prior explicit proof of the A342992 conjecture was found. The entry still lists it as a conjecture (#60, Apr 22 2021) with no later %E edits.

Closest prior material:
(1) OEIS A078239 (Murthy 2002; Robert Israel, Feb 2018). Comment: "Besides multiples of 10, 625 and its odd multiples have a(n)=0". Its Maple program implicitly assumes a prime-digit multiple exists for every n with 10∤n and 625∤n. This is an unproved assertion. A078250 (Howroyd, 2024) repeats the comment.
(2) OEIS A053316 (Henry Bottomley, Mar 2000; formula corrected by Israel, 2019): an n-digit number with digits 2 and 3 that is divisible by 2^n. This is exactly the proof's block lemma. The digits-{1,2} version is A053312, the 1971 All-Union olympiad problem (cut-the-knot.org/arithmetic/DivisibilityFromSovietMO.shtml).
(3) IMO Shortlist 1994 N7, "wobbly numbers" (prase.cz/kalva/short/soln/sh94n7.html): the same technique of combining a 2-power block with the coprime-to-10 part by repetition.
(4) Galperin & Reid, "Multiples Without Large Digits", Amer. Math. Monthly 126 (2019), as cited by John D. Cook (johndcook.com/blog/2025/12/16/multiples-with-no-large-digits/), with the citation's page numbers disputed by a reader comment. It covers digits 1–5 and does not imply this result.
(5) C. W. Wu, "Pigeonholes and repunits", Amer. Math. Monthly 121 (2014): the related {0,1} case.

The result is elementary and folklore-adjacent, but no source states or proves it for prime digits or for digits {2,3}.

assessment.follows_from: The classical block lemma (OEIS A053316, Bottomley 2000; a {2,3} variant of the 1971 All-Union Olympiad problem A053312): for every j there is a j-digit number with digits 2 and 3 that is divisible by 2^j. Combine it with Euler's theorem 10^phi(m) ≡ 1 (mod m) for m coprime to 10, and repeat the block m times, as in the IMO Shortlist 1994 N7 solution.
assessment.justification: Write n = 2^e m with m odd and coprime to 10. Take a block of L = phi(m)(e+1) digits from {2,3} that is divisible by 2^L; this is the textbook digit-by-digit induction recorded in A053316. Concatenating m copies of the block gives a number divisible by both 2^e and m, by Euler's theorem. Both steps are standard olympiad techniques and the whole argument fits in well under a page. The work is not new mathematics; it is mainly noticing that these known pieces apply directly to Sariyar's conjecture.

results.title: A344710: non-obtuse lattice triangles with sides >= sqrt(n) have |det| > (sqrt 3 / 2) n
results.summary: For every n >= 1, let a(n) be the least value of |det(B-A, C-A)| (twice the area) over lattice triangles ABC in Z^2 that are non-degenerate and non-obtuse and have all three squared side lengths >= n. Then sqrt(3/4) * n < a(n). This is Waldmann's conjectured inequality in OEIS A344710.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: Formula: "a(n) > sqrt(3/4)*n (conjectured)." Comment: "Conjectured next terms (from the conjectured inequality a(n) > sqrt(3/4)*n) are a(50,...,64) ?= 45, 48, 48, 52, 55, 55, 55, 55, 55, 56, 56, 56, 56, 56, 56." (entry by _Jonathan F. Waldmann_, May 26 2021). A344845 has the same inequality a(n) > sqrt(3/4)*m (conjectured), by the same author, May 29 2021.

Referees: A. Mazel, I. Stuhl, Y. Suhov, "High-density hard-core model on Z^2 and norm equations in ring Z[...]", arXiv:1909.11648 (v1 25 Sep 2019; v3 22 Jun 2023). Lemma 3.4.4, eq. (3.1): sqrt(3)D^2/2 < S(D) < sqrt(3)D^2/2 + sqrt(2)D. S(D) is twice the minimal area of non-obtuse Z^2-triangles with sides >= D, so A344710(n) = S(sqrt n). The paper calls the lower bound "obvious". D. Krachun, "Triangles on Z^2 and sliding phenomenon" / "Extreme Gibbs measures for high-density hard-core model on Z^2", arXiv:1912.07566 (Dec 2019 / Jun 2020). Definition 2.1 gives the same S(D) for all D > 0, and Theorem 2 gives S(D) = (sqrt3/2)D^2 + O(D^{4/5}). The underlying inequality is the classical one: a non-obtuse triangle with all sides >= D has area >= (sqrt3/4)D^2, since area = (1/2)ab sin C with the largest angle C in [60,90] degrees. Equality would need an equilateral lattice triangle, and Z^2 has none. OEIS A344710 and A344845 (local mirror and GitHub, revisions #84/#52 of Feb 2022) still list the inequality as conjectured.

results.title: A348484: no two squares two steps apart; the conjectured formula holds
results.summary: For every n >= 1, let a(n) be the largest number of squares you can choose on an n x n board so that no two chosen squares are exactly two steps apart in the same row or in the same column. Then a(n) = n^2/2 if n ≡ 0 (mod 4), a(n) = (n^2+1)/2 if n is odd, and a(n) = n^2/2 + 2 if n ≡ 2 (mod 4). (This is Yang Hong's conjecture in OEIS A348484.)
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: %F A348484 Conjectures: a(n) = n^2/2 for n == 0 (mod 4). a(n) = (n^2 + 1)/2 for n == 1 or 3 (mod 4). a(n) = n^2/2 + 2 for n == 2 (mod 4).  (Entry by _Yang Hong_, Oct 20 2021; last edit #33, Dec 06 2022.)

Referees: OEIS A348484 (Yang Hong, Oct 20 2021; latest revision #33, Dec 06 2022) still marks the formulas as "Conjectures". R. J. Mathar's Dec 2022 comment gives a 2×2-block checkerboard construction. Its g.f. -x(1+2x-2x^2+2x^3+x^4)/((1+x)(1+x^2)(x-1)^3) matches the conjectured values, but he states it only as a lower bound. Cross-reference: A048716 (the 1-D row condition, k AND 4k = 0). I found no published or online proof of the upper bound on arXiv, Math StackExchange, MathOverflow, SeqFan or general web search. The result does follow directly from the standard fact that a grid graph P_a□P_b has independence number ⌈ab/2⌉, because the "two apart" graph is a disjoint union of four such grids.

assessment.follows_from: The matching lower bound is already in the entry: R. J. Mathar's comment gives the 2x2-block checkerboard construction and a g.f. whose coefficients are the conjectured values. The upper bound follows from the standard fact that the grid graph P_r x P_s has independence number ceil(rs/2), which is proved by tiling it with dominoes plus at most one monomino. Split the cells by (i mod 2, j mod 2). The "two steps apart" graph is then a disjoint union of four grid graphs whose sides are ceil(n/2) or floor(n/2).
assessment.justification: The proof needs two observations. First, split the cells by row and column parity, so the "two apart" graph becomes four ordinary grid graphs. Second, use the textbook fact that an r x s grid graph has independence number ceil(rs/2): a checkerboard gives the lower bound and a domino tiling with at most one monomino gives the upper bound. Adding up the four grids gives the conjectured values directly. The lower-bound construction was already in the entry as Mathar's comment, and the whole argument fits in well under a page. The manuscript itself calls the result elementary. Writing the pairing as an involution on the board is a convenience for the Lean proof, not a new mathematical idea.

results.title: Signed A350557 is the matrix inverse of A350512, proved
results.summary: Let T be the A350557 triangle: T(n,0) = (2n)!/(2^n n!) = (2n-1)!!, and for 1 ≤ k ≤ n, T(n,k) = (2n-1)!! · Σ_{i=k}^{n} C(i-1,k-1)/(2i-1)!!. Set T(n,k) = 0 for k > n. Let L be the A350512 triangle: L(n,0) = 1, and for 1 ≤ k ≤ n, L(n,k) = C(n-1,k-1)(2k(n-k)+n)/k. Set L(n,k) = 0 for k > n. Define M(n,k) = (-1)^(n-k) T(n,k). Then M and L are inverse lower-triangular matrices: for all n, j ≥ 0, Σ_{k=0}^{n} L(n,k) M(k,j) = [n=j] and Σ_{k=0}^{n} M(n,k) L(k,j) = [n=j]. This is Werner Schulte's 2022 conjecture.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: %F A350557 Conjecture: M(n,k) = (-1)^(n-k) * T(n,k) is matrix inverse of A350512. (Werner Schulte, entry author, Jan 2022)

Referees: No prior resolution found. Sources checked:
(1) OEIS A350557 and A350512, in both the local mirror and the current raw.githubusercontent oeisdata. The conjecture is still marked open, there are no %E lines, and neither entry has been edited since Jan 18 2022. Across the full mirror, no other entry cross-references A350557 or A350512. I also read A286286, A249349 and A103450.
(2) google-deepmind/formal-conjectures (local checkout from Oct 2026): neither sequence is formalized.
(3) google-deepmind/alphaproof-nexus-results (Tsoukalas et al., arXiv:2605.22763): A350557 is not among the APNOutputs/OEIS files, and the paper does not mention it.
(4) Adamczewski, "OEIS Open" (arXiv:2608.11941): its appendix of resolved conjectures does not include A350557.
(5) "Further proofs of conjectures from the OEIS" (arXiv:2607.24832) and S. Fried, "Proofs of some conjectures from the OEIS" (arXiv:2410.07237): A350557 is not mentioned in either.
(6) Web searches for the A-numbers, the defining formulas, the column g.f. (1+2kx)x^k/(1-x)^(k+1), and Schulte together with the inverse: the only hit is the OEIS page, which still states the claim as a conjecture.
The result is mathematically elementary (a recurrence plus binomial inversion), but there is no published or recorded proof, so I classify it as a new result.

results.title: OEIS A350900: Schulte's gcd-ratio double sum is a Dirichlet convolution
results.summary: Let a(f; n) = Sum_{i=1..n} Sum_{k=1..n} f(gcd(i,n)/gcd(gcd(i,k),n)). Then: (1) for every complex arithmetic function f and every n > 0, a(f; n) = ((f·φ) * A057660)(n), where f·φ is the pointwise product with Euler's totient, * is Dirichlet convolution, and A057660(m) = Sum_{k=1..m} m/gcd(m,k). (2) If f is multiplicative, so is a(f; ·). (3) For n > 0, the row sum Sum_{k=1..n} T(n,k) of the A350900 triangle T(n,k) = Sum_{i=1..n} gcd(i,n)/gcd(gcd(i,k),n) equals a(id; n). (4) For n > 0, that row sum equals (A002618 * A057660)(n), where A002618(n) = n·φ(n).
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: Conjecture: Let f be an arbitrary arithmetic function. Define for n > 0 the sequence a(f; n) = Sum_{i=1..n, k=1..n} f(gcd(i,n)/gcd(gcd(i,k),n)); a(f; n) equals Dirichlet convolution of f(n)*A000010(n) and A057660(n); if f is multiplicative, then a(f; n) is multiplicative; row sums of this triangle use f(n) = n (see formula section). Also %F: Conjecture: Row sums equal Dirichlet convolution of A002618 and A057660. (Werner Schulte, Jan 21 2022)

Referees: I did not query oeis.org; OEIS entries were read from the local mirror dated 2026-10-17.
- A350900 (Werner Schulte, Jan 21 2022; last edit #13, May 24 2024): both claims are still labeled "Conjecture", and no %E line records a proof.
- A373059 (Seiichi Manyama, May 21 2024; "Row sums of A350900"): states a(n) = Sum_{d|n} phi(n/d)(n/d) sigma_2(d^2)/sigma(d^2) = (A002618*A057660)(n) without proof or conjecture label. Amiram Eldar (May 27 2024) added the multiplicative formula and the Dirichlet g.f. zeta(s)zeta(s-2)^2/zeta(s-1)^2. This is a prior unproved assertion of part 4.
- Related OEIS identities, also without proof: A350156 (Schulte, the analogous claim for f(n/gcd(i,k,n))); A371492, A371628, A373060, A373061, A372962, A372964, A372968 (Manyama, May 2024; sums of gcd(x_1,n)/gcd(x_1,...,x_k,n)).
- A057660 (= Sum_{d|n} d*phi(d)).
- Classical background: Cesaro's identity; L. Toth, "A survey of gcd-sum functions", JIS 13 (2010) 10.8.1; O. Bordelles, "A Multidimensional Cesaro Type Identity and Applications", JIS 18 (2015) 15.3.7; P. Bala, "GCD sum theorems. Two Multivariable Cesaro Type Identities" (A368743 attachment; I could not retrieve its text).
- Checked and not relevant: S. Fried, "Further proofs of conjectures from the OEIS", arXiv:2607.24832 (A350900 is not among its sequences); D. Himane, NNTDM 31 (2025) (a different Schulte conjecture, about A006472).
No prior proof or counterexample of the A350900 conjecture was found.

assessment.follows_from: Cesàro's identity Sum_{k=1..n} F(gcd(k,n)) = Sum_{d|n} F(d) phi(n/d) (Tóth's gcd-sum survey, JIS 2010), together with the formula A057660(n) = Sum_{d|n} d*phi(d), which is already in cross-referenced entry A057660. Part (4) was already stated as a formula in A373059.
assessment.justification: Set g = gcd(i,n). The summand depends on i only through g, and its dependence on k has period g. Apply Cesàro's identity once to group the i, use periodicity to collapse the k-sum to one period, apply Cesàro's identity again, and re-index the divisors. This gives a(f;n) = ((f*phi) * 1 * (id*phi))(n), and 1 * (id*phi) is A057660 by its own %F line. Multiplicativity then follows from standard closure properties, and the row-sum parts follow by exchanging the sums and taking f = id. The whole argument fits in under a page of standard gcd-sum manipulation, and the manuscript itself calls it routine.

results.title: A351743: from n = 139 the sequence is affine in 42-blocks, which proves Sycamore's, Sigrist's and the A355149 conjectures
results.summary:
Let a(1)=1 and let a(n+1) be the greatest divisor of s(n)=a(1)+...+a(n) that is prime to a(n) (OEIS A351743; s is A355149). Then:
(1) a(n)=1 for infinitely many n, and a(n)=2 for infinitely many n (Sycamore).
(2) a(2(n+21)-1) = a(2n-1) for all n >= 70 (Sigrist).
(3) There is a 21-periodic integer sequence b with a(2(n+21)) = 3645 a(2n) + b(n) for all n >= 70 (Sigrist).
(4) There is a 42-periodic integer sequence c with s(n+42) = 3645 s(n) + c(n) for all n >= 138 (A355149 conjecture).
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: A351743 (a(1)=1; a(n+1) = greatest divisor of s(n) prime to a(n), s = partial sums): "Conjecture: a(n)=1 occurs infinitely many times, and therefore so does a(n)=2." (_David James Sycamore_, Jun 07 2022) and "Conjectures from _Rémy Sigrist_, Jun 20 2022: (Start) - a(2*(n+21)-1) = a(2*n-1) for n >= 70, - a(2*(n+21)) = 3645*a(2*n) + b(n) for n >= 70 (where b is 21-periodic). (End)". A355149 (partial sums of A351743): "Conjecture: a(n + 42) = 3645*a(n) + b(n) for n >= 138 (where b is 42-periodic)."

Referees: OEIS A351743 (David James Sycamore, Jun 07 2022) states the conjecture that 1 and 2 occur infinitely often. Its formula section, from Rémy Sigrist on Jun 20 2022, adds the conjectures a(2(n+21)-1) = a(2n-1) and a(2(n+21)) = 3645 a(2n) + b(n), both for n >= 70. OEIS A355149 (De Vlieger, Sigrist and Sycamore, Jun 21 2022; last edit #11 Nov 17 2022) states the conjecture s(n+42) = 3645 s(n) + b(n) for n >= 138. Both entries still list these as open conjectures in the current oeisdata. The only other entry that cites them is A357735, which has nothing on them. I searched the full text of S. Fried's OEIS-conjecture papers (arXiv:2410.07237; J. Integer Seq. 28 (2025) 25.4.3; J. Integer Seq. 29 (2026) 26.1.8; arXiv:2607.24832) and none mentions these sequences. Searches of the web, arXiv, MathOverflow/MSE and SeqFan found no proof or counterexample.

assessment.follows_from: Sigrist's own conjectured formulas in A351743 (%F) and A355149 (%F), which already describe the block structure; the proof makes that structure an explicit affine ansatz in Y_m = (3645^m-1)/3644 and checks it by a finite computation.
assessment.justification: The proof writes a and s on each 42-term block as affine functions of Y_m = (3645^m-1)/3644. The 42 coefficient rows come from the computed data, and Sigrist's conjectures already describe this shape. Each of the 42 steps of the recursion is then shown to hold for every value of the parameter, using two elementary gcd lemmas and a finite check of small divisibility and coprimality facts. Together with a direct computation of the first 139 terms, this proves all four conjectures. This is the standard way to certify an eventually periodic or affine pattern in a recursively defined sequence, and once the ansatz is set up it reduces to a finite computation. No new idea was needed, even though the conjectures had stayed open since 2022.

results.title: Even and odd legs with odd prime factors ≡ 3 (mod 4): a(n)/n → π (A354571, A354570)
results.summary: A354571 lists the even legs k of primitive Pythagorean triangles in increasing order, each repeated once per triangle. A leg is included when every odd prime factor of k is ≡ 3 (mod 4) and k has at least one odd prime factor. A354570 lists the odd legs k in the same way, for k whose prime factors are all ≡ 3 (mod 4). Selle's conjecture says that a(n)/n → π for A354571 and A354570(n)/n → π. The formal `statement` is the conjunction of these two limits, with each sequence read as the n-th term of the list where k appears #legTriangles(k) times.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: "Conjecture: lim_{n->oo} a(n)/n = Pi. Also, lim_{n->oo} A354570(n)/n = Pi." (Lothar Selle, Jun 04 2022; same text in A354570)

Referees: No prior resolution found.
- OEIS A354571 and A354570 (Lothar Selle, Jun 2022; last edited Aug 2022) still state lim a(n)/n = Pi as a conjecture. Checked in the local mirror and in upstream raw.githubusercontent.com/oeis/oeisdata.
- Selle, "Kleines Handbuch Pythagoreische Zahlentripel" (BoD 2022), ch. 2.3.10, is cited only for the equality of the two limits; I could not access the book.
- Related unproved Selle conjectures appear in A120427, A120890 and A354569.
- Web searches (arXiv, MathOverflow, Math.SE, SeqFan) found no proof or counterexample.
- The underlying asymptotic is a standard consequence of Wiener–Ikehara/Delange applied to (1-2^-s)zeta(s)/L(s,chi4), using L(1,chi4) = pi/4. D. N. Lehmer (Amer. J. Math. 22, 1900) treats similar Pythagorean counting asymptotics, but not this restricted case.

assessment.follows_from: Classical count of primitive Pythagorean triangles with a given leg (2^(omega-1) coprime factorizations), combined with the Wiener–Ikehara / Delange Tauberian theorem applied to sum_{m odd, all p|m ≡ 3 mod 4} 2^omega(m) m^-s = (1-2^-s) zeta(s)/L(s,chi_4), with L(1,chi_4) = pi/4 and L(s,chi_4) ≠ 0 on Re s = 1.
assessment.justification: The proof counts primitive triangles with a given leg using coprime factorizations, which gives the classical multiplicity 2^(omega-1). That reduces both counting functions to the summatory function of a multiplicative weight g, whose Dirichlet series is (1-2^-s)zeta(s)/L(s,chi_4). The Wiener–Ikehara (or Delange) theorem, together with L(1,chi_4) = pi/4 and the fact that L(s,chi_4) has no zeros on Re s = 1, then gives S(N) ~ 2N/pi. A short dyadic summation and the inversion from the counting function to the n-th term finish the proof. Each step is a textbook application of standard analytic number theory, and the manuscript itself calls it routine. Most of the work went into formalization: Wiener–Ikehara had to be proved from scratch in Lean. That effort does not make the mathematics substantial.

results.title: Integer partial sums of the Calkin-Wilf ratios fusc(k)/fusc(k+1) at n = 2*4^k-1 and 2*4^k-2 (A355076)
results.summary: Let fusc be Stern's diatomic sequence (fusc 0 = 0, fusc 1 = 1, fusc(2n) = fusc n, fusc(2n+1) = fusc n + fusc(n+1)), and let a(n) be the denominator of s(n) = sum_{k=0}^{n} fusc(k)/fusc(k+1). Then for every k >= 0, a(n) = 1 when n = 2*4^k - 1 or n = 2*4^k - 2. In other words, s(n) is an integer for those n.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: Conjecture: a(n) = 1 for n of the form 2*4^k - 1 or 2*4^k - 2 for some k >= 0. (entry by _Rémy Sigrist_, Jun 18 2022)

Referees: - **Row-sum theorem (the key ingredient):** K. Siddharth Choudary and A. Satyanarayana Reddy, "Calkin-Wilf tree", arXiv:2003.13466 [math.CO], Mar 2020, accepted in Resonance. Theorem 1.1, Part 11: the sum of all elements in level n (root at level 1) is 3·2^{n−2} − 1/2, proved by induction.
- **Earlier statement of the same fact:** OEIS A052940, comment by Carl Najafi (Jul 10 2011): 3·2^n − 1 is the numerator of the sum of terms at the n-th level of the Calkin-Wilf tree.
- **Classical facts:** OEIS A002487 records a(2^k) = 1 and a(2^k − 1) = k (Adamchuk comment), and that a(n)/a(n+1) enumerates the rationals (Stern; N. Calkin and H. Wilf, "Recounting the rationals", Amer. Math. Monthly 107 (2000)).
- **The conjecture itself:** OEIS A355076 (R. Sigrist, Jun 18 2022, rev. #11) is still listed as a conjecture with no %E edits. A355075 is the matching numerators entry. I found no explicit resolution anywhere; the result follows immediately from the Choudary–Reddy row sum plus the classical facts above.

results.title: A355339: the central even run of the knight-move triangle has length 1 iff n = 2^m - 2
results.summary: Let T(n,k) be the knight-move triangle A355320. It is defined by T(0,0)=1, with zero entries outside |k| <= 2n, and T(n,k) = T(n-1,k-2) + T(n-1,k+2) + T(n-2,k-1) + T(n-2,k+1). Let a(n) be the length of the maximal block of consecutive even entries of row n that contains the centre k=0. It is 0 if T(n,0) is odd, and a(0)=0. Then for every n >= 0, a(n) = 1 if and only if n > 0 and n = 2^m - 2 for some m >= 0 (equivalently, n+2 = 2^{t+2} for some t >= 0).
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: %F Conjecture: a(n) = 1 iff n > 0 and n belongs to A000918. (Rémy Sigrist, Jun 29 2022)

Referees: - OEIS A355339 (Rémy Sigrist, Jun 29 2022): the conjecture is in %F and is still unresolved at revision #10, with no %E extensions (checked in the local mirror and upstream oeisdata on GitHub).
- OEIS A355320 (the triangle; its %F gives T(n,0)=A096609(n) and T(n,1)=A096610(n), but nothing on parity).
- OEIS A096608–A096612 (Kimberling 2004, Catalan knight paths in the right half-plane), A096587, A361292, A000918, A002605: no parity results.
- J.-L. Baril, N. Hassler, S. Kirgizov, J. L. Ramírez, "Grand zigzag knight's paths", arXiv:2402.04851 (ECA 2024): its only parity remark (Remark 3.2) concerns zigzag path counts being even when n ≡ k (mod 2), not this conjecture.
- J.-L. Baril, J. L. Ramírez, "Knight's paths towards Catalan numbers", arXiv:2206.12087: nothing on parity.
- Web searches of arXiv, MathOverflow/MSE, SeqFan and general sources found no prior proof or counterexample.
- No formalization in google-deepmind formal-conjectures.

assessment.follows_from: The row-polynomial recurrence R_{n+1}=(1+X^4)R_n+(X^3+X^5)R_{n-1} given in A355320 (%F and PARI code), reduced mod 2 using 1+X^4=(1+X^2)^2, combined with Lucas's theorem for p=2.
assessment.justification: By symmetry, the claim reduces to two parity facts: T(n,0) is even for n>=1, and T(n,1) is odd exactly when n+2 is a power of 2. Both come out of a standard technique. Reduce the row recurrence already stated in A355320 modulo 2. There 1+X^4=(1+X^2)^2 and X^3+X^5=X^3(1+X^2), so the recurrence has an explicit binomial closed form (a sum over compositions of n). The coefficient parities then follow from Lucas's theorem (equivalently, Kummer's carry criterion) by a short carry argument. The whole argument is about a page of elementary mod-2 polynomial algebra and binomial parity, the kind of thing a competent combinatorialist would find quickly. The conjecture most likely stayed open because the entry is obscure, not because it is hard.

results.title: A356360: the continued-fraction denominators are 1 or prime
results.summary: For n >= 3, let a(n) be the denominator, in lowest terms, of the continued fraction 1/(2 - 3/(3 - 4/(4 - ... ((n-1) - n/(n+1))))). Then every a(n) is 1 or a prime. This is the conjecture Mohammed Bouras stated in OEIS A356360 (2022).
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: A356360: "Conjecture: The sequence contains only 1's and the primes." (_Mohammed Bouras_, Oct 15 2022). The same sentence appears in A369797 (Feb 2024), A370726 (Feb 2024) and A372763 ('Conjecture 1', May 2024). A372761: "Conjecture 1: Except for 4, the sequence contains only 1's and the primes." A362086: "Conjecture: Except for 9, every term of this sequence is either a prime or 1." A363482: "Conjecture: Except for 49, every term of this sequence is either a prime or 1." (all by Bouras)

Referees: OEIS A356360 (mirror 2026-10-17, rev #31 Aug 2024): still marked "Conjecture". It has an unproved comment "Same as A128059(n), A145737(n-1), A097302(n-2) for n>5", and its formula "a(n)=2n-1 if prime else 1 (n != 5)" is labeled "From the conjecture". M. Bouras, "The Distribution Of Prime Numbers And The Continued Fractions", Zenodo doi:10.5281/zenodo.7212512 (2022; also viXra 2209.0101): proves only the closed form (Thm 1.1) and states Conjecture 3.1, verified to n=10000. M. Bouras, "A New Primes-Generating Sequence", arXiv:2509.09745 (2025), Table 2 (k=1 row = A356360): observation only, no proof. Bouras slides, Zenodo 10992128: "Conjecture 2", no proof. AlphaProof Nexus results / formal-conjectures auto_oeis THEOREM_MAPPING and T. Adamczewski, "OEIS Open", arXiv:2608.11941: A356360 is not included; only the sibling A372761 Conj. 2 was resolved.
