Related but distinct: A356247 conjectures proved by B. Cloitre (2025, OEIS attachment). No prior proof or counterexample found.

assessment.follows_from: The closed form and gcd formula already in the entry, a(n) = (2n-1)/gcd(2n-1, A051403(n-2)+A051403(n-3)), proved as Theorem 1.1 of Bouras's linked paper. Combined with A051403(j) = (j+2)*A003422(j+1)/2, this reduces the question to the elementary fact that an odd composite 2m+3 with m >= 4 divides m!. The same denominator-of-factorial pattern appears in A145737 (Detlefs: a(n) = denominator(n!*3n(n+1)/(2(2n+1))) = 2n+1 if prime, else 1).
assessment.justification: The gcd formula already in the entry gives a(n) | 2n-1 at once, so the prime case is immediate. The composite case needs only that an odd composite c = 2m+3 with m >= 4 divides m!, a textbook Wilson-style lemma with a short case split on whether c = p^2. Together with checking n = 3, 4, 5 directly, the whole argument fits in under a page and uses no new idea. The longer Lean development is formalization effort and does not make the mathematics deeper.

results.title: Internal n-gons in a regular n-gon: triple points occur only for n = 3, 4, 6, and otherwise there are n k^2 + 1 regions (Shannon's A357216 conjecture)
results.summary:
Take the regular n-gon with vertices V_j = exp(2πij/n). Divide each side into k+1 equal parts. For m = 1..k, the m-th internal n-gon joins the m-th division points of consecutive sides. Its side (j, m-1) is the segment from the m-th division point of side j to the m-th division point of side j+1. The statement has two parts.
(1) For n >= 3, some k gives a point lying on three distinct drawn sides if and only if n is 3, 4 or 6.
(2) For n = 5 and for every n >= 7 and every k >= 0, the open polygon minus all n*k drawn sides has exactly n*k^2 + 1 connected components.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: %C Conjecture: the only n-gons that contain non-simple intersections are the 3-gon (triangle), 4-gon (square), and 6-gon (hexagon). %F Conjectured formula for all columns for n >= 7: T(n,k) = n*k^2 + 1. %F Conjectured formula for all rows except for n = 3, 4, 6: T(n,k) = n*k^2 + 1. (Scott R. Shannon, Sep 18 2022; the same conjecture appears in A357235 (vertices n*k^2+n) and A357254 (edges 2n*k^2+n))

Referees: I found no prior resolution. The OEIS entries A357216, A357235 and A357254 (Scott R. Shannon, Sep 2022, last revised Sep 21 2022, no %E lines) still list both claims as conjectures, in the local mirror and the current GitHub oeisdata. The related entries for the triangle (A356984, with Talmon Silver's classification for n = 3 only), the square (A357058) and the hexagon (A357196) give no general proof. arXiv API searches for "A357216" and "internal n-gons" returned nothing. Web searches covering MathOverflow, Math StackExchange, SeqFan and Google-Scholar-style queries found only the OEIS entries themselves. Sela Fried, "Proofs of some Conjectures from the OEIS" (arXiv:2410.07237) is unrelated. The key tool, Niven's theorem (cos(2*pi/n) is rational only for n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 6), is classical.

assessment.follows_from: Niven's theorem (cos(2*pi/n) is rational only for n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 6), combined with the Euler-formula count of regions already cited in the entry's %F line (T = edges - vertices + 1).
assessment.justification: The proof first notes that two chords can only cross if they cut off the same corner or adjacent corners. So any triple point involves just four consecutive vertices, and in an affine frame these depend only on u = 2cos(2*pi/n). With every chord parameter rational, the condition for three chords to meet is linear in u with a nonzero rational coefficient, so u would be rational, which Niven's theorem rules out for n = 5 and n >= 7. Explicit rational triple points for n = 3, 4, 6, and the standard count (a chord crossed at p distinct interior points adds p + 1 regions) giving n*k^2 + 1, complete the proof. The whole argument is about a page of elementary coordinate geometry plus a classical theorem. The long Lean file reflects the effort of formalizing the topology, not a hard mathematical idea.

results.title: OEIS A362086: every denominator of 1/(2-3/(3-4/(...(n-1)-n/(-3)))) except 9 is 1 or a prime
results.summary: For n >= 3 let a(n) be the reduced denominator of 1/(2 - 3/(3 - 4/(4 - ... ((n-1) - n/(-3))))), evaluated in Q from the inside out. Then for every n >= 3 with a(n) != 9, a(n) is 1 or a prime. (Mohammed Bouras's conjecture; the value 9 occurs at n = 5.)
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: Conjecture: Except for 9, every term of this sequence is either a prime or 1. (Mohammed Bouras, May 28 2023)

Referees: OEIS A362086 (local mirror, revision #35, May 09 2024): "Conjecture: Except for 9, every term of this sequence is either a prime or 1." No proof is recorded. Related prior work, none of which settles A362086:
- M. Bouras, "A New Primes-Generating Sequence", arXiv:2509.09745 (2025). Lists A362086 in its Table 1 family; the primality property is stated only as a conjecture.
- B. Cloitre, "On the sequence A356247" (2025), OEIS attachment a356247_1.pdf. Proves Conjectures 1-3 for the innermost -1 analogue, A356247.
- T. Adamczewski, "OEIS Open: How many conjectures can language models turn into theorems?", arXiv:2608.11941 (2026), together with the AlphaProof Nexus Lean files oeis_363347_conjecture_2.lean and oeis_a363102_conjecture_1.lean. Proves the analogues for innermost -2 (A363102) and -4 (A363347).
A362086 appears in neither the alphaproof-nexus-results repository nor the epoch-research LeanOpenProblems and LeanOpenProblems-results repositories. Searches of arXiv, MathOverflow and Math StackExchange found no proof or counterexample.

assessment.follows_from: The entry's own formula a(n) = (n^2+n-3)/gcd(n^2+n-3, 3*A051403(n-3) + n*A051403(n-4)), with A051403 written in left factorials (its %F), combined with the factorial-valuation and size argument already used for the sibling conjectures A363102 (Adamczewski, arXiv:2608.11941, Appendix A), A356247 (Cloitre) and A363482.
assessment.justification: The closed form for the unreduced fraction is essentially the gcd formula already listed in the entry. It reduces the denominator to N/gcd(N, 3(n-1)(n-3)!) with N = n^2+n-3, which is roughly n^2. The rest is the standard template from the solved sibling sequences: a prime p up to n-3 that survives in the denominator must divide N to a higher power than it divides (n-3)!, and this is impossible because of size, apart from a small N = 3p^2 case. Prime factors above n must be at least n+1, so at most one fits, and the cases n < 36 are a finite check. The argument is about a page and a direct adaptation of known proofs, with no new idea, so it is routine.

results.title: OEIS A363482: apart from 49, every denominator of 1/(2-3/(3-4/(...(n-1)-n/(-5)))) is 1 or a prime
results.summary: For n >= 3 let t_n = -5 and t_k = k - (k+1)/t_{k+1} for k = n-1, ..., 2. Let a(n) be the denominator, in lowest terms, of 1/t_2 = 1/(2-3/(3-4/(...(n-1)-n/(-5)))). Then for every n >= 3, either a(n) = 49, or a(n) = 1, or a(n) is prime. This is Bouras' conjecture (2023). The value 49 occurs only at n = 6.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: Conjecture: Except for 49, every term of this sequence is either a prime or 1. (Mohammed Bouras, Jun 04 2023; 'The conjecture holds through n=10000' - Bill McEachen, Jul 08 2025)

Referees: No prior resolution of A363482 found. Sources checked:
- OEIS A363482 (local mirror, identical to upstream oeisdata #29, Jul 13 2025): conjecture plus a numerical check to n = 10000 (McEachen), no proof.
- Bouras, "A New Primes-Generating Sequence", arXiv:2509.09745 (2025): lists A363482 as the k=5 case of n^2+(k-2)n-k, with observations only.
- Epoch OEIS Open benchmark (github.com/epoch-research/LeanOpenProblems-results, metadata/oeis/conjectures.json): A363482 is absent.
- google-deepmind/formal-conjectures: no A363482 file.
- google-deepmind/alphaproof-nexus-results: no A363482 file.

Related prior results on sibling sequences:
- A363102 (endpoint -2) proved: T. Adamczewski, "OEIS Open: How many conjectures can language models turn into theorems?", arXiv:2608.11941 (2026), Appendix A; also AlphaProof Nexus oeis_a363102_conjecture_1.lean.
- A356247 (endpoint -1) proved: B. Cloitre, "On the sequence A356247" (2025, OEIS-hosted PDF a356247_1.pdf; not readable here).
- A363347 (endpoint -4) conjectures 1-2 proved: AlphaProof Nexus oeis_363347_conjecture_2.lean; Adamczewski, arXiv:2608.11941.

The proof here follows the same template as the A363102 proof.

assessment.follows_from: The entry's own formula a(n) = (n^2+3n-5)/gcd(n^2+3n-5, 5*A051403(n-3)+n*A051403(n-4)), which reduces to N/gcd(N, 5(n-1)(n-3)!), combined with the p-adic/Legendre-bound template of Adamczewski's proof of the sibling conjecture A363102 (arXiv:2608.11941, Appendix A, linked from cross-reference A363102).
assessment.justification: The closed form for the reduced denominator, a(n) = N/gcd(N, 5(n-1)(n-3)!) with N = n^2+3n-5, is essentially the formula already in the entry, and it comes from a standard convergent recurrence. From there the proof is about a page of elementary number theory, and it is the same argument already published for the sibling sequence A363102 (endpoint -2) and its relatives. If a prime p <= n-3 divides a(n), Legendre's bound forces a high power of p to divide N, which is too big except in a small case (N = 3p^2) that is easy to handle. Any prime factor above n-3 is in fact at least n+2, because N + c factors for c = 0, 1, 5, 7, and since N < (n+2)^2 there is room for only one such factor. The cases n <= 35 are a finite check. The manuscript itself says it adapts the existing template, so no new idea was needed.

results.title: A363609: a(k^3) = 6k(k+2), the cube is the optimal polycube of k^3 dice
results.summary: Each standard die has opposite faces summing to 7, all dice have the same chirality, and each die may take any of its 24 rotations. Build a face-connected polycube from n dice. A face is visible when the neighbouring cell is empty; faces underneath and faces facing an internal cavity also count. a(n) is the least possible number of visible pips. Claim: for every k > 1, a(k^3) = 6(k+2)k.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: %F A363609 Conjecture: a(k^3) = 6*(k+2)*k for k > 1.  (Unattributed formula line. Entry by _Matt Donahoe_, Jun 11 2023; last edit #45, Sep 03 2023.)

Referees: I found no prior resolution.
- OEIS A363609, by Matt Donahoe, Jun 11 2023 (revision #45, Sep 03 2023): the local mirror is identical to oeis/oeisdata main on GitHub, and it still states the formula as "Conjecture: a(k^3) = 6*(k+2)*k for k > 1".
- Michael S. Branicky's formulas in the same entry, Jun 11 and Jun 15 2023: these give only upper bounds and loose bounds.
- Donahoe's program, https://github.com/mdonahoe/oeis/blob/main/A363609/dice.py, with its out.txt: a heuristic search over box-plus-slab layouts, with no optimality proof.
- OEIS A193416, minimum surface area of polycubes: the unweighted analogue, a(n^3) = 6n^2.
- AMC 10A 2002 Problem 18 (https://artofproblemsolving.com/wiki/index.php/2002_AMC_10A_Problems/Problem_18): computes the minimum for the 3x3x3 cube alone, 90. It does not show that the cube is optimal among all polycubes.
- Loomis and Whitney, Bull. AMS 55 (1949) 961-962: the classical inequality behind the projection step.
- Searches of arXiv, MathOverflow, Math StackExchange, Puzzling and SeqFan turned up no proof and no counterexample.

assessment.follows_from: Discrete Loomis-Whitney inequality (Loomis and Whitney 1949), the standard projection bound behind A193416's a(n^3)=6n^2, and AM-GM, together with a 64-case finite check per die
assessment.justification: The value 6k(k+2) splits as surface area 6k^2 plus 12k. That second term counts the pairs of perpendicular exposed faces on the cube. The proof matches this split. First it checks a finite inequality for one die: the pips shown are at least the number of exposed faces plus the number of exposed perpendicular pairs. Then it bounds the faces by projections and Loomis-Whitney, as in the known surface-area result (A193416). It bounds the perpendicular pairs by taking an extreme cell in each slice, then uses |P| <= l1*l2*l3 and AM-GM. The edge term is a neat observation, but it is a direct analogue of the standard projection argument. The whole proof fits in about a page and uses only standard tools, so a competent mathematician working on the problem would likely find it quickly.

results.title: Edges of the all-chords graph of a triangle with n general-position points per side (A367119)
results.summary: Take the equilateral triangle with corners 0, 1 and 1/2 + (√3/2)i. Let B be the three corners together with exactly n points in the relative interior of each side, and no other points. Draw the segment between every pair of distinct points of B; pairs on a common side give pieces of that side. Assume general position: no interior point of the triangle lies on three pairwise distinct drawn segments. Form the planar graph whose vertices are the points of B together with every point where two drawn segments meet in a single point. Two distinct vertices are adjacent when they lie on a common drawn segment and no vertex lies strictly between them. Then for every n ≥ 0 this graph has (3/2)(3n^4 + 4n^3 + 3n^2 + 4n + 2) edges. This was conjectured by Shannon and Sloane for OEIS A367119.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: %F Conjecture: a(n) = (3/2)*(3*n^4 + 4*n^3 + 3*n^2 + 4*n + 2). (Scott R. Shannon and N. J. A. Sloane, Nov 05 2023)

Referees: OEIS sources (read from the local mirror and checked against GitHub oeisdata main):
- A367119 (Shannon and Sloane, Nov 05 2023): the edge formula is still marked "Conjecture"; last edited Nov 09 2023.
- A367117: "Theorem: a(n) = (3/4)*(n+1)*(3*n^3+n^2+4)" for the vertex count of the same configuration. This is the key prior result, since the edge formula follows from it by degree counting: E = 2V + 3(n^2−1).
- A213827: "a(n) = (A367177 [sic, i.e. A367117](n) − 3*(n+1))/3 – Shannon & Sloane, Nov 09 2023". This is the interior-crossing count n^2(n+1)(3n+1)/4 per side-orbit.
- A367183 (Nov 13 2023): T(3,k) = A367117(k) appears apart from its "Conjectured" rows.
- A365929: Sloane's proof (Nov 07 2023) of the crossing count for the corner-free triangle variant.
- A366932 and A367015: the analogous edge and region conjectures, marked "now a theorem" by Sloane on Dec 31 2025.
- A392261, A392282, A392228 (Shannon and Sloane, Jan 2026): Shannon's attached proof (a392261.txt) of the general vertex, edge and region formulas for k general points per side of a regular n-gon without corners. The local mirror holds only a git-lfs pointer and the file could not be fetched; oeis.org was not queried, as instructed.
- A367190 and A366253: the triangle row (n=3) with corners is listed as a conjecture.

Web searches (arXiv, Math StackExchange, general) found no paper or post that explicitly proves the A367119 or A367118 conjecture. The general method is the classical Euler-formula and crossing-count argument for chord arrangements (Moser's circle problem; Poonen–Rubinstein, arXiv math/9508209).

results.title: The least number of inequivalent cells of a (6k+5)-iamond is 3(k+1)
results.summary: For every k >= 0, the least number of inequivalent cells over all polyiamonds with n = 6k+5 cells is 3(k+1). Two cells of P are equivalent when a symmetry of the triangular grid maps P onto itself and one cell to the other. This is Exley's conjecture in OEIS A369366, a(6k+5) = 3(k+1).
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: %C A369366 Conjecture: a(6k+5) = 3(k+1) for all k >= 0. Observed for k = 0, 1, 2 (n = 5, 11, 17). The next test case is a(23), predicted to be 12.  (From _Peter Exley_, Apr 07 2026)

Referees: OEIS A369366 (local mirror revision #14, Apr 14 2026, identical to oeisdata main): Exley's comment of Apr 07 2026 states the conjecture and already proves the lower bound a(6k+5) >= 3(k+1) (no rotations are possible when n = 6k+5, so |G_max| = 2). No upper-bound construction or full proof appears in the entry or its %E history. Cross-references checked: A369365, A369367, A369363, A369364, A367758, A367759, A373637, A376798, A376799. The only related proof is Mason and von Brömssen's formula proof for the polyomino analog A367758 (square lattice, a different problem). Exley's linked GitHub repo github.com/pexley-math/oeis-A369366 and the account page return 404 and could not be inspected. Web searches (arXiv, general web) found no prior resolution.

assessment.follows_from: Exley's own comment in A369366, which already sketches the lower bound a(6k+5) >= ceiling(n/2) = 3(k+1) (an odd n rules out half-turns, and n = 2 mod 3 rules out 3-fold rotations). The matching upper bound comes from the straight row of 6k+5 triangles, which has one mirror symmetry.
assessment.justification: The lower bound was already argued in the entry's own comment. The only missing part was a polyiamond that reaches the bound. The obvious candidate works: a straight row of 2m+1 triangles is symmetric under the mirror through its middle cell, so it has at most m+1 classes, which is 3(k+1) when n = 6k+5. Both halves are a few lines of elementary symmetry counting, and the paper itself calls them elementary. The Lean work is careful, but the mathematics needed no new idea.

results.title: Row lengths of the Schreier-set triangle A373345 are A007895 (number of Zeckendorf summands)
results.summary: Let A371176 be the increasing sequence of positive integers k whose binary weight (number of ones) is at most the ruler function v2(2k), i.e. at most one more than the index of the lowest set bit. Equivalently, these are the encodings sum 2^(s-1) of the finite Schreier sets S, meaning nonempty sets of positive integers with |S| <= min S. Row n of A373345 is the Schreier set encoded by A371176(n). Claim: for every n >= 1, row n has exactly as many elements as the Zeckendorf representation of n has terms. In the formal statement, (T n).length = (Nat.zeckendorf n).length.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: %Y A373345 Cf. A007895 (conjectured row lengths) ... (Paolo Xausa, Jun 01 2024). Likewise %Y A373557 Cf. ... A007895 (conjectured row lengths) (Paolo Xausa, Jun 09 2024).

Referees: OEIS A371176 (Mikhail Kurkov, 2024): the formula a(n) = b(n)*A001316(b(n))/2 with b(n) = A048679(n), and the recursion a(n) = 2^(A072649(n)-1) + [c(n)>0]*2*a(c(n)), were present by Apr 20 2024 (oeisdata commit 6ea59dd), before the A373345 conjecture of Jun 1 2024. Both were stated without proof and imply popcount(A371176(n)) = A007895(n). Kurkov's comment of Oct 21 2024 states the explicit Zeckendorf-rewriting description of A371176(n).
H. V. Chu, "The Fibonacci Sequence and Schreier-Zeckendorf Sets", J. Integer Sequences 22 (2019), Art. 19.6.5 (arXiv:1906.10962), Theorem 3: a cardinality-preserving bijection between Schreier sets and Zeckendorf sets, which also preserves colex/binary order.
GitHub issue the-omega-institute/trureturing #9050 ("Research: full Schreier-Zeckendorf row-length identity (OEIS A373345)", by AlyciaBHZ, Sep 20 2026; confirmed when the manuscript was checked) presents the identity as an elementary consequence of Chu's bijection, as paper mathematics with no Lean formalization.
Background only: A. Bird, "Jozef Schreier, Schreier sets and the Fibonacci sequence", Out Of The Norm blog, 2012, gives the binary ordering and the R/S block recursion but does not mention Zeckendorf. H. V. Chu, arXiv:2606.21865 (2026), is a survey and does not state the identity.
No prior Lean formalization found.

results.title: A373359: Schreier-set row lengths equal the Zeckendorf weight A007895
results.summary: Let A371176 be the increasing sequence of positive integers k with popcount(k) <= v_2(2k), i.e. popcount(k) <= (index of the lowest 1-bit of k) + 1. These are the binary codes of the Schreier sets X (|X| <= min X). Row n of A373359 is the set of 1-based positions of the 1-bits of A371176(n). For every n >= 1, row n has as many elements as there are terms in the Zeckendorf representation of n. Equivalently, popcount(A371176(n)) = A007895(n).
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: %Y A373359 Cf. A007895 (conjectured row lengths), A373346 (row sums), A373347. (_Paolo Xausa_, Jun 04 2024; the same 'conjectured row lengths' cross-reference appears in A373345 and A373579)

Referees: - OEIS A373359 and A373345 (Paolo Xausa, Jun 2024): "A007895 (conjectured row lengths)". Local mirror and upstream are unchanged.
- OEIS A371176 (Mikhail Kurkov, Mar 14 2024):
  - formula a(n) = 2^(A072649(n)-1) + [c(n)>0]*2*a(c(n)) with c = A066628;
  - formula a(n) = b(n)*A001316(b(n))/2 with b = A048679;
  - Kurkov comment of Oct 21 2024: A371176(n) is the Zeckendorf representation of n with the 01->1 rewrite and k-1 zeros appended. Each implies popcount(A371176(n)) = A007895(n).
- A007895 formula a(n) = A000120(A003714(n)) (Zumkeller 2005).
- GitHub issue the-omega-institute/trureturing #9050 (Sep 20 2026): https://github.com/the-omega-institute/trureturing/issues/9050. An informal proof of the A373345/A373359 row-length identity, via Chu's bijection plus order preservation and via Bird's recursive blocks.
- H. V. Chu, "The Fibonacci Sequence and Schreier-Zeckendorf Sets", J. Integer Seq. 22 (2019), Art. 19.6.5 (arXiv:1906.10962): the bijection between Schreier sets and Zeckendorf sets.

results.title: A375522: S2(n) - S1(n) = 1 fails at n = 42 (the difference is 5)
results.summary: Let p_k be the k-th prime. Define s(0) = 0 and s(k) = s(k-1) + 1/(p_k b(k)), where b(k) = 1 + floor(1/((1 - s(k-1)) p_k)) (this is A375781). Write s(n) = S1(n)/S2(n) in lowest terms (S2 = A375522, S1 = A375521). Sigrist and Sloane conjectured that S2(n) - S1(n) = 1 for every n >= 1 except n = 4 and n = 6. This is false: S2(42) - S1(42) = 5. Lean: theorem result : ¬ statement.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: The differences S2(n) - S1(n) are surprisingly small: for n = 1,2,...,34 the values S2(n) - S1(n) are: 1, 1, 1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 1, ..., 1 suggesting the conjecture that they are always 1 except for n = 4 and 6 (compare the Theorem in A374983). (Rémy Sigrist and N. J. A. Sloane, Aug 30 2024)

Referees: The conjecture is in OEIS A375522 (R. Sigrist and N. J. A. Sloane, Aug 30 2024; comment added Aug 31 2024; current revision #25, Apr 22 2025). It is restated as still open ("it seems") in A375528 (Sloane, Sep/Oct 2024). Related: A375521, A375781, A374983/A375516 (harmonic analogue, proved by Sigrist), and Sloane, "A Nasty Surprise in a Sequence and Other OEIS Stories", Rutgers Experimental Math Seminar, Oct 10 2024 (slides list these sequences and a general Conjecture 4, with no counterexample). Sigrist and Sloane, "Dampening Down a Divergent Series", is still cited on OEIS as a manuscript in preparation. No prior counterexample or proof turned up in the OEIS histories, arXiv (e.g. Fried arXiv:2607.24832 does not cover it), web searches, or google-deepmind/formal-conjectures. The SeqFan archive could not be reached.

assessment.follows_from: The entry's own recursion (its Maple/Mathematica programs), run as a finite computation modulo a smooth modulus such as (190!)^2. If 1 - s(n-1) = 1/D, then 1 - s(n) = m/(D(D+m)) with m = p_n - (D mod p_n).
assessment.justification: The conjecture is refuted by one computed value: S2(42) - S1(42) = 5. Note that S2(42) has about 4*10^11 digits, so it cannot be computed directly. The only idea needed is a standard one. The difference S2(n) - S1(n) is the small numerator of the remainder 1 - s(n), and it depends only on the huge denominator modulo small numbers, so you track that denominator modulo a large smooth modulus and account for the precision lost when you cancel the gcd at each step. That bookkeeping lemma takes about a page and is elementary. Once it is set up, the result is a finite computation, so the work is routine, although the counterexample is real and was out of reach of the authors' direct computation up to n = 34.

results.title: A386538: moving the circle's center off the grid enlarges the max lattice polygon (counterexample at n = 7)
results.summary: Conjecture (OEIS A386538, Felix Huber): for every n ≥ 0, the largest area of a polygon with vertices on Z^2 inside the closed disk of radius n is the same whether the disk's center is a grid point or any point of the plane. In the frozen encoding: for all n : ℕ, ⨆_{c ∈ ℝ²} vol(conv(Z² ∩ B(c, n))) = vol(conv(Z² ∩ B(0, n))). We prove the negation. At n = 7 with center c0 = (5/12, 5/24), the convex hull of the lattice points in B(c0, 7) has area at least 277/2 = 138.5. The convex hull for the center 0 has area at most 3457/25 = 138.28; its true value is 138 = a(7).
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: "Conjecture: The maximum possible area of a polygon within the circle would be the same if only the vertices but not the center were fixed on grid points." (entry by _Felix Huber_, Aug 05 2025). The same conjecture appears for ellipses in A386539, which has T(n,n) = A386538(n).

Referees: Sources checked:
- Local OEIS mirror and raw.githubusercontent.com/oeis/oeisdata, A386538: #23, Aug 19 2025, no %E lines. A386539: #19, Aug 19 2025.
- Entries that cite A386538/A386539: A398490, A396223, A391113. None addresses the conjecture.
- Cross-references read: A066643, A123690, A125228, A288247, A322106, A322107, A357577, A108126. None resolves it. A123690 and A295344 concern lattice-point counts with an off-grid center, not polygon areas.
- Web searches for the A386538 number, the entry's wording, Felix Huber plus counterexample, SeqFan, and MathOverflow/Math.SE on convex hulls of lattice points in a shifted disk.

Related but not resolving:
- J. Zhao, "The Largest Circle Enclosing n Lattice Points", https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.06234, and its sequel https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.16081
- Bárány–Larman and Balog–Deshouillers on the integer convex hull of a disk (vertex counts, origin-centered only), e.g. https://www.renyi.hu/~barany/cikkek/73.pdf

No prior proof or counterexample found.

assessment.follows_from: Direct finite search: exact convex-hull area computation of the lattice points in disks of radius n around rational centres, compared with a(7)=138 from the entry's own data.
assessment.justification: The conjecture is refuted by one explicit counterexample. With radius 7 and centre (5/12, 5/24), the lattice points in the disk have a convex hull of area 281/2, which beats a(7) = 138. Finding it took only a search over rational centres with exact hull areas, and checking it means comparing the areas of two explicit lattice polygons, a 12-gon and a 15-gon. No new idea was needed, and the extra work in Lean (trapezoid decompositions and measure-theory bookkeeping) does not change that. This is the conjecture as the author meant it, not a degenerate case, so it is genuinely settled, but the mathematics is routine.

results.title: A386655 modulo 6 is eventually periodic with pattern [1, 0, 3, 0, 3, 2]
results.summary: Let a(n) = sum_{k=0..n} C(n,k) 2^(k(k+1)) (2^k - (n-k))^(n-k-1), where the k = n term is read as 2^(n^2) and 0^0 = 1. Then for every n >= 6, a(n) mod 6 equals the entry with index (n-6) mod 6 of [1, 0, 3, 0, 3, 2]. Equivalently, a(n) mod 6 = 1, 0, 3, 0, 3, 2 for n ≡ 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 (mod 6). (Paul D. Hanna's conjecture, OEIS A386655.)
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: A386655 (E.g.f.: Sum_{n>=0} (2^n*x + LambertW(x))^n / n!): "Conjecture: for n >= 6, a(n) (mod 6) equals [1, 0, 3, 0, 3, 2] repeating." (_Paul D. Hanna_, Aug 23 2025). Analogues: A386656 (q=3) [4,3,2,1,0,1], A386657 (q=4) [1,2,3,2,3,4], A386658 (q=5) [4,3,0,3,0,5].

Referees: I found no earlier resolution.
- OEIS A386655 (local mirror and current GitHub oeisdata, revision #14, Aug 24 2025) still states the mod-6 claim as a conjecture by Paul D. Hanna, with no %E edit or proof note.
- The cross-referenced sister entries A386656, A386657 and A386658 (q = 3, 4, 5) state analogous mod-6 conjectures, none marked proved. The related entry A386648 also has an open mod-6 conjecture.
- Web searches turned up only OEIS pages (e.g. https://oeis.org/A386648, https://oeis.org/A136524) and no paper, arXiv preprint, MathOverflow/Math StackExchange post or SeqFan message proving or refuting the A386655 conjecture.
- The classical tool used is the expansion e^(cW(x)) = Sum_k c(c-k)^(k-1) x^k/k! (the tree-function/Lambert W identity), together with Fermat's little theorem and the binomial-transform identity Sum_m C(n,m)C(m,j)x^m = C(n,j)x^j(1+x)^(n-j).

assessment.follows_from: The entry's explicit formula a(n) = Sum_{k=0..n} C(n,k) 2^(k(k+1)) (2^k-(n-k))^(n-k-1), combined with Fermat's little theorem mod 2 and mod 3 and the standard identity Sum_m C(n,m) C(m,j) x^m = C(n,j) x^j (1+x)^(n-j).
assessment.justification: The proof starts from the explicit sum formula already given in the entry and works modulo 2 and modulo 3 separately. Modulo 2 only the k=0 term survives, which is immediate. Modulo 3, writing 2 = -1 and using Fermat's little theorem makes each summand a 6-periodic function of n-k. Such a function can be written with C(m,j), j <= 2, and (-1)^m, and a standard binomial-transform identity then gives a(n) = 1-n^2 or n^2-n mod 3; CRT finishes. This is an elementary argument of about a page, the kind of residue computation a competent mathematician would carry out quickly, so it is routine. The scout had already outlined it before the proof attempt.

results.title: Column sums of strictly superdiagonal reversed partitions by maximum are A000245
results.summary: Let T(n,k) be the number of reversed integer partitions y = (y_1 <= ... <= y_m) of n (positive parts, weakly increasing, sum n) that are strictly superdiagonal (y_i > i for all i) and have maximum part k. Then for every k >= 1, sum_n T(n,k) = A000245(k-1), where A000245(0) = 0 and A000245(K) = 3(2K)!/((K+2)!(K-1)!) for K >= 1.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: Conjecture: Column sums are A000245. - _Gus Wiseman_, Sep 24 2025

Referees: OEIS A388724 (rev #12, Oct 06 2025; the conjecture is still listed and no %E resolution is recorded). M. Archibald, A. Blecher, S. Elizalde, A. Knopfmacher, "Subdiagonal and superdiagonal partitions", Afrika Matematika 36:77 (2025), doi:10.1007/s13370-025-01282-0. Theorem 2.3 and its proof give a bijection from superdiagonal weakly increasing partitions with largest part m to pairs (P in D_m, 0 ≤ h < final E-run length of P), plus the generating function for fixed largest part. Theorem 2.2's proof gives a bijection from partitions with k parts and largest part s to the ballot paths B_{k-1,s}. Combined with the shift y_i -> y_i - 1 and the classical identity sum over D_m of final descent length = A000245(m) (E. Deutsch, "Dyck path enumeration", Discrete Math. 204 (1999); the A000245 comment by Homberger on total returns), or with Catalan-triangle row sums (A009766, which has A000245 as a diagonal), this yields the conjecture immediately. No explicit prior statement or proof of the column-sum identity was found on OEIS, arXiv, MathOverflow, Math StackExchange or the web.

results.title: No primitive Heronian triangle has integer circumradius
results.summary: Let x, y, z be positive integers satisfying the strict triangle inequalities, with gcd(x, y, z) = 1, and let K be a natural number with 16K^2 = (x+y+z)(-x+y+z)(x-y+z)(x+y-z), i.e. K is the area. Then there is no natural number R with 4KR = xyz. In other words, no primitive Heronian triangle has integer circumradius. This is Felix Huber's conjecture in OEIS A392943.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: "Conjecture: There is no primitive Heronian triangle with integer circumradius." (entry by _Felix Huber_, Feb 04 2026)

Referees: Ronald van Luijk, "The diameter of the circumcircle of a Heron triangle", Elemente der Mathematik 63 (2008), 118–121. The relevant parts are:
- Theorem 2, (4)⇒(5): if gcd(a,b,c,d) = 1, every prime divisor of the circumdiameter d is ≡ 1 mod 4.
- Corollary 5: for a prime p ≢ 1 mod 4, p^{v_p(d)} divides gcd(a,b,c).
- Proof of Theorem 1: it states explicitly that a Heron triangle with integer circumradius has all sides even.

Earlier related work:
- A.-V. Kramer & F. Luca, "Some remarks on Heron triangles", Acta Acad. Paedagog. Agriensis Sect. Mat. (N.S.) 27 (2000) 25–38. Shows no power of 2 is the circumradius of a Heron triangle.
- M. Aassila, "Some results on Heron triangles", Elem. Math. 56 (2001) 143–146.

Also related, with full text not checked: E. Read, "Integer triangles with integer circumradii", Math. Gazette 107 (2023) 241–248.

OEIS A392943 (Huber, Feb 2026) cites none of these, and no proof has been added to the entry.

results.title: The 1089-trick map has two 9-digit fixed points (A393794 uniqueness conjecture is false)
results.summary: Let rev(m) be the decimal reversal of m (leading zeros dropped), and let T(x) = D + rev(D) with D = |x - rev(x)|. Havenaar's conjecture in A393794 says that for every n >= 1, a(n) = 110*(10^(n+1) - 1) is the only fixed point of T with exactly n+4 decimal digits. This is false. For n = 5, x = 108910890 has 9 digits and satisfies T(x) = x, but x is not a(5) = 109999890.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: "a(n) is the unique fixed point of the 1089-trick map T among all (n+4)-digit numbers (verified exhaustively for n = 1..4; conjectured for all n >= 1)." (comment in A393794, entry by _Remco Havenaar_, Feb 27 2026; the entry names the sequence 'Fixed points of the 1089-trick map' and gives a(n) = 110*(10^(n+1)-1))

Referees: OEIS A393794 (Havenaar, Feb 27 2026; #19, Mar 10 2026, no correction as of GitHub oeisdata mirror). OEIS A001232 (numbers k with 9k = rev k; includes non-primitive 10891089; structure theorem by D. W. Wilson 1997 and M. F. Hasler 2022), from which 10*A001232 ⊂ Fix(T) follows trivially. R. Havenaar, SYNTRIAD/digit-dynamics GitHub repo (initial commit 2026-03-09): papers/paper_A.tex still states the uniqueness conjecture, while data/results_export.json experiment id 10 (truc_1089, 7-digit domain, 2026-02-25) lists 108910890 among T's fixed points without remark. Neither source states the contradiction. Y. Almirantis and W. Li, arXiv:2408.02527 and arXiv:2410.11784 (Fibonacci Quart. 64 (2026) 281-310) study the related two-option reversal map Phi, with Phi(Phi(x)) = T(x) in the relevant range; arXiv:2410.11784, which predates the conjecture, lists 108910890 twice: in Table 2 as part of the 2-cycle {10891089, 108910890} of Phi, and in Appendix A.2 among the outputs of the two-step 1089 trick on eight-digit numbers; it does not consider the fixed points of T. OEIS A124074 (S. Dumortier, 2006) studies a variant of Phi whose example already shows the 2-cycle 1089 -> 10890 -> 1089. No published refutation found: this is the first explicit refutation, and it is mathematically elementary.

assessment.intended_status: The counterexample answers the conjecture as its author meant it. 108910890 is an ordinary 9-digit positive fixed point of T, which is exactly the uniqueness the conjecture claims. Nothing in the entry sets numbers of this kind apart.
assessment.follows_from: The entry's own proof that T(a(n)) = a(n) works for any k with 9k = rev(k): rev(10k) = 9k, so D = k and T(10k) = 10k. Cross-reference A001232 lists such k, including the non-primitive term 10891089 (its 5th term; Hasler's comment there describes the concatenated terms 1089 0...0 1089). This gives 10*10891089 = 108910890, a second 9-digit fixed point. A direct exhaustive search of 9-digit numbers also finds it.
assessment.justification: The refutation is one explicit 9-digit number whose fixed-point property is checked by a few lines of arithmetic. Where it comes from is immediate from the entry itself: the entry's proof uses only 9k = rev(k), and it points to A001232, whose listed data includes the non-primitive term 10891089. Extending this to every n >= 5 (using 1089 0...0 1089) is equally elementary. The number had also already appeared in the conjecturer's own computational output and in Almirantis-Li. No new idea was needed, so this is routine.

results.title: Bar tilings of the smallest-perimeter rectangle: a(n+1) = 4 a(n) for odd n >= 3 (A394981)
results.summary: Let a(n) be the number of tilings, counted up to the symmetries of the rectangle, of the rows(n) x cols(n) rectangle by the n bars 1x1, 1x2, ..., 1xn, each used exactly once. Here rows(n) = floor((n+1)/2) and cols(n) = (n(n+1)/2)/rows(n). For n = 2m+1 the rectangle is (m+1) x (2m+1), and for n = 2m+2 it is (m+1) x (2m+3). In Lean, a(n) is the frozen bitmask-search definition: it sums the stabilizer sizes of all tilings found by the search and divides by the order of the symmetry group (Burnside). Claim (A394981 conjecture, read for odd n >= 3): for every odd n >= 3, a(n+1) = 4 a(n). The literal case n = 1 fails, a(2) = 1 != 4 = 4 a(1), and the statement excludes it.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: %F A394981 Conjecture: If n is odd, then a(n+1) = 4*a(n).  (Unattributed formula line. Entry by _Gary Yane_, Apr 08 2026; a(1)-a(2) corrected by _Pontus von Brömssen_, May 13 2026.)

Referees: The OEIS A394981 entry (Gary Yane, Apr 08 2026; a(1)-a(2) corrected by Pontus von Brömssen, May 13 2026; revision #42, May 16 2026, the same in the local mirror and upstream oeisdata) still states the identity as a conjecture, with keyword "more" and no proof reference. No other OEIS entry cites it. Cross-references A254414/A254458/A254607/A329279 are unrelated counts. Searches found no proof or counterexample on arXiv, MathOverflow, Math StackExchange, SeqFan or the general web. Nearest work, all on a different problem: arXiv:2606.05439, Blanco, Dougherty-Bliss, Ter-Saakov and Zeilberger, "In How Many Ways can a Rectangle be Rectangled?" (tilings by bars of any length); arXiv:2607.29369, Martinez (L-tetromino tilings).

assessment.justification: The proof is short and elementary, about a page of informal argument. Because all bar lengths differ, no tiling has a nontrivial symmetry, so a(n) is a quarter of the raw tiling count. Every bar longer than half the width must lie horizontally, and these bars take one row each, so they all cover the middle column. A case split on where bar m+1 sits divides the larger rectangle's tilings into four classes. Deleting one or two middle or edge columns gives a bijection from each class to the tilings of the smaller rectangle. This pigeonhole and column-deletion argument would come quickly to a competent combinatorialist. The 2400-line Lean file reflects the work of formalizing it, not the difficulty of the mathematics. The proof needs the hypothesis n >= 3 because the identity fails at n = 1. That case is a degenerate exception, and the intended conjecture is fully settled.

results.title: Alexandersson's recurrence for the row polynomials of A395454 holds (rows counted from 1)
results.summary:
Let E2(j,i) be the second-order Eulerian numbers (A201637): E2(0,0)=1, E2(0,i)=0 for i>=1, and E2(j+1,i) = (2j+1-i)E2(j,i-1) + (i+1)E2(j,i). Let T(n,k) = sum_{j=0}^n (-1)^{n-j} C(n,j) E2(j,n-k), the triangle A395454, and let P_m(t) = sum_{k=0}^m T(m,k) t^k be its row polynomials in the entry's numbering (P_0 = 1, P_1 = 0, P_2 = 2t, ...). Then for every m >= 2, in Z[t],
P_m = (m-1)(1+t) P_{m-1} + (t - t^2) P'_{m-1} + 2(m-1) t P_{m-2}.
Equivalently, with the rows counted from 1 (P1(n) = P_{n-1}), for every n >= 3: P1(n) = (n - 2t + nt - 2) P1(n-1) + (t - t^2) P1'(n-1) + t(2n-4) P1(n-2). This is Alexandersson's conjecture in the form fixed by the frozen statement.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: %F A395454 Conjecture: Let P(n) be the generating polynomial (in t) of row n. Then P(n) = (n - 2*t + n*t - 2)*P(n-1) + (t - t^2)*P'(n-1) + t*(2*n-4)*P(n-2). - Per W. Alexandersson, Jun 27 2026

Referees: No earlier resolution found. Closest related work:
- S.-M. Ma and Y.-N. Yeh, "Eulerian polynomials, Stirling permutations of the second kind and perfect matchings," Electron. J. Combin. 24(4) (2017) #P4.27, arXiv:1607.01311. Its Thm 17 is an analogous recurrence for Stirling-derangement polynomials by cycle ascent plateaus (a different family). Its Cor 18 is the A053871 row-sum recurrence. Its Prop 9 implies that A395454 row n is the distribution of n - casc over Stirling derangements.
- G.-H. Duh, Y.-C. R. Lin, S.-M. Ma and Y.-N. Yeh, arXiv:1612.07391 (2016).
- S.-M. Ma, S. Kitaev, J. Yeh and Y.-N. Yeh, arXiv:2601.20665 (2026).
- S. Fried, "Further proofs of conjectures from the OEIS," arXiv:2607.24832 (2026). Does not cover A395454.

OEIS A395454 (#30, Oct 14 2026; Luschny's entry, Alexandersson's conjecture of Jun 27 2026) still lists the formula as a conjecture, with no proof recorded in any comment, %E line or link. Read with the entry's offset-0 numbering the formula is false; read with rows counted from 1 it holds.

assessment.follows_from: The standard differential recurrence for second-order Eulerian polynomials, E_{j+1}(x) = (1+2jx)E_j(x) + x(1-x)E_j'(x). This is a direct reformulation of the triangle recurrence in A201637 and Graham-Knuth-Patashnik Section 6.2. It is pushed through the alternating binomial transform that defines A395454 using Pascal's rule.
assessment.justification: The proof takes the standard recurrence for the reversed second-order Eulerian polynomials, applies it inside the alternating binomial transform (Pascal's rule and k*C(n,k) = n*C(n-1,k-1)), and then compares coefficients term by term. Altogether this is about a page of index bookkeeping, and the paper itself calls the argument routine. The result proves the reading the author evidently meant, with rows counted from 1 (an off-by-one in the indexing). That reading reduces at t=1 to the A053871 recurrence. The literal offset-0 reading fails trivially at n=2. No new idea or construction was needed.

results.title: A397315: a 14-point blackout of the 5 x 8 grid refutes T(n,m) = n + m
results.summary: Pemmasani's conjecture in OEIS A397315 says this. Let T(n,k) be the largest number of points that can be blacked out of the grid {0..k-1} x {0..n-1} so that every lattice rectangle (tilted rectangles included) is still determined by its set of visible vertices. Then T(n,m) = n + m whenever min(n,m) >= 4, except T(4,4) = 7 and T(4,5) = T(5,4) = 8. We prove the negation. The 5 x 8 grid (n = 5, k = 8) has a valid blackout of 14 points, so T(5,8) >= 14, which is more than the predicted 5 + 8 = 13.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: "Conjecture: T(n,m) = n+m whenever min(n,m) >= 4, except T(4,4) = 7 and T(4,5) = 8 (verified on seven cells through 6 X 6)." (entry by _Arjun Pemmasani_, Sep 02 2026; comment in the entry, which was last revised Sep 12 2026)

Referees: The refutation is in Arjun Pemmasani's GitHub repository "Kagey-Problems" (https://github.com/apemm/Kagey-Problems), which the OEIS entry A397315 links in its %H line. These are the files that record it:
- kagey-problems/problem001/data/ledger.md, "Outcomes, part 2 (2026-10-17)", commit 45b175b, 2026-10-17: blackout(5,8) = 14 and blackout(6,8) = 15. The 5 x 8 maximum blackouts form one orbit of 4.
- The JIS paper draft kagey-problems/problem001/jis/pemmasani.tex, file sections/sec07_five.tex. Its Theorem "the guess fails" states f(5,8) = 14 and f(6,8) = 15. Theorem "five rows" states f(5,m) = m+6 for every m >= 8.
- The Lean proof kagey-problems/lean/KageyProblems/Problem001/Kernel.lean, theorem kfvalue_5_8 (f(5,8) = 14, kernel-checked), commit 8df4162, 2026-10-18. CollarBoards.lean has fval_five: f(5,m) = m+6 for m >= 8.
- kagey-problems/problem001/README.md says: "The guess f = h+m for both sides at least 4 fails at 5 x 8 and 6 x 8."

The source problem is Peter Kagey's Open Problem Collection, Problem 001 (https://peterkagey.com/problems/001/); his page lists no values. The companion entry A399580 has nothing on 5 x 8. Neither OEIS entry, in the local mirror or on GitHub (#38 and #24), has been updated with the refutation yet.

results.title: No odd n with a(n) > 1 has b^n ≡ b^{a(n)} (mod n) for all b (OEIS A051903)
results.summary: Let a(n) be the largest exponent in the prime factorization of n (OEIS A051903; a(1) = 0). Thomas Ordowski (Dec 2019) asked: are there odd numbers n with a(n) > 1 and b^n ≡ b^{a(n)} (mod n) for every natural number b? The upstream formal statement says such an n exists. We prove its negation: there is no odd n with a(n) > 1 such that b^n ≡ b^{a(n)} (mod n) for all b ∈ ℕ.

results.title: An odd n with a(n) > 1 and 2^n ≡ 2^{a(n)} (mod n), where a(n) is the largest prime exponent of n (OEIS A051903, Ordowski)
results.summary: Let a(n) be the largest exponent in the prime factorization of n (OEIS A051903). Ordowski (Dec 2019) asked whether some odd n has a(n) > 1 and 2^n ≡ 2^{a(n)} (mod n). The answer is yes. The formal statement is ∃ n : ℕ, Odd n ∧ 1 < a n ∧ 2 ^ n ≡ 2 ^ (a n) [MOD n], with a n defined as the foldr max of the multiplicities over n.primeFactorsList. The witness is n = 9687963167864344937 = 7 · 631 · 881 · 3511² · 201961.
